questionBank.prompt: Priya believes people who drink coffee in the morning are friendlier. At a conference she notices every friendly coffee drinker she meets and barely registers the unfriendly ones. Which habit is Priya showing?
options: Replication — repeating someone else's study
Confirmation bias — favoring information that supports what she already believes
Falsifiability — designing a study that could prove her wrong
Empiricism — collecting systematic observations
questionBank.explanation: Priya is seeking out evidence that confirms her belief and ignoring evidence that would contradict it, which is confirmation bias as defined by the APA and summarized by Simply Psychology. Replication repeats studies, falsifiability invites disproof, and empiricism demands systematic observation — none of which describes selective noticing.
questionBank.skill: Applying the concept of confirmation bias to an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: Dr. Okafor predicts: 'If students review their notes within 24 hours of a lecture, they will remember more on a one-week test than students who do not review.' Why is this a good hypothesis?
options: It matches what most people already believe
It is too general to be tested in a single study
It is testable and could be shown wrong by evidence
It was published in a peer-reviewed journal
questionBank.explanation: The prediction names its variables, states a direction, and could be contradicted by data — the testable, falsifiable qualities OpenStax and Simply Psychology identify in a good hypothesis. Popularity, vagueness, or publication status are not what make a prediction scientific.
questionBank.skill: Applying the criteria of testability and falsifiability to an original hypothesis

questionBank.prompt: A research team finds that sleep-deprived participants respond more slowly on a reaction-time task. A second lab repeats the study with the same methods and gets the same pattern of results. What has happened?
options: The first study's conclusion has been disproven
The hypothesis has been promoted to a theory
The result is now a fact that cannot be questioned
The finding has been replicated — the results held when the study was repeated
questionBank.explanation: Repeating a study with the same methods to check whether the results are consistent is replication, as the Noba Project defines it; matching results make the finding more trustworthy. It does not disprove the first study, promote anything to a theory, or make the result immune to future testing.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing replication when a study is repeated with the same methods

questionBank.prompt: In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration repeated about a hundred psychology studies drawn from prestigious journals and found that only about a third produced the same results. Why is this outcome part of how science works rather than proof that psychology is untrustworthy?
options: Failed replications are never published, so the failures are invisible
A single study is never the last word — science advances by testing ideas repeatedly and correcting itself
The original researchers deliberately faked most of their data
Replication only matters in laboratory sciences, not psychology
questionBank.explanation: The Noba Project reports the roughly one-third replication rate from the 2015 Open Science Collaboration effort and treats non-replication as a problem the field confronts through re-testing and self-correction. The other options contradict the record: failed replications are discussed openly, fraud does not explain the pattern, and replication matters across psychology.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why failed replications are part of science's self-correcting process

title: Research Methods
in30Seconds: Psychologists do not rely on hunches. They gather evidence with research methods — systematic approaches such as surveys, case studies, naturalistic observation, correlational studies, and experiments. Each method has strengths and blind spots, and the research question shapes which one fits. Findings come from samples, subsets of the people researchers ultimately want to describe. No single method gives a perfect picture, so good research combines methods, treating each as one lens on behavior rather than a mirror of the whole truth.
whyItMatters: Every psychology claim you meet — in news, health advice, product marketing, or policy debates — rests on a method someone chose, and knowing how psychologists gather evidence tells you how much a finding can support. Academically, research methods are the backbone of the discipline: later courses on experiments, correlation, and statistics refine the toolbox this lesson introduces. Practically, these are everyday critical-thinking tools. When you hear that a survey of two hundred people proves something about everyone, you can ask who was sampled and what the method can and cannot show. Looking ahead, the habit of asking which method fits which question, and what each method misses, transfers to any field that makes claims about people — which is most of them.
learningObjectives: Define research methods as the systematic, evidence-based approaches psychologists use to study behavior, and explain what makes them empirical.
Identify surveys, case studies, naturalistic observation, correlational studies, and experiments, and state one strength and one limitation of each.
Apply the principle that the research question shapes the choice of method to a new scenario.
Explain what a sample is and why a sample should represent the larger population a researcher wants to describe.
Analyze why no single method gives a complete picture and why combining methods strengthens psychological evidence.

collegeVersion.heading: What research methods are
collegeVersion.body: Research methods are the systematic approaches psychologists use to gather evidence about behavior and the mind. OpenStax's Psychology 2e textbook puts the working definition plainly: psychologists have many research methods available in their efforts to understand, describe, and explain behavior and the cognitive and biological processes that underlie it. The key word is evidence. The same textbook explains that scientific knowledge is empirical — grounded in objective, tangible evidence that can be observed and checked — which is what separates research from intuition, rumor, or personal experience. Every method in the toolbox is a disciplined way of collecting that evidence, and each one makes different tradeoffs.

collegeVersion.heading: The toolbox: five methods
collegeVersion.body: Surveys are fixed lists of questions given to many people, and they can be delivered on paper, online, or verbally. A campus recreation office might email every enrolled student twelve questions about how often they exercise and which facilities they use. The honest limitation is self-report: people may not answer accurately, so a student who skips the gym may still check the box for four workouts a week. Case studies focus intensely on one person or a few individuals. A memory researcher might spend two years with a single woman who recalls her childhood days in unusual detail, mapping how her memory is organized. The honest limitation is reach: someone that unusual may not represent anyone else. Naturalistic observation means watching behavior where it naturally happens, staying unobtrusive because people act differently when they know they are being watched. A team might stand at the end of a grocery aisle and record how shoppers pause, compare, and move on. The honest limitation is control: researchers cannot make the behavior happen on schedule, and observers can unconsciously see what they expect. Correlational studies measure variables as they naturally occur and ask whether they move together. Researchers might track students' nightly sleep and exam scores across a semester and find that more sleep goes with higher scores. The honest limitation is that a relationship is not proof that one thing caused the other — that question belongs to experiments. Experiments actively change one variable and measure the effect under controlled conditions, which is the strongest tool for causal questions, though the controlled setting can be artificial. Experiments get their own full lesson; here they are one tool among five.

collegeVersion.heading: Choosing a method: the question shapes the method
collegeVersion.body: There is no single best method, only the method that fits the question. The Noba Project's research-methods chapter states the principle directly: which method you choose depends on the type of questions you are asking, as well as what resources are available. An original example makes it concrete. A researcher who wants to know how often first-year students visit the counseling center and how they feel about it chooses a survey, because it reaches many students cheaply and lets them answer privately. A researcher who wants to see what students actually do during orientation week chooses naturalistic observation, because she needs real behavior, not reported behavior. A researcher who wants to test whether a specific study-skills workshop raises grades needs an experiment. Time and money matter too: a quick survey can map a question before anyone invests in a costly long-term study.

collegeVersion.heading: Samples: who is studied
collegeVersion.body: Psychologists almost never study everyone they care about. They study a sample — a subset of individuals selected from a population, which is the overall group the researcher is interested in — and then seek to generalize the findings to that population. Representativeness is the catch: a sample should resemble the population it came from. If a survey about dining-hall hours is mostly answered by students who eat late dinners, the late-evening diners are overrepresented, and the results will not describe the whole campus. The same logic explains why a case study of one extraordinary person cannot stand for everyone: the sample is real and detailed, but it does not represent the group. Big samples help, but a big, lopsided sample still misleads.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note: lenses, not mirrors
collegeVersion.body: Every method has blind spots, and pretending otherwise is how bad studies happen. Surveys buy breadth at the cost of honest self-reports; case studies buy depth at the cost of narrowness; naturalistic observation buys realism at the cost of control; correlational studies buy real-world patterns at the cost of causal proof; experiments buy control at the cost of artificial settings. The Noba chapter draws the honest conclusion: all methods have limitations, which is why the best research uses a variety of methods. Think of methods as lenses, not mirrors. A lens magnifies some features and distorts others; no single lens shows the whole object. Psychology builds trustworthy knowledge by pointing several lenses at the same question and checking whether they agree. That is also why one study is never the final word — and why asking which method produced a claim is a good reflex for anyone reading psychology.

vocabulary.definition: The systematic, evidence-based approaches psychologists use to study behavior, including surveys, case studies, naturalistic observation, correlational studies, and experiments.
Grounded in observable, tangible evidence that can be checked, rather than in intuition or personal opinion.
A fixed set of questions administered to a group of people, often used to gather information from large numbers of participants quickly.
An intensive, in-depth examination of one person or a small number of individuals, often chosen because they have a rare or revealing characteristic.
Watching and recording behavior as it occurs in its natural setting, while the observer stays unobtrusive.
A study that measures variables as they naturally occur and examines whether the variables are related to one another.
A subset of individuals selected from a larger population to be studied; researchers generalize from the sample to the population.
The overall group of individuals a researcher is interested in describing; the sample is drawn from this group.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Psychologists want to know how people actually think and behave, but you cannot just trust what people say or what seems obvious. So they use research methods: organized ways of collecting evidence, and each method answers a certain kind of question. Want to hear from thousands of people quickly? Survey them. Want to understand one remarkable person deeply? Do a case study. Want to see real behavior? Watch people where it actually happens. Want to know whether two things move together? Use a correlational study. Want to test what causes what? Run an experiment. No method is perfect: surveys depend on honest answers, case studies focus on unusual people, watching gives little control, and correlations do not prove causes. That is why researchers mix methods and why one study is never the whole story.
eli10.analogy: Think of research methods as different tools for fixing up a house. A hammer, a saw, and a level are all useful, but you would not saw a nail or level a board with a hammer. The job decides the tool. And no single tool builds a house alone — a good builder switches tools and checks the work from several angles. Psychologists do the same: the question picks the method, and solid conclusions come from combining them.
eli10.analogyLimits: The toolbox analogy makes methods sound interchangeable, but research choices are heavier than tool choices. A hammer does not change the wood it hits, while a method shapes what a researcher can see and what they miss. Tools are also neutral, whereas methods carry ethical rules about treating participants well, and a poorly run study can mislead people even when the method itself is a sensible one.

workedExample: Dr. Reyes wants to know whether students who use the campus tutoring center feel more confident in their courses. She starts with a survey: all 1,200 first-year students are emailed eight questions about tutoring use and confidence, and 300 reply. The 300 are her sample; the 1,200 are the population she wants to describe. Checking the replies, she notices they skew toward students who visited the center at least once — a sample that does not represent the whole class. So she adds a second method: during exam week she sits in the tutoring center's open study area and quietly records how students arrive, work, and leave, without interrupting. The survey gives her breadth, and the observation gives her real behavior. She does not claim the center causes confidence — that would take an experiment — but she now has two lenses on the same question, and each lens's blind spot is covered by the other.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating one study as the final answer.
commonMistakes.correction: Every method has blind spots, so a single study is rarely conclusive. Findings earn trust when different methods point the same way.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming whoever answered a survey represents everyone.
commonMistakes.correction: Respondents are a sample, and claims about a population are only as strong as the sample's representativeness. A lopsided sample, even a large one, misleads.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a correlation as proof of cause.
commonMistakes.correction: Correlational studies show that variables are related; they cannot show that one caused the other. Causal claims require experiments, which have their own lesson.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting one method to answer every kind of question.
commonMistakes.correction: The question shapes the method: surveys for breadth, case studies for depth, observation for real behavior, experiments for cause. Matching method to question is the skill.

compareContrast.distinction: A survey trades depth for breadth, gathering thin data from many people; a case study trades breadth for depth, gathering rich data from one person or a few.
Observation keeps behavior natural but gives up control over when and how it occurs; experiments gain control by changing a variable deliberately, sometimes at the cost of an artificial setting.
The population is everyone a researcher wants to describe; the sample is the subset actually studied, and findings generalize only as far as the sample represents the population.

keyTakeaway: Research methods are the evidence-gathering tools of psychology: the question chooses the method, every method has a blind spot, and trustworthy conclusions come from representative samples and from methods that check one another.

questionBank.prompt: What makes scientific research different from intuition or personal experience as a way of understanding behavior?
options: It is faster and cheaper to carry out.
It relies on evidence that can be observed and checked.
It never produces contradictory findings.
It requires a laboratory setting.
questionBank.explanation: Scientific knowledge is empirical: it is grounded in observable evidence that can be checked, which is exactly what separates research from intuition and personal experience. Speed and cost are not what define research, contradictory findings do occur, and much research happens outside laboratories.

questionBank.prompt: A psychologist spends two years following one stroke survivor, documenting her memory, mood, and daily routines in detail. Which method is she using?
options: Survey
Naturalistic observation
Case study
Correlational study

A survey would involve many people answering fixed questions, naturalistic observation would mean watching behavior in its natural setting, and a correlational study would measure how variables relate.

questionBank.prompt: A team wants to record how often commuters glance at their phones in a train station without influencing the behavior they are studying. Which method should they use, and why must the observers stay unobtrusive?
options: A survey, because people answer honestly in writing.
A case study, because it covers many people at once.
An experiment, because it controls the setting.
Naturalistic observation, because people may behave differently when they know they are being watched.
questionBank.explanation: Watching behavior where it naturally happens is naturalistic observation, and observers must stay unobtrusive because people change their behavior when they know they are watched. Surveys depend on self-reports, case studies focus on one person or a few, and an experiment would deliberately change the situation rather than record it as it is.

questionBank.prompt: A headline claims that people who drink more coffee score higher on memory tests, and a researcher's correlational study found exactly that relationship. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The study shows the two variables are related, but it cannot prove coffee improves memory.
The study proves coffee improves memory because the sample was large.
The study proves weak memory leads people to drink more coffee.
The study is worthless, because correlational data can never be informative.
questionBank.explanation: Correlational studies can describe relationships between variables, but they cannot establish cause and effect — a large sample does not change that, and neither does reversing the direction of the claim. The data are still informative about a relationship; they just cannot prove what caused it.

questionBank.prompt: A student organization surveys 200 of its members about study habits and wants to describe the habits of all 4,000 members. What does the 200-person group represent?
options: The population, because it is a group of people.
A sample, a subset chosen to stand in for the larger population.
A case study, because it covers a single organization.
An experimental group, because surveys are experiments.
questionBank.explanation: The 200 respondents are a sample — a subset of the population (all 4,000 members) — and the findings generalize only as far as the sample represents that population. The population is the whole group of interest, a case study would mean studying one person or a few in depth, and surveys are not experiments.

title: Experiments
in30Seconds: An experiment is a controlled test: the researcher changes one thing — the independent variable — while holding everything else steady, and measures what happens to a second thing, the dependent variable. Participants are split into an experimental group and a control group by chance, and because only one thing changed, a difference between the groups can be credited to that change. Experiments are the gold standard for claims about cause and effect.
whyItMatters: Psychology's most confident claims — that a therapy works, that a study habit helps, that a cue affects memory — rest on experiments. A relationship you simply observe can always be explained by some third factor you did not notice; an experiment exists to close that loophole by changing one thing and controlling the rest. Learning how experiments are built teaches you how to read them: where the manipulation sits, which group is the comparison, and whether the setting was artificial enough to doubt. That skill carries into every psychology course that follows, and into everyday decisions about which studies deserve your trust.
learningObjectives: Define an experiment as a controlled test in which the researcher changes one variable and measures its effect on another, following the APA Dictionary of Psychology's definition.
Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable, and the control variables in an experiment, using original examples.
Distinguish the experimental group from the control group and state what each contributes to the comparison.
Explain random assignment in plain terms — who goes where is decided by chance — and why it matters for comparing groups fairly.

Analyze the logic and the limits of experiments: why changing one thing while holding the rest steady supports cause-and-effect claims, and why artificial or impossible experiments qualify those claims.

collegeVersion.heading: What an experiment is
collegeVersion.body:
An experiment is a controlled test. The American Psychological Association's Dictionary of Psychology defines an experiment as a series of observations conducted under controlled conditions to study a relationship, with the purpose of drawing causal inferences about that relationship. In plainer language, the Noba Project's Research Designs module puts it this way: in experiments, researchers actively make changes in one variable and watch for changes in another variable. That is the gold-standard idea. Psychology reaches its strongest conclusions — this caused that — through experiments, because the researcher, not nature, decides what happens to whom and when.

An original example holds the shape together. Suppose a researcher wants to know whether a short nap helps people stay alert. She cannot simply ask people how alert they feel after napping, because people who nap may differ from people who do not in a hundred ways. Instead she runs an experiment: some participants nap for ten minutes, others do not, and everyone then works on the same timed puzzle. The nap is the one thing that differs between the two conditions; everything else — the room, the hour, the puzzle, the instructions — is the same. If the nappers solve more puzzles, the difference has one clear suspect.

collegeVersion.heading: The variables: independent, dependent, and control
collegeVersion.body:
Every experiment runs on three kinds of variables. The independent variable is the one the researcher deliberately changes — in the nap study, whether a participant napped. The dependent variable is the one the researcher measures afterward to see whether anything happened — the number of puzzles solved. The names encode the logic: the outcome depends on the manipulation. The APA dictionary defines the independent variable as the variable that is specifically manipulated in order to assess its effect, and the dependent variable as the outcome observed to change after variation of the independent variable.

The third kind is quieter but just as important. A control variable is something that could affect the measured outcome but is not what the study is about; the researcher holds it constant so it cannot be the cause of any difference. The same room, the same time of day, the same puzzle difficulty — each is a control variable. Hold them steady and they are removed from the running as explanations. The nap study's clean result depends on the control variables staying truly constant.

collegeVersion.heading: Experimental group, control group, and random assignment
collegeVersion.body:
Participants in an experiment are divided into groups. The experimental group is exposed to the manipulation of the independent variable — the nap. The control group is the comparison: its members receive no intervention, or an established one, so it shows what happens without the manipulation. In the nap study, the control group simply waits quietly for ten minutes and then does the same puzzle. The experimental group's score means little on its own; it means something only against the control group's score.

Who lands in which group cannot be left to preference, because people who volunteer for a nap and people who refuse it may differ in alertness before the experiment even starts. So the researcher decides by chance: random assignment. The APA dictionary defines it as assigning participants to conditions entirely at random, so that each participant has an equal likelihood of being assigned to any particular condition. A coin flip, a die roll, or a random-number list will do. The honest reason this matters: random assignment makes the two groups approximately comparable in every respect except the treatment — the nappers and the non-nappers end up with similar ages, sleep histories, and moods on average. When the groups start out comparable and only one thing differs, a difference at the end has one credible cause.

collegeVersion.heading: The logic, the limits, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body:
The core argument is short: change one thing, hold everything else steady, compare. If the groups differed only in the manipulation and were comparable before it, then the manipulation is the best explanation for any difference in the outcome. That is the experiment's claim to the title of gold standard.

The honest note is that the claim comes with two limits. First, experiments can be artificial. As OpenStax's Psychology textbook observes, experiments are often conducted in very artificial settings, which calls into question how well the findings apply to real-world settings. A quiet lab room with a word list is not a dorm hallway with a phone buzzing. Second, some experiments are impossible — practically or ethically. A researcher cannot randomly assign children to different parenting styles and follow them for twenty years, however much she would like an answer. Where the manipulation cannot be done, experiments cannot go, and psychology must lean on other methods with weaker claims.

That is the reality check: experiments trade realism for control. You gain the ability to say “this caused that”; you pay for it in settings that may not match ordinary life. Reading an experimental result well means asking both questions at once — did they control enough, and does this artificial setting still tell us about the real world?

vocabulary.definition: A controlled test in which the researcher changes one variable and measures the effect on another while holding the rest steady, conducted in order to support a cause-and-effect claim.
The variable the researcher deliberately changes (manipulates) in an experiment in order to see what effect it has.
The outcome the researcher measures to see whether it changed after the manipulation of the independent variable.
A factor that could affect the measured outcome but is not the focus of the study; the researcher holds it constant so it cannot explain the result.
The group of participants who are exposed to the manipulation of the independent variable.
The comparison group whose members receive no intervention, or an established one; its responses are the baseline against which the experimental group is judged.
Deciding by chance — a coin flip, a die roll, or a random-number list — which participants go into which condition, so each participant has an equal chance of any condition.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: An experiment is the most reliable way psychologists have to answer “does this cause that?” Instead of watching the world and guessing, the researcher builds a small test: two groups that start out alike, one change, everything else identical. If the groups end up different, the one change is the only thing left to blame. It is like troubleshooting: to find out which ingredient made a dish taste off, you do not change three things and hope; you change one thing, taste, and repeat. The power of the experiment is not that it is complicated — it is that it is simple enough for one change to have one suspect.
eli10.analogy: Imagine baking two identical cakes. You add extra sugar to one and nothing else; both go into the same oven for the same time. If one cake comes out sweeter, you know the sugar did it — because the only difference between the cakes was the sugar. That is the whole design: a matched pair, one difference, a comparison. Random assignment plays the part of shuffling a deck before dealing: it decides which cake gets the sugar, so the two cakes start out with the same ingredients on average.
eli10.analogyLimits: Cakes do not argue. People bring their own histories, moods, and expectations into the lab, so two groups are never identical — random assignment only makes them comparable on average, not equal. And a baker's kitchen is the experimenter's lab: perfectly controlled, which is exactly why a recipe that works there may need adjusting in a real kitchen with a real oven. The trade of realism for control is built into the method.

workedExample: Dr. Rivera wants to know whether writing a short gratitude note before studying improves students' recall of course material. She recruits 60 volunteers and assigns each one to a condition with a random-number list: 30 will write a two-minute gratitude note — the experimental group — and 30 will write a two-minute note about their morning routine instead — the control group, same writing activity, no gratitude. Both groups then study the same 20-item vocabulary list for ten minutes in the same room and take the same recall quiz. The independent variable is the type of note; the dependent variable is the quiz score; the room, the list, and the time limits are control variables. If the gratitude group scores higher on average, Dr. Rivera can credit the gratitude note — because random assignment made the groups comparable at the start and only the note differed. She will also note that the quiet lab setting is cleaner than a real dorm room, so the finding may not fully transfer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping the independent and dependent variables — saying the dependent variable is what the researcher changes.
commonMistakes.correction: The independent variable is what the researcher changes; the dependent variable is what she measures afterward. The name is a memory hook: the outcome depends on the manipulation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the control group is the group that gets the new treatment.
commonMistakes.correction: The control group is the comparison — its members receive no intervention, or an established one. It exists so the experimental group has a baseline to be judged against.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing random assignment means picking participants at random.
commonMistakes.correction: Random assignment decides who goes into which condition, not who gets to take part. Deciding who participates is a separate step; random assignment's job is to make the groups comparable at the start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating an experiment's result as proof that holds in every setting.
commonMistakes.correction: Experiments control tightly but often run in artificial settings, so a clean lab result may not survive contact with real-world conditions — and some questions cannot be experimented on at all.

compareContrast.distinction: The experimental group receives the manipulation of the independent variable; the control group receives none (or an established alternative) and provides the baseline. The difference between them is the whole point of the comparison.
The independent variable is changed by the researcher; the dependent variable is the measured outcome that may change as a result. One is the suspected cause, the other the suspected effect.
Both are chosen by the researcher, but for opposite reasons — the independent variable is changed on purpose to test its effect, while a control variable is held constant so it cannot have an effect.

keyTakeaway: An experiment earns the title of gold standard by changing one thing, holding the rest steady, and letting chance decide who is in which group — but it pays for that control with artificial settings, so its claims always deserve a second look.

questionBank.prompt: In a psychology experiment, which term names the variable that the researcher deliberately changes in order to see its effect?
options: The dependent variable
The control variable
The independent variable
The outcome variable
questionBank.explanation: The independent variable is the one the researcher deliberately manipulates; the APA dictionary defines it as the variable that is specifically manipulated in order to assess its effect. The dependent variable is the outcome measured afterward, a control variable is held constant rather than changed, and “outcome variable” is another name for the dependent variable, not for the manipulation.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the definition of the independent variable

questionBank.prompt: A researcher tests whether a two-minute breathing exercise lowers anxiety before a quiz. One group does the breathing exercise; the other group sits quietly for the same two minutes before the same quiz. Which group is the control group?
options: The group that sits quietly, because its members receive no intervention and serve as the comparison baseline
The group that does the breathing exercise, because it controls the situation
Both groups, because everyone takes the same quiz
Neither group, because no medication is involved
questionBank.explanation: The control group is the comparison group whose members receive no intervention — here, the students who simply sit quietly (APA Dictionary). The breathing-exercise group is the experimental group, exposed to the manipulation. Both groups take the quiz, but that is the measurement, not the manipulation; medication has nothing to do with whether a group is a control.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the control group in a new scenario

questionBank.prompt: To decide which students use a new study app and which use their usual method, a researcher flips a coin for each participant: heads means the app, tails means the usual method. What is this procedure called?
options: Convenience sampling
Random assignment
Experimental control
A control condition
questionBank.explanation: Assigning participants to conditions by coin flip is random assignment — the APA dictionary defines it as assigning participants to conditions entirely at random, with every participant equally likely to land in any condition. Convenience sampling is about who gets recruited, not where they are placed; experimental control is the broader practice of holding things steady; and a control condition is a group, not the assignment procedure.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing random assignment and distinguishing it from other procedures

questionBank.prompt: Two researchers find that people who drink more coffee also tend to sleep fewer hours. Why would they still want to run an experiment before concluding that coffee reduces sleep?
options: Because observing a relationship is never useful information
Because experiments cost less than surveys
Because experimental settings perfectly match real life
Because only an experiment that changes one thing while holding the rest steady can support a cause-and-effect claim; the observed relationship alone could have other explanations
questionBank.explanation: Observing that two things go together cannot rule out other explanations; the only way a researcher can support a cause-and-effect claim is to perform an experiment, as OpenStax's Psychology textbook states and the Noba module echoes. Observation is useful — it just cannot settle causation. Experiments are not cheaper than surveys or perfectly realistic; that is precisely the honesty check, not a reason to skip experiments.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why experiments are needed for cause-and-effect claims

questionBank.prompt: A researcher tests whether room temperature affects typing speed. All participants type the same passage in the same room at the same hour on identical keyboards, and only the temperature changes between conditions. What are the identical factors called?
options: Dependent variables
Independent variables
Control variables
Experimental groups
questionBank.explanation: Factors that could affect the measured outcome but are held constant so they cannot explain the result are control variables (APA Dictionary). The dependent variable is the typing speed being measured; the independent variable is the temperature being changed; and the experimental group is a set of participants, not a factor held steady.
questionBank.skill: Identifying control variables held constant in a design

title: Correlation
in30Seconds: A correlation is a measure of how two variables move together. Two things are correlated when they rise and fall in step — same direction, opposite directions, or with no pattern at all. The tighter the pattern, the stronger the correlation, and a scatterplot is its picture. Correlations are useful for prediction and for generating hypotheses, but a link between two variables is not proof that one causes the other. Correlation is a clue, not a verdict.
whyItMatters: Correlations are everywhere in daily life — in news headlines, app reports, health trackers, and product claims — and most people never learn to read them. A sleep app that shows later bedtimes alongside more evening screen time is reporting a correlation, and so is a headline that ties one habit to some outcome. The skill is knowing what the pattern does and does not say: a correlation can point you toward a prediction and spark a question worth studying, but it cannot by itself tell you what causes what. Psychology courses build on this idea constantly — every claim about the relationships between behavior, thought, and biology passes through it.
learningObjectives: Define correlation as a measure of how two variables move together, and identify the three directions a correlation can take.
Distinguish positive, negative, and near-zero correlations, using an original example for each.
Explain what strength means — how tightly the pattern holds — and describe the range of the correlation number honestly, without computing statistics.
Read a scatterplot as the picture of a correlation, describing what a tight band of dots versus a scattered cloud shows.
Explain what a correlation can and cannot show, and why a link between variables is not evidence of cause.
Apply correlation to real situations: use it for prediction and hypothesis generation, and state its honest limits.

collegeVersion.heading: What a correlation is
collegeVersion.body: The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines correlation as the degree of a relationship between two variables. In plainer words, two things are correlated when they move together: a change in one tends to come with a change in the other. Consider a fictional sleep-tracking app called Nightowl, which records two numbers per user each night — minutes of screen time after 9 p.m. and the time that person fell asleep. Sorted by screen time, the pattern jumps out: nights with more evening screen time come with later bedtimes, and nights with little screen time come with earlier ones. The two variables move together, and that co-movement is exactly what a correlation measures. Correlation always describes a pair of variables at a time — this and that, not the whole picture at once.

collegeVersion.heading: Three directions: positive, negative, and zero
collegeVersion.body: A correlation has a direction: the story of how the two variables relate. A positive correlation means they move in the same direction — as one goes up, the other tends to go up too, and as one falls, the other tends to fall. The sleep-app link is positive: more screen time, later bedtime. A negative correlation means they move in opposite directions — as one goes up, the other tends to go down. Original example: a running coach finds that athletes who take more rest days have fewer injuries — rest up, injuries down. A zero correlation — more precisely, near-zero — means no consistent pattern: the variables do not move together. The same app records shoe size, which has no relationship with bedtime. One caution from OpenStax: a negative correlation is not the same as no correlation. Opposite directions are still a relationship; no relationship means no pattern of any direction.

collegeVersion.heading: Strength: how tightly the pattern holds
collegeVersion.body: Direction tells you which way the variables move; strength tells you how reliably. A strong correlation is one where the pattern holds almost every time. A weak one holds sometimes — the variables lean in the same general direction, but exceptions are common. In the Nightowl data, screen time and bedtime move together on most nights but not all: a tired user might scroll for an hour and still fall asleep early. So the pattern is real but not perfect. When researchers put a number on a correlation, it runs from -1 to +1: the closer the number sits to either end, the more strongly the variables are related, and the more predictable one becomes from the other. A number near zero means little or no pattern. The honest note: the arithmetic behind that number is the statistics subject's territory, not this lesson's.

collegeVersion.heading: Scatterplots: the picture of a correlation
collegeVersion.body: A scatterplot draws the pattern so you can see it. Each dot is one person, one night, or one anything, carrying two pieces of information: left-to-right is the value of one variable, up-down is the value of the other. Dots that climb from the lower-left corner to the upper-right corner show a positive correlation; dots that slope down from upper-left to lower-right show a negative one. The shape of the whole cloud is the story. When the dots hug a line, the correlation is strong; when they scatter loosely around it, it is weak. If the dots form no shape at all, the variables are essentially unrelated. In one picture, a scatterplot answers two questions: which direction, and how tightly.

collegeVersion.heading: What a correlation can and cannot show
collegeVersion.body: Here is the boundary that matters. What a correlation can show: that two variables are linked — that they move together in a consistent way. What it cannot show: why they move together. OpenStax puts it directly: establishing that a relationship exists tells us little about cause and effect. Consider the sleep-app link: it could mean screen time delays sleep, or that people who naturally stay up late reach for their phones while they wait for drowsiness. Or a third factor — a demanding work schedule, a noisy household — could be pushing both at once. The data, taken alone, cannot choose among these stories, because every one of them produces the same pattern. The deeper question — how researchers ever do decide what causes what — is its own lesson. Here, hold the boundary: correlation shows links, not causes.

collegeVersion.heading: What correlations are for: prediction and hypothesis generation
collegeVersion.body: A correlation earns its keep even when it explains nothing. First, prediction: when two variables move together, knowing one helps you anticipate the other. OpenStax notes that correlations have predictive value — an admissions office might use the link between high-school grades and first-year performance to anticipate which applicants will succeed. Second, hypothesis generation: a pattern suggests possible explanations, and each possible explanation is a question worth testing. The Noba Project makes the point with the generosity-and-happiness example: the correlation could mean generosity causes happiness, or happiness causes generosity, or a third variable drives both. A researcher who sees the sleep-app pattern now has a testable question — does cutting evening screen time actually move bedtimes earlier? Testing it is a different method's job, covered in its own lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Correlation is a clue, not a verdict. It tells you where to look, and it never closes the case. The pattern in the data is real and useful — for predicting, for raising questions, for narrowing the possibilities. But the pattern alone cannot prove any explanation, no matter how obvious the story seems. Read correlations the way a careful detective reads a clue: note it, let it point you somewhere, and keep looking for the test that decides between the stories.

vocabulary.definition: A measure of the degree to which two variables move together — the extent of their relationship.
Any characteristic or quantity that can take different values across people, events, or time.
A pattern in which two variables move in the same direction, rising and falling together.
A pattern in which two variables move in opposite directions: as one increases, the other tends to decrease.
A situation in which two variables show no consistent pattern; changes in one carry no information about the other.
How tightly a correlation's pattern holds — how consistently the two variables move together.
A graph in which each dot represents one data point, positioned by its values on two variables.
Using the value of one variable to anticipate the value of a related variable, based on how they move together.
A candidate explanation, stated clearly enough to be tested with evidence.
The relationship in which one thing produces a change in another; a correlation alone cannot establish it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A correlation is a way of saying that two things move together. Some pairs rise and fall in step — more screen time, later bedtime: that is a positive correlation. Some move in opposite directions — more rest days, fewer injuries: that is a negative one. And some show no pattern at all: near-zero. Correlations also have strength: a strong one holds almost every time, a weak one only sometimes. A scatterplot shows all of this in one picture, one dot per person. Correlations are handy — they let you predict, and they hand you questions to test — but they never say what causes what. The pattern is a clue; the explanation still has to be earned.
eli10.analogy: Think of a wooden dock floating on the water. When the tide rises, the dock rises; when the tide falls, the dock falls. Watch the dock and you can predict the tide's direction quite well — yet the dock does not cause the tide, and the tide does not lift the dock. Something else, the moon's gravity, moves both. That is what a correlation is: a real, useful, visible link — with the true driver standing off to the side.
eli10.analogyLimits: The dock and the tide are almost perfectly synchronized — a very strong correlation — while most real correlations are loose, with plenty of exceptions. And in the tide example the hidden cause is famous and easy to name; in real research, third variables are usually invisible and hard to hunt down, which is why the honest lesson ends where it does: a clue, not a verdict.

workedExample: Priya opens the fictional Nightowl sleep app's anonymized dataset: 10,000 users, two numbers per person per night. She plots evening screen time on one axis and bedtime on the other, one dot per user. The dots form a loose band climbing to the right — positive, moderate strength: plenty of people fit the pattern, plenty do not. Next she plots shoe size against bedtime: the dots go everywhere, no shape at all — near-zero. Then she reads a forum post claiming the app proves that screen time causes late sleep. She stops: the data show a link, not a cause. The pattern can predict — a heavy scroller is more likely to be a late sleeper — and it generates a testable question: does reducing evening screen time move bedtimes earlier? But answering that question needs a method the app's data cannot supply. She writes her summary: "Screen time and bedtime move together in this dataset. That is a correlation — a useful clue, not a verdict."

commonMistakes.mistake: "Negative correlation means there is no relationship."
commonMistakes.correction: Negative is a direction, not an absence. Variables that move in opposite directions are related — sometimes strongly. No relationship lives near zero, in the middle of the range, where no pattern of any direction shows up.

commonMistakes.mistake: "The stronger the correlation, the more likely one variable causes the other."
commonMistakes.correction: Strength says how tightly the pattern holds, not why it holds. A very tight pattern can still be driven by a hidden third factor, so strength never upgrades a correlation into a cause.

commonMistakes.mistake: "One exception disproves a correlation."
commonMistakes.correction: Correlations describe patterns across many data points, and exceptions are normal. Strength is a matter of how many exceptions there are, not whether any exist.

commonMistakes.mistake: "If two things are correlated, one must be causing the other."
commonMistakes.correction: A link is not proof of a cause. Usually several explanations fit the same pattern — the sleep-app link, for example, has at least three plausible stories. Deciding among them requires other research methods, which this subject covers in separate lessons.

compareContrast.distinction: Both are real relationships; they differ only in direction — same direction versus opposite directions. In both cases, knowing one variable helps anticipate the other.
A correlation is a measured link between variables; causation is one variable producing a change in another. A correlation never establishes causation on its own — that question is its own lesson.

Strength is how tightly the pattern holds: a strong correlation shows few exceptions, a weak one shows many. Direction and strength are independent — a strong negative correlation is just as tight as a strong positive one.

keyTakeaway: A correlation measures how two variables move together — same direction, opposite directions, or not at all — and a scatterplot shows the pattern at a glance. It is a clue, not a verdict: useful for prediction and hypothesis generation, never proof of cause.

questionBank.prompt: A researcher records two sets of numbers for the same group of people and wants one concept that describes whether those numbers move together — rising and falling in step, moving in opposite directions, or showing no pattern at all. What is that concept called?
options: A scatterplot — a graph, not the measure itself.
A hypothesis — a candidate explanation to be tested.
A correlation — a measure of how two variables move together.
An experiment — a method for testing what causes what.
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines correlation as the degree of a relationship between two variables, which is what the researcher wants to measure. A scatterplot pictures a correlation rather than naming the measure, a hypothesis is a candidate explanation, and an experiment is a research method — none of them is the concept itself.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the definition of a correlation

questionBank.prompt: A fictional sleep-tracker app finds that on nights when users spend more time on their phones after 9 p.m., they also fall asleep later, and on nights with little phone time they fall asleep earlier. Which description fits this pattern?
options: A positive correlation — the two variables move in the same direction.
A negative correlation — the two variables move in opposite directions.
A zero correlation — the variables show no consistent pattern.
Proof that phone use delays sleep.
questionBank.explanation: Screen time and bedtime rise and fall together, which is the definition of a positive correlation — same direction. A negative correlation would show later bedtimes with less screen time, a zero correlation would show no pattern, and the app data alone cannot prove that phone use delays sleep.
questionBank.skill: Applying the direction of a correlation to an original data pattern

questionBank.prompt: A running coach tracks each athlete's monthly rest days and injuries. Athletes who take more rest days have fewer injuries, and athletes who rest less get hurt more often. What does this pattern describe?
options: A positive correlation — rest causes injuries.
A negative correlation — as rest days increase, injuries tend to decrease.
A zero correlation — the two variables are unrelated.
Proof that rest prevents injuries.
questionBank.explanation: Rest days and injuries move in opposite directions — more rest, fewer injuries — which is a negative correlation, as OpenStax describes it. A positive correlation would mean injuries rise with rest days, a zero correlation would show no pattern, and the measured link alone does not prove rest prevents injuries.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing a negative correlation in an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: A researcher plots each participant as one dot on a graph: hours of evening screen time on the horizontal axis and bedtime on the vertical axis. The dots form a tight band climbing from the lower-left corner to the upper-right corner, with few stragglers. What does the picture show?
options: A strong positive correlation — the variables move together and the pattern holds tightly.
A strong negative correlation — the variables move in opposite directions.
A zero correlation — no relationship between the variables.
Proof that screen time causes later bedtimes.
questionBank.explanation: In a scatterplot, dots climbing from lower left to upper right show a positive correlation, and dots that hug a line rather than scattering widely show a strong one — Noba describes the bottom-left-to-upper-right pattern and OpenStax ties closeness to the line to strength. The slope rules out negative and zero, and a scatterplot alone proves no cause.
questionBank.skill: Reading a scatterplot for direction and strength

questionBank.prompt: A hospital's wellness app reports that patients who walk more steps each day also report better mood scores, and the pattern is consistent across thousands of users. The hospital wants to know whether walking improves mood. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: Walking definitely improves mood, since the pattern is consistent across thousands of users.
The variables are unrelated, because the app only measures and does not experiment.
The hospital should stop tracking steps, since a correlation cannot be used for anything.
The pattern is a correlation — useful for prediction and as a starting hypothesis — but it does not by itself prove that walking causes better mood.
questionBank.explanation: The steps-and-mood pattern is a correlation with predictive value, and it suggests a hypothesis worth testing — but establishing a relationship tells little about cause and effect, as OpenStax states, so it cannot prove walking improves mood. Consistency across users strengthens the pattern, not the causal claim; the variables are clearly related; and correlations are useful for prediction and hypothesis generation.
questionBank.skill: Applying the correlation-versus-cause boundary and the uses of correlation

title: Correlation Versus Causation
in30Seconds: Correlation means two things tend to change together; causation means one thing makes another happen. The two are not the same, and confusing them is the most common mistake in science reporting. A link between variables can be real yet have nothing to do with cause: a hidden third factor may drive both, or the arrow may point the other way. Experiments, which actively change one variable and watch for changes in another, are the method that can test a cause-and-effect claim.
whyItMatters: Every day, headlines convert a study's correlation into a confident cause: screens damage attention, late nights wreck grades, walking improves mood. Most of those headlines are wrong, not because the studies are fake but because a link is not a cause. Learning to spot the difference changes how you read news, evaluate health advice, and argue with evidence in any course that uses research. It also protects you from your own mind: humans are pattern-seeking animals, and the pattern the brain loves to see is cause. In college writing and in professional life, the person who can say this study shows a link, not a cause, is the one who reasons clearly. This lesson gives you that move.
learningObjectives: Define correlation and causation, and state the difference between a link and a cause-and-effect relationship.
Explain why the human tendency to see patterns makes correlational findings easy to over-read as causal.
Identify the third-variable problem and reverse causation as two ways a real correlation can exist without causation.
Apply the correlation-versus-causation distinction to evaluate a research headline or finding.
Explain why experiments are the method that can test a cause, and why even good experiments leave questions open.

collegeVersion.heading: The two words, defined
collegeVersion.body: Correlation and causation are easy to say and easy to confuse, so psychologists start with a plain working definition. A correlation is a relationship between two variables: when one changes, the other tends to change too, in a predictable direction. OpenStax's Psychology 2e puts it directly: when two variables are correlated, it simply means that as one variable changes, so does the other. Causation is a stronger claim: it says one thing makes another happen, that changes in one variable cause changes in another. Noba's Research Designs module makes the same distinction in method terms: correlational research measures variables as they naturally occur and computes how they go together, while experiments actively change one variable and watch for changes in another. The two-word summary researchers repeat is simple: correlation does not mean causation. The rest of this lesson is about what that phrase means and why everyone, including experts, has to keep saying it.

collegeVersion.heading: Why the mind leaps from link to cause
collegeVersion.body: Humans are pattern-seeking animals, and that is usually a feature. Spotting that dark clouds mean rain, or that a certain rustle means danger, kept our ancestors alive. The same machinery runs in modern life, but it overproduces: the brain treats a few coincidences as a reliable rule and then dresses the rule up as a cause. OpenStax flags exactly this as a standard topic in analyzing findings: our tendency to look for relationships between variables that do not really exist. Here is an original example. A fan notices that his team has won the last three games he watched while wearing his lucky socks, and he now refuses to watch without them. His sock-wearing and his team's winning are, in his memory, correlated, and he has quietly decided the socks cause the wins. Nothing about the socks explains the games; the pattern is a product of attention, not of the socks. That is the engine behind most bad causal headlines: a real or imagined link, a mind that loves patterns, and a story that turns goes-with into causes.

collegeVersion.heading: The third-variable problem
collegeVersion.body: Sometimes a correlation is real, meaningful, and still not causal, because a hidden factor drives both variables. Researchers call that hidden factor a third variable, or a confounding variable. Consider a fictional dataset from a seaside town. Across a summer, the town records daily sunshine hours, sunglasses sold at the boardwalk, and first-aid visits for minor beach injuries. All three rise together. A careless headline could claim that buying sunglasses causes beach injuries. The real driver is simpler: sunny days draw bigger crowds to the beach, and bigger crowds mean more sunglasses sold and more scrapes and sunburns treated. The sunshine, not the sunglasses, is the third variable. OpenStax describes the same structure: while variables are sometimes correlated because one does cause the other, it could also be that some other factor is actually causing the systematic movement in both variables of interest. Whenever you meet a link, ask first: what else moves with both of these?

collegeVersion.heading: Reverse causation
collegeVersion.body: The second trap is the direction of the arrow. A correlation says two things move together; it does not say which one is pulling. Consider a fictional workplace study: employees who drink more coffee report worse sleep, and a wellness newsletter concludes that coffee ruins sleep. That may be true, but the data alone cannot rule out the opposite reading: people who sleep badly arrive tired and reach for more coffee. The arrow may point from poor sleep to coffee, not from coffee to poor sleep. This is why the OpenIntro statistics textbook notes that correlation does not specify which variable is explanatory and which is the outcome. The same two variables, the same correlation, two completely different causal stories. Before accepting any headline, ask the direction question: which one could plausibly make the other happen, and could the story work in reverse?

collegeVersion.heading: Experiments: the method that can test cause
collegeVersion.body: If correlation can only raise questions, what answers them? Experiments, the subject of a sibling lesson. In an experiment, the researcher actively changes one variable, the suspected cause, while controlling the conditions around it, then measures whether the other variable changes in response. Noba's module states the logic plainly: experiments allow researchers to make causal inferences. OpenStax agrees: correlational research can find a relationship between two variables, but the only way a researcher can claim that the relationship is cause and effect is to perform an experiment. The honest note is equally important. Experiments are powerful but imperfect: they often take place in artificial settings, and many questions cannot be tested experimentally for ethical or practical reasons. So the honest framing for this whole topic is: correlation is a question, and experiments are the best available answer, a good answer that still deserves more studies, more checks, and more questions.

vocabulary.definition: A statistical relationship in which two variables tend to change together; the link may or may not be causal.
A cause-and-effect relationship in which changes in one variable produce changes in another.
A hidden factor that influences both of the variables being studied, creating the appearance of a direct link between them.
A situation in which the causal arrow runs opposite to the assumed direction, so the outcome actually drives the cause.
A perceived relationship between variables that does not really exist, produced by the mind's tendency to notice matches and overlook mismatches.
A research method in which the investigator actively changes one variable while controlling conditions, in order to test cause and effect.
Any measurable characteristic that can take different values, such as hours of sleep, exam scores, or coffee consumption.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Correlation and causation are two different claims about the same pair of things. Correlation says: these two move together. Causation says: this one makes that one move. The first is a description; the second is a story about a mechanism, and a description never proves the story. Two things can move together because one drives the other, because the other drives the one, because a third thing drives both, or because your mind simply noticed the times they matched and ignored the times they did not. That is why researchers keep the phrase correlation does not mean causation close at hand: not because links are unimportant, they are the starting point of every investigation, but because a link alone does not tell you which story is true.
eli10.analogy: Think of a correlation as two friends who always arrive at the same party together. Seeing them walk in side by side tells you they are connected, and you can predict that if one shows up, the other probably will too. But it does not tell you who invited whom, or whether a third friend organized the whole evening and drove them both.
eli10.analogyLimits: The party analogy breaks down because people can simply ask the friends how they got there; variables cannot answer questions. A correlation also never reveals whether the connection is causal, coincidental, or shared, because the data are silent on the story. And unlike friends, who either show up together or do not, correlations are matters of degree: two variables can be weakly or strongly linked, and even a strong link says nothing about cause.

workedExample: A campus newspaper runs the headline Breakfast Boosts Exam Scores after a survey finds that students who eat breakfast average higher marks on morning exams. A careful reader applies this lesson. First, is the claim correlation or causation? The survey shows a link, nothing more. Second, could a third variable drive both? Students who eat breakfast may also sleep more regularly, arrive on time, and keep steadier routines, any of which could explain the scores. Third, does the arrow have to point from breakfast to grades? It could point the other way: students who are already organized and doing well may be the ones with time for breakfast. The headline is a question, not an answer. To test it, a researcher would need an experiment, randomly assigning students to eat or skip breakfast before the same exam and comparing results. Until that happens, the honest summary is: breakfast goes with better scores; whether it causes them is still open.

commonMistakes.mistake: A strong correlation proves causation.
commonMistakes.correction: Strength describes how reliably the variables move together; it says nothing about why. Even a near-perfect link can be driven by a third variable, so strength is never proof of cause.

commonMistakes.mistake: If a finding is not causal, it is worthless.
commonMistakes.correction: Correlational evidence is how research discovers leads. A link raises the question that an experiment can then answer, so correlation is valuable even when it cannot settle causation.

commonMistakes.mistake: The direction of the arrow is obvious from the data.
commonMistakes.correction: Correlational data do not show direction. Reverse causation is always a live possibility, so the arrow has to be argued for, not assumed.

commonMistakes.mistake: One good experiment settles it forever.
commonMistakes.correction: Experiments are the best tool for causal claims, but they are often run in artificial settings, and a single study still needs replication and converging evidence before it becomes a confident conclusion.

compareContrast.distinction: Correlation says two variables move together; causation says one makes the other happen. A link can be real without any mechanism connecting the two.
With a third variable, a hidden factor drives both observed variables; with reverse causation, the two variables are truly connected but the causal arrow points opposite to the headline's story.
A correlational study observes and measures variables as they naturally occur; an experiment manipulates one variable under controlled conditions, which is what allows a causal test.

keyTakeaway: Correlation shows that things move together; causation means one thing makes another happen. A link raises a question, a well-run experiment is the best way to answer it, and even then good science keeps asking.

questionBank.prompt: A researcher reports that hours of sleep and next-day exam performance are positively correlated. What does that finding alone establish?
options: That the two variables tend to change together, so more sleep goes with better performance
That more sleep causes better exam performance
That exam performance causes students to sleep more
That sleep and exam performance have no relationship at all
questionBank.explanation: A positive correlation means the variables tend to move together: as one increases, so does the other. That is a link, not a mechanism, so it does not establish cause in either direction.
questionBank.skill: Recalling what a correlation does and does not establish

questionBank.prompt: Why do researchers say that correlational findings cannot support cause-and-effect claims on their own?
options: Because correlational studies are always poorly designed
Because correlations are too weak to matter
Because a hidden third variable or the reverse direction of influence could explain the same link
Because no two variables are ever truly related
questionBank.explanation: A correlation can arise from a third variable driving both measured variables, or from influence flowing the opposite way. Neither possibility is ruled out by the link itself, which is why causation needs a different method.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why correlation alone cannot establish causation

questionBank.prompt: In a fictional seaside town, daily sunshine hours, sunglasses sold at the boardwalk, and first-aid visits for beach injuries all rise together across the summer. A headline claims that buying sunglasses causes beach injuries. Which explanation best fits the data?
options: Sunglasses genuinely cause beach injuries
Sunny days draw larger crowds to the beach, and more people on the beach means both more sunglasses sold and more injuries treated
Beach injuries cause people to buy sunglasses
The three measures are unrelated and the pattern is meaningless
questionBank.explanation: Sunshine is the third variable: it drives crowd size, and the crowd drives both sunglasses sales and first-aid visits. The correlation is real, but the sunglasses-to-injury link is an illusion created by the shared cause.
questionBank.skill: Applying the third-variable explanation to a fictional dataset

questionBank.prompt: A fictional workplace survey finds that employees who drink more coffee report worse sleep, and a newsletter concludes that coffee ruins sleep. What is the strongest reason to doubt the newsletter's conclusion?
options: The survey included too few employees to count
Coffee drinkers are probably lying about their sleep
The correlation is too weak to report
The arrow may point the other way: people who sleep badly may drink more coffee to get through the day
questionBank.explanation: Reverse causation is a live possibility: poor sleep may drive coffee consumption rather than coffee causing poor sleep. Correlation does not specify which variable influences which, so the newsletter has overclaimed.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a finding for reverse causation

questionBank.prompt: A student wants to know whether a link between social media use and mood is causal. Which next step best fits how researchers test cause?
options: Run an experiment that actively changes social media use while controlling other conditions, then measure mood
Gather a larger correlational dataset and look for a stronger correlation
Ask people which direction they think the influence runs
Conclude that the link proves cause because it appears in many studies
questionBank.explanation: Experiments allow causal inferences because the researcher manipulates the suspected cause and controls the surrounding conditions. More correlation, even from bigger samples, still cannot isolate cause; neither can opinion or repetition.
questionBank.skill: Choosing the experimental test of a causal question

quickCheck.prompt: A researcher reports that hours of sleep and next-day exam performance are positively correlated. What does that finding alone establish?
options: That the two variables tend to change together, so more sleep goes with better performance
That more sleep causes better exam performance
That exam performance causes students to sleep more
That sleep and exam performance have no relationship at all
quickCheck.explanation: A positive correlation means the variables tend to move together: as one increases, so does the other. That is a link, not a mechanism, so it does not establish cause in either direction.
quickCheck.skill: Recalling what a correlation does and does not establish

quickCheck.prompt: Why do researchers say that correlational findings cannot support cause-and-effect claims on their own?
options: Because correlational studies are always poorly designed
Because correlations are too weak to matter
Because a hidden third variable or the reverse direction of influence could explain the same link
Because no two variables are ever truly related
quickCheck.explanation: A correlation can arise from a third variable driving both measured variables, or from influence flowing the opposite way. Neither possibility is ruled out by the link itself, which is why causation needs a different method.
quickCheck.skill: Explaining why correlation alone cannot establish causation

quickCheck.prompt: In a fictional seaside town, daily sunshine hours, sunglasses sold at the boardwalk, and first-aid visits for beach injuries all rise together across the summer. A headline claims that buying sunglasses causes beach injuries. Which explanation best fits the data?
options: Sunglasses genuinely cause beach injuries
Sunny days draw larger crowds to the beach, and more people on the beach means both more sunglasses sold and more injuries treated
Beach injuries cause people to buy sunglasses
The three measures are unrelated and the pattern is meaningless
quickCheck.explanation: Sunshine is the third variable: it drives crowd size, and the crowd drives both sunglasses sales and first-aid visits. The correlation is real, but the sunglasses-to-injury link is an illusion created by the shared cause.
quickCheck.skill: Applying the third-variable explanation to a fictional dataset
