title: Intelligence
in30Seconds: Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems — the working definition used here, drawn from the APA Dictionary of Psychology and the Noba Project. Experts still debate exactly what intelligence is, and an IQ score, from an intelligence test, captures only part of the picture. Psychologists have proposed one general ability (Spearman's g), many separate abilities (Gardner's multiple intelligences), and three interacting kinds (Sternberg's triarchic theory). Genes and environment both shape it. No number captures a person.
whyItMatters: Almost everyone has met an IQ score — their own, a friend's, or one quoted in a headline. Understanding what that number does and does not mean changes how you read it: in schools, where tests help decide who gets support; in hiring and placement, where scores influence decisions; and in everyday talk, where people quietly rank themselves and others. The measurement debate matters academically because it sits at the center of psychology's oldest questions — what the mind is and how to study it. Practically, it keeps a useful tool in its place: a sample of some abilities, not a verdict on a person. And honestly, it is a reminder that the most important measures of a person rarely come with a scale.
learningObjectives: Define intelligence using the working definition — the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems — and explain why experts continue to debate the definition.
Explain what an IQ score is and describe the original purpose of Alfred Binet's intelligence test.
Distinguish Spearman's theory of general intelligence (g), Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences, and Sternberg's triarchic theory, with attribution to each theorist.
Explain what modern intelligence tests measure and what they leave out.
Analyze the evidence that genes and environment both shape intelligence.
Evaluate the claim that no single test score captures a person.

collegeVersion.heading: What intelligence is
collegeVersion.body: Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems. That working definition compresses the ones psychologists actually use. The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines intelligence as the ability to derive information, learn from experience, adapt to the environment, understand, and correctly utilize thought and reason. The Noba Project's intelligence module, by psychologist Robert Biswas-Diener, describes intellectual ability as encompassing the ability to learn, remember, and use new information, to solve problems, and to adapt to novel situations. Compress both and you get the working definition of this lesson: learn, reason, solve. The honest note comes immediately: experts do not agree on a single definition. OpenStax Psychology 2e puts it directly — what exactly is intelligence? The way researchers have defined the concept has been modified many times since the birth of psychology. Some argue for one broad ability; others argue for many separate ones. That debate is part of the topic, not a gap in it.

collegeVersion.heading: The IQ idea: a score with a history
collegeVersion.body: IQ stands for intelligence quotient, and it describes a score earned on a test designed to measure intelligence. The APA Dictionary defines IQ as a standard measure of an individual's intelligence level based on psychological tests; the average is customarily set at 100, and most scores fall within fifteen points of it. The score has a specific origin story. In the early 1900s, the French government asked Alfred Binet to develop an intelligence test to use on children — not to rank them, but to determine which ones might have difficulty in school, so they could get help. American researchers saw the value of the idea: Louis Terman, a Stanford professor, standardized Binet's work into the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale, still used today. In 1939, David Wechsler built his own test from subtests covering verbal and nonverbal skills, because he believed intelligence was a global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment. Modern IQ tests descend from those tools.

collegeVersion.heading: Three theories of intelligence
collegeVersion.body: Over the last century, psychologists have proposed very different answers to what intelligence is. Charles Spearman, a British psychologist, argued that intelligence consists of one general factor, called g, which could be measured and compared among individuals — the observation behind it being that people who perform well in one intellectual area tend to perform well in others. The APA Dictionary credits the idea of the general factor (g) to Spearman in 1904. Howard Gardner, a Harvard psychologist, took the opposite direction: his theory of multiple intelligences holds that each person possesses at least eight relatively independent intelligences — linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, spatial, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic. Gardner's theory is widely used in education, though OpenStax notes it has been heavily criticized among cognitive psychologists for lacking empirical evidence. Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory of intelligence offers three parts: analytical intelligence, close to academic problem solving — analyzing, evaluating, judging, comparing; creative intelligence, inventing or imagining novel solutions; and practical intelligence, sometimes called street smarts — finding solutions that work in everyday life by applying knowledge from experience.

collegeVersion.heading: Tests today: some abilities, not the whole person
collegeVersion.body: Modern IQ tests measure real abilities. The APA Dictionary describes the intelligence test as an individually administered test measuring the ability to solve problems, form concepts, reason, acquire detail, and perform other intellectual tasks. But those abilities are a sample, not the whole person — and the people who built the tests said so. Wechsler was suspicious of using a single score to capture all of intelligence, and he designed his test to tap a variety of verbal and nonverbal skills. OpenStax reports that IQ tests have been debated throughout their development and use: they have sometimes been used for harmful purposes, such as supporting the eugenics movement, and the question of how valid they are remains open. Scores even drift across generations: the Flynn effect is the observation that each generation scores higher than the last, which Flynn argued does not necessarily mean greater intelligence. A score is a measurement of some abilities at one moment, not a biography.

collegeVersion.heading: What shapes intelligence: genes and environment
collegeVersion.body: Genes and environment both matter. The classic evidence comes from twin studies. In the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart, researchers found that identical twins raised together and identical twins raised apart show higher correlations between their IQ scores than siblings or fraternal twins raised together — a finding OpenStax reports as revealing a genetic component to intelligence. At the same time, other psychologists emphasize the developmental environment; OpenStax's summary of the field is direct: aspects of each idea are probably correct. The range-of-reaction idea captures the balance: a person's genetic potential is a fixed quantity, but whether that potential is reached depends on the environmental stimulation experienced, especially in childhood. No single gene, classroom, or number explains a person's intelligence.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: a verb, not a noun
collegeVersion.body: The reality check that holds the lesson together: a number does not capture a person. A score is a measurement taken at one time, from one set of tasks, under one set of conditions; the person is a learner who changes, practices, and adapts. That is why the honest framing of this lesson is that intelligence is a verb, not a noun — it is something people do, learning, reasoning, solving, more than something they have. Treating it as a fixed noun, a rank carried for life, is where the measurement debate does its damage. Treating it as activity keeps both the science and the humility: measure what can be measured, and remember what the measurement leaves out.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to learn, reason, and solve problems — the working definition used in this lesson; psychologists continue to debate the exact definition.
A standard score earned on a test designed to measure intelligence; the average score is customarily set at 100.
The single general factor proposed by Charles Spearman that is believed to underlie performance across many kinds of intellectual tasks.
Howard Gardner's theory that each person possesses several relatively independent kinds of intelligence, such as linguistic and spatial, rather than one general ability.
Robert Sternberg's theory that intelligence has three parts — analytical, creative, and practical.
A standardized test that measures abilities such as solving problems, forming concepts, and reasoning.
A statistical estimate of how much of the variation in a trait within a population comes from genetic differences.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Intelligence is the name psychologists give to the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems. No one owns a perfect definition — the experts debate it, and that debate is part of the story. The number you have probably heard of is IQ, the score from an intelligence test, and it measures real abilities: solving puzzles, reasoning, remembering facts. But it is a sample, not the whole person. Over a century, three famous theories have emerged. Spearman said intelligence is one general thing, g, that shows up across everything you do. Gardner said no — people have at least eight different intelligences, from musical to spatial to interpersonal. Sternberg said it is three: analytical, creative, and practical. What makes it grow? Genes and environment, together — twin studies show a genetic hand, and experience shows the environment's. The honest bottom line: intelligence is a verb, not a noun — something you do, more than a rank you carry. No number captures a person.
eli10.analogy: Think of a kitchen and a chef. The pantry holds the ingredients — that is the genetic starting material. The chef's training, the recipes tried, and the kitchen she practices in are the environment. The dish she produces on a given night depends on the task in front of her. Now imagine rating the chef's entire ability by a single number from one taste test of one dish. The number says something real about that dish on that night — and almost nothing about the hundreds of dishes she could still learn to cook.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a chef can be retrained and a kitchen restocked, while a person cannot swap genes, and intelligence is not only visible in performances. It also risks sounding like scores are worthless — they are not. A well-built test does measure real abilities. The point is that a measurement is a sample, not the whole.

workedExample: Dev, a sophomore, took an IQ-style test for a research study and scored near the middle of the distribution. The research assistant handed him the number with a caution: it samples some abilities, it does not describe a person. That same semester, the irrigation system in his family's greenhouse kept failing. Dev spent three weekends diagnosing it — forming a hypothesis about a blocked valve, testing it, learning from the failure, trying again — until he found the real culprit, a corroded sensor. No test he had ever taken asked about corroded sensors, and none had measured his patience for failure. A year later he retook the study's test and scored higher, with no coaching in between. Neither score was a lie. Each was a real sample of some abilities at one moment. The number was part of the story; Dev was the rest.

commonMistakes.mistake: "An IQ score measures your total intelligence, once and for all."
commonMistakes.correction: A score reflects some measured abilities on one test at one time. Psychologists note that the validity of intelligence tests is still debated, scores shift across generations (the Flynn effect), and no single number captures a person.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Binet invented IQ testing to rank people by ability."
commonMistakes.correction: Binet's test, requested by the French government, was meant to identify children who might have difficulty in school so they could get help — a purpose of finding who needs support, not a lifetime ranking.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Gardner's multiple intelligences is the settled scientific theory of intelligence."
commonMistakes.correction: Gardner's theory is influential and widely used in education, but cognitive psychologists have heavily criticized it for lacking empirical evidence; it is one theory among several, not a settled answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Intelligence is fixed by genes, or else purely made by the environment."
commonMistakes.correction: Research supports both: twin studies show a genetic component, and the range-of-reaction view holds that reaching your potential depends on environmental stimulation, especially in childhood.

compareContrast.distinction: Spearman proposed a single general factor that underlies performance across many kinds of intellectual tasks; Gardner proposed at least eight relatively independent intelligences. The one-ability versus many-abilities question is the heart of the measurement debate.

In Sternberg's triarchic theory, analytical intelligence is close to academic problem solving — analyzing, evaluating, comparing — while practical intelligence means finding solutions that work in everyday life by applying knowledge from experience, sometimes called street smarts.

Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems; an IQ score is a measurement of some of those abilities taken from one test at one time. The score is a sample of part of the ability; intelligence is the whole activity.

keyTakeaway: Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems — an activity, not a fixed rank. IQ scores measure some abilities, not the whole person, and genes and environment both shape the person behind the number.

questionBank.prompt: In the early 1900s, the French government asked Alfred Binet to develop a test of intelligence for children. What was the original purpose of that test?
options: To identify children who might have difficulty in school so they could get help.
To rank the entire population by intellectual worth.
To measure creativity and artistic talent.
To prove that intelligence is inherited.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax Psychology 2e reports that Binet was asked by the French government to develop an intelligence test to use on children to determine which ones might have difficulty in school. The purpose was identifying who could use help, not ranking the population, measuring creativity, or proving inheritance.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the original purpose of Binet's intelligence test

questionBank.prompt: A student reads that a classmate scored an IQ of 115 on a modern intelligence test. Which description of what that number means is most accurate, according to the APA Dictionary of Psychology?
options: The classmate answered 115 questions correctly on the test.
The classmate is guaranteed to succeed at any intellectual task.
The classmate earned a standard score on an intelligence test, with the average set at 100.
The classmate's mental age, measured in years, is 115.
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary defines IQ as a standard measure of an individual's intelligence level based on psychological tests, with the mean customarily 100 and most scores within fifteen points of it. It is a standardized score, not a raw count of correct answers, a guarantee of success, or a literal mental age in modern use.
questionBank.skill: Recalling what an IQ score represents

questionBank.prompt: Rosa's car battery dies in a cold parking lot. Instead of calling for help, she wraps the battery in a warm blanket, waits, and the car starts — a fix she learned from years of maintaining farm equipment, not from a manual. In Sternberg's triarchic theory, which kind of intelligence is Rosa showing?
options: Analytical intelligence — analyzing the problem step by step.
Practical intelligence — applying knowledge from experience to solve an everyday problem.
Linguistic intelligence — explaining the fix clearly to others.
General intelligence (g) — the single factor behind all tasks.
questionBank.explanation: Sternberg's practical intelligence is sometimes compared to street smarts — finding solutions that work in everyday life by applying knowledge based on experience, as OpenStax describes. Rosa's fix comes from experience, not from analyzing and comparing ideas (analytical), from language (linguistic), or from a single general factor (Spearman's g).
questionBank.skill: Applying Sternberg's practical intelligence to an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: A school newsletter announces that a new intelligence test 'tells you everything about a student's potential.' Which response best reflects what the evidence in this lesson supports?
options: True — intelligence tests measure the whole person.
False — the tests measure nothing useful at all.
Partly true — a single score predicts how someone's whole life will go.
Overstated — intelligence tests measure some real abilities, but no single number captures a person.
questionBank.explanation: IQ tests measure real abilities such as problem solving and reasoning, yet David Wechsler was himself suspicious of using a single score to capture all of intelligence, and OpenStax notes the question of test validity remains open. Option A overclaims what tests measure, B denies they measure anything, and C treats one score as a life verdict.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing an overclaim about what intelligence tests measure

questionBank.prompt: In the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart, identical twins raised apart showed higher correlations between their IQ scores than siblings or fraternal twins raised together. Which conclusion does this finding best support?
options: Intelligence is completely determined by genes.
Intelligence is completely determined by the environment.
Genes contribute to intelligence, while the environment also shapes it.
IQ scores change randomly and show nothing stable.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax reports the twin finding as revealing a genetic component to intelligence, while also noting psychologists who emphasize the developmental environment — and concluding that aspects of each idea are probably correct. The finding supports a genetic contribution, not complete genetic determination (A), environment-only (B), or randomness (D).
questionBank.skill: Analyzing twin-study evidence on genes and environment

title: Motivation
in30Seconds: Motivation is the internal process that directs and energizes behavior — the impetus, as the APA Dictionary of Psychology puts it, that gives purpose or direction to what we do. Some motivation is intrinsic, arising from pleasure in the activity itself; some is extrinsic, coming from outside rewards and punishments. Drives like hunger and thirst push us to restore balance; the need for achievement pushes us to do things well; goals give the energy a target. Real motivation is a mix, not a switch — and it is the why behind every action.
whyItMatters: Motivation is the closest thing psychology has to an answer for the question behind every other question: why do people do what they do? Academically, it connects the foundations of this course — learning, emotion, development, and personality — because each of those topics describes a different engine of behavior. Practically, understanding motivation changes how you read your own choices: why a task you love feels effortless, why a reward can drain the pleasure from a hobby, why a goal pulls you forward. And it matters honestly: motivation is rarely pure, and knowing that keeps you from misreading yourself and everyone around you.
learningObjectives: Define motivation as the internal processes that direct and energize behavior, and attribute the working definition to the APA Dictionary of Psychology and OpenStax Psychology 2e.
Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, using an original example of each.
Explain the drive idea — that needs arising from imbalance push behavior toward restoring balance — and name hunger, thirst, and achievement as motives.
Describe Maslow's hierarchy of needs, and explain why it is a theory rather than a law.
Explain how goals direct motivation, and analyze why real motivation is usually a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic forces.

collegeVersion.heading: What motivation is
collegeVersion.body: Psychologists define motivation as the internal process that directs and energizes behavior. The APA Dictionary of Psychology calls it the impetus that gives purpose or direction to behavior, and notes that it operates in humans at a conscious or unconscious level. OpenStax Psychology 2e states the same idea more simply: motivation describes the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal. The Noba Project's Motives and Goals module calls it the psychological driving force that enables action in the pursuit of a goal. Three ideas recur across the definitions. Motivation is internal — it lives in the person, not in the situation. It directs — it aims behavior at something. And it energizes — it supplies the push that turns possibility into action. Because motivation is internal, psychologists cannot observe it directly; they infer it from what people choose, how hard they try, and how long they persist. The study of motivation is behavior read backward: every action is evidence of the motive behind it.

collegeVersion.heading: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
collegeVersion.body: The most useful distinction in the field separates motivation that comes from inside the person from motivation that comes from outside. Intrinsic motivation is an incentive to engage in an activity that derives from pleasure in the activity itself, as the APA Dictionary puts it — you do the thing because doing it feels good or interesting. Original example: Keiko spends Saturday afternoons repairing old bicycles in her garage; nobody pays or asks her, and she keeps at it because untangling a stuck gear train is satisfying in its own right. Extrinsic motivation is an external incentive to engage in an activity, especially motivation arising from the expectation of reward or punishment. Original example: Tomás drives for a weekend delivery service; he does not especially enjoy city traffic, but the paycheck makes the hours worthwhile. OpenStax gives the same split: intrinsically motivated behaviors are performed for the personal satisfaction they bring, while extrinsically motivated behaviors are performed to receive something from others. The two kinds behave differently and can interact in surprising ways.

collegeVersion.heading: Needs, drives, and the push to restore balance
collegeVersion.body: A classic explanation of where motivation comes from is the drive idea. According to drive theory, as OpenStax presents it, deviations from homeostasis create physiological needs, and those needs produce psychological drive states that direct behavior toward restoring balance. A drive, in the APA Dictionary's terms, is a generalized state of readiness that motivates activity, usually created by deprivation of something needed. The clearest examples are the classic drive states of hunger and thirst: hunger pushes you to find and eat food; thirst pushes you to drink fluids. (The biology of those signals belongs to another subject; the point here is psychological — a felt state aims behavior at a goal.) Drives are not only bodily. Psychologists also study social motives, and among them the need for achievement stands out — the APA Dictionary defines it as a strong desire to accomplish goals and attain a high standard of performance and personal fulfillment, proposed by Henry Murray and investigated extensively by David McClelland. Original example: Amara does not care about the certificate at the end of her community coding course, but she refuses to submit a project she knows has a flaw; the pull is toward doing something well.

collegeVersion.heading: Maslow's hierarchy: a theory, not a law
collegeVersion.body: Abraham Maslow (1943) proposed a framework meant to span the whole range of motives, from biological to personal to social. His hierarchy of needs is usually drawn as a pyramid: at the base sit the physiological needs for survival; above them, needs for safety and security; then the need to belong and be loved; then esteem, the need for self-worth and confidence; and at the top, self-actualization, which Maslow described as achieving one's full potential. The organizing idea is that lower needs generally take priority: someone struggling to find enough food is unlikely to spend much energy wondering whether others admire them. The honest note: this is a theory, not a law. OpenStax records that Maslow's theory has been criticized for its subjective nature and its inability to account for real-world phenomena, and the ordering plainly fails sometimes — people pursue dignity, love, or meaning while basic needs go unmet, as hunger strikers show. Treat the pyramid as a map of the kinds of motives people have, not a strict checklist.

collegeVersion.heading: Goals, the honest note, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Motivation needs a target, and the target is a goal. The APA Dictionary defines a goal as the end state toward which an organism is striving — the purpose of an activity. The Noba Project adds that goals are fundamental guides for human behavior: a goal is the cognitive representation of a desired state. Stated simply: goals direct motivation — the clearer the goal, the more directly the energy has somewhere to go. First, motivation is a mix, not a switch. OpenStax is direct: in reality, our motivations are often a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and the nature of the mix changes over time. The overjustification effect shows why: an external reward added to an activity you already enjoy can weaken the intrinsic pull until the activity feels like work. Calling yourself intrinsically or extrinsically motivated as a fixed label misses how much the blend shifts with context. Second, the honest framing: motivation is the why behind every action. Ask why someone chose this, tried that hard, or quit early, and you are asking a motivation question; motivation, though invisible itself, is visible in the behavior it produces.

vocabulary.definition: The internal process that directs and energizes behavior; the impetus that gives purpose or direction to action, operating at a conscious or unconscious level.
An incentive to engage in an activity that comes from pleasure or interest in the activity itself, rather than from outside benefits.
An incentive to engage in an activity that comes from outside the person, such as an expected reward or the avoidance of punishment.
A generalized state of readiness that motivates activity, typically created by deprivation of something the organism needs, such as food or water.
The account of motivation holding that deviations from homeostasis create needs, which produce drive states that direct behavior toward restoring balance.
The tendency of an organism to maintain stable conditions across its physiological systems, such as body temperature or water levels.
A strong desire to accomplish goals and reach a high standard of performance and personal fulfillment; proposed by Henry Murray and studied extensively by David McClelland.
Abraham Maslow's 1943 theory that human motives range from basic physiological needs up to self-actualization, often drawn as a pyramid; a theory, not a law.
The end state toward which a person is striving; the purpose of an activity or endeavor.
The top tier of Maslow's hierarchy, in which a person strives to achieve their full potential.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Motivation is the engine of behavior — the internal push that points your actions at something and gives them power. Psychologists describe it as the process that directs and energizes what you do. Part of the push comes from inside: you do something because you enjoy it, like Keiko repairing bicycles for the fun of untangling gears. Part comes from outside: you do something for what it brings you, like Tomás driving deliveries for the paycheck. Some motives are built-in drives — hunger pushes you to eat, thirst pushes you to drink — and some are standards you hold yourself to, like the need to finish a job well. Goals give the engine a destination. And real motivation is almost never pure: it is a blend of inside and outside pulls that shifts with time and circumstance.
eli10.analogy: Think of a car. Motivation is the engine, and a goal is the destination in the navigation system. The engine supplies the power — how hard the car pushes forward — and the destination decides the direction. The engine runs on a fuel blend, and in people the blend is a mix of pleasure in the driving itself (intrinsic) and the rewards waiting where you arrive (extrinsic). A car with a full tank but no destination burns fuel pointlessly; a car with a destination but no engine goes nowhere. You need both, and the mix of fuels changes along the way.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down in two ways. A car's engine and its destination are separate things, but in people the same motive can be both the push and the aim — the joy of solving a puzzle can be the reason you start and the reward you finish for. And a car runs on a fixed fuel blend, while a person's motivation is unstable: the same activity can shift from pleasure to obligation when deadlines, pay, or prizes enter, and the mix changes over time. Motivation is also rarely a single engine — several motives usually push at once, sometimes in different directions.

workedExample: Jordan has been sketching comic pages every night for two years, purely because inventing characters is fun — intrinsic motivation, the pleasure of the activity itself. Then a local magazine offers to publish a monthly strip for a small fee. Suddenly the sketching has deadlines, an audience, and a check. For the first two months Jordan still enjoys it; by month four the evenings feel like work, and the urge to sketch for fun fades — the pattern OpenStax describes through the overjustification effect, where added external rewards can diminish intrinsic motivation. Meanwhile the usual drives still run, and the need for achievement shows up when a page comes out wrong and Jordan redoes it until the layout is right, not because the editor asked. The lesson of the example is that no motive switched off; the blend simply changed. Jordan's motivation is still a mix — the magazine pays, the drawing pleases, the standard pulls — and the mix will keep shifting with context.

commonMistakes.mistake: "I am an intrinsically motivated person."
commonMistakes.correction: Motivation is not a fixed personality label. The same person's blend of intrinsic and extrinsic forces shifts with the activity and the circumstances; OpenStax notes that motivations are often a mix of both factors that changes over time.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Rewards always make people want something more."
commonMistakes.correction: Not necessarily. In the overjustification effect, adding an external reward to an activity someone already enjoys can diminish intrinsic motivation, so the behavior may fade once the reward is gone.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Maslow's pyramid is a proven law of human behavior."
commonMistakes.correction: It is a theory, proposed by Abraham Maslow in 1943, and it has been criticized for its subjective nature and for failing to account for real-world cases where people pursue higher needs while basic needs go unmet.

commonMistakes.mistake: "If there is no visible reward, there is no motivation."
commonMistakes.correction: Motivation is internal and often operates below awareness — the APA Dictionary notes it works at a conscious or unconscious level. Hunger can push you to find food, and achievement can push you to redo flawed work, with no reward in sight.

compareContrast.distinction: The behavior can look identical — the difference is the source of the incentive. Intrinsic motivation comes from pleasure in the activity itself; extrinsic motivation comes from outside benefits such as rewards or avoided punishments.

A drive pushes from behind — a felt state of need, like hunger, that presses you toward food. A goal pulls from ahead — the desired end state you are aiming at, like a marathon finish line. Both direct behavior, but from opposite directions.

Drive theory explains the push of specific needs toward restoring balance; Maslow's hierarchy organizes the full range of human motives — biological, personal, and social — into a priority pyramid. They answer different questions about the same behavior.

Motivation directs and energizes behavior toward goals; emotion is the felt response to events. They constantly interact — fear can energize escape — but emotion is its own topic elsewhere in this course.

keyTakeaway: Motivation is the internal process that directs and energizes behavior — a shifting blend of intrinsic pleasure, extrinsic rewards, drives, and goals that is the why behind every action.

questionBank.prompt: According to the APA Dictionary of Psychology, which description best captures what motivation is?
options: The impetus that gives purpose or direction to behavior, operating at a conscious or unconscious level.
A reward or punishment delivered after a behavior to encourage or discourage it.
The biological process of growing and developing on a built-in timetable.
A relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge that results from experience.
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines motivation as the impetus that gives purpose or direction to behavior, operating at a conscious or unconscious level, and OpenStax points the same way. Option B describes external factors that can encourage or discourage behavior — not motivation itself; C describes maturation; D describes learning, both covered elsewhere in this course.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the APA Dictionary's working definition of motivation

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following is the clearest example of extrinsic motivation?
options: Keiko repairs bicycles on weekends because untangling the mechanics satisfies her.
Tomás drives weekend deliveries because he wants the paycheck.
Amara redoes a flawed coding project because her own standard demands it be right.
Jordan sketches comic pages because inventing characters is fun.
questionBank.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is an external incentive — motivation arising from the expectation of a reward, exactly Tomás's paycheck. Options A and D are intrinsic: the satisfaction comes from the activity itself. Option C is the need for achievement, an internal standard rather than an outside benefit.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing extrinsic motivation in an original example

questionBank.prompt: Maya skips breakfast, and by mid-morning she keeps thinking about the sandwich shop two blocks away and walks there instead of her usual route. Which concept best explains the shift in her behavior?
options: The need for achievement — she wanted to accomplish the walk to the shop.
Extrinsic motivation — the sandwich was an outside reward she expected to receive.
A drive state — hunger, created by a need, directed her behavior toward food.
Self-actualization — she was fulfilling her full potential as a walker.
questionBank.explanation: Hunger is a classic drive state: deprivation creates a need, and the resulting drive directs behavior toward restoring balance — here, finding food. Option A misreads a routine walk as an accomplishment goal, B confuses the goal object with an external incentive for a task, and D invokes Maslow's top tier, which has nothing to do with a skipped breakfast.
questionBank.skill: Applying the drive concept to an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: Nadia studies for her nursing exam partly because she finds the material genuinely interesting and partly because she needs a passing grade for her program. Her grandmother calls her intrinsically motivated; her roommate calls her extrinsically motivated. Which claim is best supported?
options: The roommate is right — any grade attached to studying makes the motivation purely extrinsic.
The grandmother is right — interest in the material makes the motivation purely intrinsic.
Both labels oversimplify — real motivation is usually a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic factors that changes over time.
Neither applies, because exam study is not a goal-directed behavior.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax is explicit: in reality, motivations are often a mix of both intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and the nature of the mix changes over time. Nadia's case shows both at once, so labeling her as one type oversimplifies. Option D is wrong because exam study is exactly a goal-directed behavior.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing whether motivation is purely intrinsic or extrinsic

questionBank.prompt: A community center pays volunteers a small hourly stipend to run its after-school reading program. The coordinator notices that children who were already enthusiastic about choosing books become less interested in reading on their own. Which concept from the lesson best explains this pattern?
options: Drive theory — the stipend created a need that the children tried to satisfy by reading less.
Maslow's hierarchy — the children moved down the pyramid toward physiological needs.
The need for achievement — the stipend lowered the children's performance standards.
The overjustification effect — adding an external reward can diminish intrinsic motivation for an activity someone already enjoys.
questionBank.explanation: The overjustification effect is the pattern OpenStax describes: intrinsic motivation is diminished when extrinsic motivation is given, which can create dependence on the reward. Options A, B, and C misapply drive theory, Maslow's hierarchy, and the need for achievement — none of which predicts that paying children for reading would reduce their interest in reading.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing an original scenario with the overjustification effect

title: Emotion
in30Seconds: Emotion is a complex reaction that involves the body, the mind, and behavior at once — a subjective state that combines physiological responses, cognitive appraisal, and expression. Psychologists distinguish emotions, which are short and tied to a specific trigger, from moods, which are long and diffuse. Classic theories disagree about the order of the parts, and the basic emotions — happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust — appear recognizable across cultures, even though display rules shape when people show them. The honest framing: emotion is data, not noise.
whyItMatters: Emotions run underneath nearly everything psychology studies — how you remember an event, how you decide, how you get along with other people. Academically, this lesson is the foundation: motivation, stress, and social psychology all build on the feeling states described here, and the theories of emotion are a clean introduction to how psychologists argue with evidence. Practically, understanding the components lets you read your own reactions — the racing heart, the quick judgment, the urge to act — as parts of one system instead of a mystery. And it matters honestly: if emotion is data, then learning to listen to it without letting it drive is a real skill, not self-help talk.
learningObjectives: Define emotion as a complex reaction involving physiological, cognitive, and behavioral components, and attribute the working definition to OpenStax Psychology 2e.
Name the six basic emotions from the classic Ekman list, and explain why lists of basic emotions vary by theory.
Distinguish emotion from mood, using an original example of each.
Explain the James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, and Schachter-Singer two-factor theories, describing how each orders the components of emotion.
Describe how emotion is expressed through faces and bodies, and explain how cultural display rules shape expression.
Analyze the framing of emotion as information rather than noise, using an original scenario.

collegeVersion.heading: What emotion is
collegeVersion.body: An emotion is a subjective state of being that we often describe as our feelings. That working definition comes from OpenStax Psychology 2e, which also says what an emotion is made of: emotions result from combining subjective experience, expression, cognitive appraisal, and physiological responses. In plainer terms, an emotion is a complex reaction involving the body, the mind, and behavior at once. The body contributes physiological responses — a racing heart, faster breathing, sweating. The mind contributes a cognitive appraisal — a quick judgment about how the situation affects you. Behavior contributes expression — the face, the voice, and the posture that carry the emotion outward. Honest caveat: psychologists have not settled on one perfect definition, and the order of the parts is still debated. The component account — body, mind, and behavior together — is the common thread across sources.

collegeVersion.heading: The three components: body, mind, and behavior
collegeVersion.body: Physiological: the body's automatic changes during an emotion — heart rate, breathing, sweat, muscle tension. Original example: as the exam begins, Priya's palms go damp and her heart hammers against her ribs before she has even read the first question. Cognitive: the appraisal — the evaluation of whether and how the situation matters to you. Original example: when the 7:42 train is late, Mira appraises the delay as free reading time and feels almost cheerful, while Jonas appraises the same delay as a ruined meeting and feels hot frustration. Same train, two appraisals, two emotions. Behavioral: the expression and action side — the smile, the frown, the slumped shoulders, the urge to flee. Original example: after the rejection email lands, Omar's shoulders drop, his voice goes flat, and he cancels the plans he had been looking forward to. The three run together so fast they usually feel like one thing — exactly what the classic theories argue about.

collegeVersion.heading: The basic emotions
collegeVersion.body: Paul Ekman's cross-cultural research found that certain facial expressions are recognized in very different cultures, which led to the idea of basic emotions. The classic list names six. Happiness: the felt state of joy or contentment. Sadness: the response to loss. Fear: the response to threat. Anger: the response to being blocked or wronged. Surprise: the response to the unexpected. Disgust: the response to something repulsive. The honest note: lists vary by theory. OpenStax presents seven universal expressions, adding contempt to the six, and some researchers, like Lisa Feldman Barrett, argue that emotions are constructed from experience rather than hardwired. Treat the six as the standard teaching list, not a final census.

collegeVersion.heading: The classic theories: what order do the parts come in?
collegeVersion.body: Three theories dominate the textbooks, and each answers the order question differently. The James-Lange theory, named for William James and Carl Lange, holds that emotions arise from physiological arousal: the body reacts first — heart racing, breathing fast — and the feeling of fear is your experience of that bodily reaction. The Cannon-Bard theory, developed by Walter Cannon and Philip Bard in response, holds that physiological arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently: you see the snake and feel fear at the same moment your body mobilizes, and neither causes the other. The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory holds that emotion has two factors — physiological arousal plus a cognitive label — and you interpret your arousal using the context; in their 1962 experiment, people injected with adrenaline reported euphoria or anger depending on how the person beside them behaved. Appraisal theories (Magda Arnold, Richard Lazarus) put the thought first — and the field has not declared a winner.

collegeVersion.heading: Emotion versus mood
collegeVersion.body: The words are used interchangeably in everyday speech, but psychologists draw a clean line. An emotion is a relatively intense affective state that occurs in response to something — short and specific. A mood is a prolonged, less intense affective state that does not occur in response to something specific — long and diffuse. Original example: Sam's jaw tightens and his voice rises when a driver cuts him off — an emotion, sharp and gone in minutes. His partner has felt flat and listless for three weeks with no single event behind it — that is a mood. Emotion is the weather; mood is the season.

collegeVersion.heading: Expression: faces, bodies, and culture
collegeVersion.body: Faces and bodies signal emotion. Recognition of basic facial expressions appears universal — Ekman's research in an isolated New Guinea community, and the finding that people born blind produce the same expressions, both point that way — and bodies carry emotion too, through posture, movement, and tone of voice. The honest note: expression varies by culture. Display rules are culturally specific standards for which emotions may be shown, when, and to whom. Matsumoto found that Americans expressed negative emotions like anger and fear both alone and in company, while Japanese participants mainly expressed them alone. The same feeling can wear different public faces in different places — recognition is universal, display is not.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: emotion is data, not noise
collegeVersion.body: Emotions look like interruptions — the flush of anger mid-meeting, the dread before a test — and it is tempting to treat them as static. The functional view says the opposite. The Noba Project's Functions of Emotions module, summarizing Tooby and Cosmides, describes emotions as rapid information-processing systems that help us act with minimal thinking. They evolved to handle recurring problems fast — flee, fight, help, reject, approach. An emotion is a message about what you value, what threatens you, what just changed — delivered fast and loud. The skill is not to silence the message but to read it: the knot in your stomach before a decision is information about what the decision means to you; the anger in an argument is information about a boundary crossed. Data, not noise.

vocabulary.definition: A subjective state of being — what we often describe as feelings — that combines physiological responses, cognitive appraisal, and expression; a complex reaction involving body, mind, and behavior at once.
The body's automatic physical changes during an emotion, such as changes in heart rate, breathing, or sweating.
The evaluation of how a situation affects you; the thought that helps determine which emotion you feel.
The outward display of an emotion through nonverbal and verbal behavior, including the face, voice, and posture.
The emotions thought to be recognized across cultures, classically listed as happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust.
A prolonged, less intense affective state that is not tied to a specific trigger, unlike an emotion.
Culturally specific standards that govern which emotions may be displayed, when, and to whom.
The theory that emotions arise from physiological arousal: the body reacts first, and the emotion is the experience of that reaction.
The theory that physiological arousal and emotional experience occur at the same time, independently.
The Schachter-Singer account holding that emotion combines physiological arousal with a cognitive label supplied by the context.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: An emotion is your whole self reacting at once — body, mind, and behavior. Your heart races while your thoughts size up the situation while your face does something about it. Psychologists call the three parts the physiological response, the cognitive appraisal, and the expression. The classic six — happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust — show up on faces in similar ways around the world, though different cultures have different rules about when it is okay to show them. Emotions are short and tied to something specific; moods are long and vague. The big theories argue about the order: does the body react and then you feel (James-Lange), do both happen at once (Cannon-Bard), or do you feel whatever your arousal plus the situation suggests (two-factor)? Nobody has won the argument outright.
eli10.analogy: Think of a car's dashboard. The check-engine light comes on, and you have two options: cover it with tape because the beeping is annoying, or read it as data — something under the hood needs attention. Emotions are the same: the rush of anger in an argument is a warning light about a boundary; the knot in your stomach before a choice is a signal about what the choice means to you. Tape over the lights and you lose the information; stare at them and you never drive. The skill is noticing the light, reading what it points to, and driving anyway.
eli10.analogyLimits: A dashboard light is a clean binary signal with a known meaning; an emotion is fuzzy, built from body, mind, and context at once, and can be misread — excitement and anxiety can feel identical in the body. A light never changes because you interpret it, but labeling an emotion can change the emotion itself, which is the two-factor insight. And the light's wiring is fixed, while emotions are shaped by culture, experience, and even the theories you happen to know.

workedExample: Ravi has a job interview at nine. As the panel enters, his heart pounds and his mouth goes dry — physiological response. His mind races through an appraisal: the interviewer's nod is friendly, this is going well. He hears his own voice stay steady and notices himself leaning forward — expression and behavior. Later, in the waiting room before the second round, the same pounding heart returns, and this time Ravi, remembering the two-factor theory, tells himself: this is excitement, not danger — and the feeling shifts. One honest footnote: when a question stings, he keeps his face neutral, because in his workplace culture showing frustration to an interviewer is not done — a display rule at work. The flutter in his chest was never noise; it was information about how much this mattered to him.

commonMistakes.mistake: Emotion and mood are the same thing — two words for one feeling.
commonMistakes.correction: An emotion is short, intense, and tied to a specific trigger; a mood is prolonged, less intense, and diffuse. The panic that spikes when a bus lurches is an emotion; the flatness that has followed you for weeks is a mood.

commonMistakes.mistake: The feeling comes first, and the body just follows.
commonMistakes.correction: The order is exactly what the classic theories dispute. James-Lange puts the body first; Cannon-Bard says body and feeling happen at once; two-factor adds the label. None of them supports the simple feeling-first story.

commonMistakes.mistake: A racing heart always means fear.
commonMistakes.correction: The same arousal can be labeled fear, excitement, or anger depending on the context — that is the two-factor insight. A pounding heart on a dark street reads as fear; a pounding heart on a dance floor reads as excitement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Since facial expressions are universal, everyone expresses emotion the same way.
commonMistakes.correction: Recognition appears universal, but display rules are cultural. What you feel and what you show are governed by different rules in different places.

commonMistakes.mistake: The goal is to not feel emotions at all.
commonMistakes.correction: Emotions are information-processing systems that evolved to help you act fast. The goal is to read the message, not to delete the messenger.

compareContrast.distinction: Emotion is short, intense, and tied to a specific trigger; mood is prolonged, less intense, and diffuse. Weather versus season.
James-Lange says physiological arousal comes first and the emotion follows from it; Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur at the same time, independently. Same snake, different orders.
The ability to recognize basic facial expressions appears universal, while the rules for showing emotions vary by culture. You can read the face; you cannot assume you know its rules.

keyTakeaway: Emotion is a complex reaction of body, mind, and behavior — short, specific, and full of information; the skill is reading it, not silencing it.

questionBank.prompt: A psychology text describes an emotion as a subjective state that combines several ingredients at once. Which set names those ingredients?
options: Physiological responses, cognitive appraisal, and expression
Memory, attention, and language
Reward, punishment, and habit
Sleep, hunger, and thirst
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax Psychology 2e describes emotions as resulting from the combination of subjective experience, expression, cognitive appraisal, and physiological responses — the body, the mind, and the behavior. Option B names cognitive processes, C names learning concepts, and D names drive states; none of them is the component set for emotion.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the three components of emotion from the working definition

questionBank.prompt: Lena's panic spikes when her bus lurches and fades within minutes, while her roommate has felt vaguely low for weeks with no single cause. Which pairing matches the psychology distinction?
options: Lena's panic is a mood; the roommate's low feeling is an emotion
Lena's panic is an emotion — intense and tied to a trigger; the roommate's low feeling is a mood — prolonged and diffuse
Both are moods, because both are feelings that last more than a minute
Both are emotions, because both involve feelings
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax distinguishes an emotion — a relatively intense affective state that occurs in response to something — from a mood — a prolonged, less intense state that does not occur in response to something specific. Option B matches exactly. A swaps the two; C and D collapse the distinction the lesson draws.
questionBank.skill: Applying the emotion-versus-mood distinction to a scenario

questionBank.prompt: Diego's heart is racing and his breathing is fast on a crowded dance floor. He looks around, decides the music and the friendly crowd mean excitement, and feels excited. Which theory best matches his experience?
options: James-Lange — his emotion caused his physiological arousal
Cannon-Bard — his emotion and his arousal happened simultaneously, with no labeling involved
Schachter-Singer two-factor — he labeled his physiological arousal using the context
Facial feedback — his smile produced the feeling on its own
questionBank.explanation: The two-factor theory holds that emotion combines physiological arousal with a cognitive label drawn from the context — exactly Diego's sequence: arousal, then a label from the scene, then the emotion. A reverses James-Lange's direction, B ignores the labeling step, and D names a different mechanism (facial feedback) that does not describe his reasoning.
questionBank.skill: Matching a scenario to the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory

questionBank.prompt: A hiker spots a coiled snake on the trail. According to the James-Lange theory, what happens as she sees it?
options: She feels fear at the same moment her body reacts, and the two are independent
She appraises the snake as dangerous first, and the appraisal produces both her arousal and her fear
She feels fear first, and her racing heart follows as a result of the feeling
Her body reacts first — racing heart, fast breathing — and the feeling of fear follows from that arousal
questionBank.explanation: The James-Lange theory asserts that emotions arise from physiological arousal: the body's reaction comes first, and the emotion is the experience of that reaction. Option A describes the Cannon-Bard theory, B describes appraisal-first views, and C reverses James-Lange's order.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a scenario through the James-Lange theory's ordering of components

questionBank.prompt: Ekman's cross-cultural research found that people in very different cultures can recognize certain facial expressions. Which conclusion fits the evidence in this lesson?
options: Recognition of basic facial expressions appears universal, but display rules shape when and how people actually show emotions
Facial expressions mean completely different things in every culture
Only people raised in the same culture can reliably read each other's faces
Facial expressions are learned entirely from media like film and television
questionBank.explanation: The lesson's evidence — Ekman's New Guinea research, the identical expressions produced by people born blind, and the display-rules findings (Matsumoto; Noba's Culture and Emotion module) — supports universal recognition plus cultural variation in display. Option B and C deny the universal side, and D denies both, which the blind-born finding contradicts.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating conclusions about universal recognition and cultural display rules

title: Social Psychology
in30Seconds: Social psychology is the study of how other people shape our thoughts, feelings, and behavior — through their actual presence, the ones we imagine, and the ones we only carry in mind. Its central claim is the power of the situation: context steers us more than we usually notice. Its big topics are attribution, attitudes, conformity, obedience, and group behavior. Classic studies by Solomon Asch, Stanley Milgram, and Philip Zimbardo showed ordinary people bending under social pressure. We are social animals with social minds.
whyItMatters: Social psychology sits at the meeting point of the individual and everyone else. Academically, it explains how the mind works in company — which is where minds actually work most of the time — and it connects to personality, emotion, and learning. Practically, it helps you read your own behavior: why you act differently in a crowd, why a team decision went wrong, why a first impression of a rude coworker may be a misread of a bad day. Forward-looking, the same principles show up in teamwork, public health campaigns, online communities, and leadership. The honest value is the biggest one: knowing that situations shape us is the first step toward choosing situations that bring out the best in us.
learningObjectives: Define social psychology using the attributed working definition and explain what actual, imagined, and symbolically represented presence means.
Explain the power-of-the-situation argument with an original example of context changing behavior.
Define attribution and attitude, and describe how each relates to behavior.
Name the major topic areas of social psychology — attribution, attitudes, conformity, obedience, and group behavior — with an original example of each.
Describe the historical studies of Solomon Asch, Stanley Milgram, and Philip Zimbardo in one line each, with findings attributed.
Evaluate why attitudes do not always predict behavior, using the distinction between explicit and implicit attitudes.

collegeVersion.heading: What social psychology is
collegeVersion.body: Social psychology is the study of how other people shape what we think, feel, and do. The working definition used here comes from Gordon Allport, carried in the APA Dictionary of Psychology: social psychology is the study of how an individual's thoughts, feelings, and actions are affected by the actual, imagined, or symbolically represented presence of other people. Actual presence is a friend in the room; imagined presence is the audience you picture while rehearsing alone; symbolized presence is the standard you carry, like a coach's voice on the last lap. OpenStax Psychology 2e: social psychology examines how people affect one another, and it looks at the power of the situation. The Noba Project's introduction module investigates the same ground: the ways other people affect our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Three authoritative sources, one object of study.

collegeVersion.heading: The big topics
collegeVersion.body: The field organizes around a handful of big questions. Attribution concerns inferences about the causes of behavior — the APA Dictionary: an inference regarding the cause of a person's behavior or an interpersonal event. Original example: Priya's coworker snaps at a customer, and Priya's first thought is rudeness; the coworker had just learned her father was hospitalized — the situational explanation never occurred to Priya. Attitudes are relatively enduring evaluations of objects, people, groups, issues, or concepts, ranging from negative to positive, per the APA Dictionary. Original example: Ravi quietly dislikes cilantro, and the evaluation colors every menu he reads, guiding his orders. Conformity is the adjustment of opinions, judgments, or actions to match other people or group standards; it has its own sibling lesson, so we name it here. Original example: at a concert, Delia claps along with the encore though she found the song merely fine. Obedience is behavior in compliance with a direct command, often from a person in authority, per the APA Dictionary. Original example: a new hire keeps the outdated spreadsheet template because the manager told her to, though a better one exists. Group behavior is what happens when two or more interdependent people influence one another through roles, norms, and shared goals (the APA Dictionary's social group). Original example: four students split a presentation into speaker, slide maker, timer, and fact-checker — a result none would have produced alone.

collegeVersion.heading: The situation idea
collegeVersion.body: The core argument of social psychology is that context shapes behavior powerfully. OpenStax is blunt: people will change their behavior to align with the social situation at hand. The field's signature demonstration of how much we underrate this is the fundamental attribution error, named by Ross (1977): overestimating character and underestimating situation when explaining behavior. Original example: at his cousin's wedding, Daniel — famously quiet in the office — delivers the toast with a confidence no colleague has ever seen: the celebration, the microphone, the room expecting a speech drew out behavior his personality alone would not predict. The honest note: the power of situations is real but not absolute. Reviews find the error varies with context and culture — stronger in individualistic societies, as OpenStax and the APA Dictionary both note. Situations steer us; they do not erase us.

collegeVersion.heading: Attitudes: evaluations that guide — sometimes
collegeVersion.body: An attitude is a relatively enduring evaluation of an object, person, group, issue, or concept on a negative-to-positive scale, often assumed to grow out of beliefs, emotions, and past behaviors (APA Dictionary). The natural assumption is that attitudes guide behavior — and often they do. But the honest note from the research: attitudes do not always predict action. The Noba Project's social cognition module explains that explicit attitudes, the ones we can report, can diverge from implicit attitudes — automatic evaluations beyond awareness — and both can lose to the situation. Original example: Mila tells a survey interviewer she strongly supports recycling, but late for a train she drops a plastic bottle into a general trash bin — no recycling bin is nearby. Her stated attitude and her action parted ways — not dishonesty, but the situation outrunning the evaluation.

collegeVersion.heading: The classic studies
collegeVersion.body: Three landmark studies anchor the field's history, each earning one line here as an attributed historical study. Solomon Asch's line-judgment studies of the 1950s showed that people often give an obviously wrong answer to match a unanimous group — conformity in action. Stanley Milgram's obedience research at Yale (1963) showed participants following an experimenter's instructions in what they believed was a learning study, further than most people predicted, and it raised lasting ethical questions about research with human participants. Philip Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment (1971) assigned student volunteers to guard and prisoner roles in a mock prison, showing the power of social roles, norms, and scripts. All three are described in OpenStax Psychology 2e (sections 12.2 and 12.4), and the Asch and Milgram studies appear in the Noba Project's conformity and obedience module. What they share is a finding that surprised their era: ordinary people, in ordinary situations, can behave in ways their friends would swear they never would.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The reality check that ties the lesson together: we are social animals with social minds. Being shaped by others is not a flaw in our design — it is the design. The same machinery that produces conformity also produces teamwork, cooperation, and kindness, and the same sensitivity to authority keeps classrooms and surgical teams functioning. When your own behavior surprises you, or someone else's does, look at the context before you write the verdict on character. The situation is part of the story — often the bigger part.

vocabulary.definition: The study of how an individual's thoughts, feelings, and actions are affected by the actual, imagined, or symbolically represented presence of other people.
The idea that context — roles, norms, and the presence of others — shapes behavior powerfully, often more than personality alone predicts.
An inference about the cause of a person's behavior or an interpersonal event.
The tendency to overestimate a person's traits and underestimate the situation when explaining their behavior.
A relatively enduring evaluation of an object, person, group, issue, or concept, ranging from negative to positive.
An evaluation a person can deliberately report when asked.
An automatic evaluation that can operate without awareness and may differ from what a person reports.
Behavior in compliance with a direct command, typically issued by a person in a position of authority.
The adjustment of one's opinions, judgments, or actions to match other people or group standards.
Two or more interdependent individuals who influence one another through roles, norms, and shared goals.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Social psychology is the study of how other people get inside your head. Not just the people in the room: the ones you imagine, and the ones you have never met whose standards you have absorbed. The field's big lesson is that your behavior is not only yours. The situation — who is watching, what role you are playing, what everyone else is doing — steers you more than you notice. That is why the same person can be patient at home and sharp at the office, and why a confident speaker can go quiet in a meeting. The classic studies by Asch, Milgram, and Zimbardo made this point by showing ordinary people doing surprising things under social pressure.
eli10.analogy: Think of a swimmer in a river. The swimmer brings skill, strength, and habits — that is the person. The river brings current, banks, and weather — that is the situation. Two equally strong swimmers can end up in completely different places because the rivers differ, and a strong swimmer can be carried along by a current they never noticed. Social psychology is the science of the river: it maps the currents of roles, norms, and other people that move us.
eli10.analogyLimits: The river only pushes one way; people push back. We choose situations, shape them, and sometimes swim hard against the current — a person under pressure still has agency. The same current moves different swimmers differently, so situations steer personality rather than erase it. And rivers have no intentions, while situations are made by people with expectations, which means they can be negotiated, questioned, and changed.

workedExample: Nadia usually studies alone, reading in silence. For the final exam she joins a study group at the library. Omar, the group's strongest student, announces a plan: each person explains one chapter aloud while the others listen. Nadia finds herself explaining the memory chapter out loud, matching the group's format — behavior she never shows at home. When Omar declares that forgetting is mostly a matter of time passing, Nadia, who read the interference research, hears herself nod along before she quietly corrects him. Same person, different situation: the group's norms, roles, and a confident leader changed how she studied and even what she said before she thought it through. Later she tells a friend she is a group person — a trait explanation for behavior the situation produced.

commonMistakes.mistake: Social psychology is just common sense about people.
commonMistakes.correction: Common sense explains events after the fact; social psychology tests its claims with systematic research. The classic studies produced results most people did not predict — that is why they became classics.

commonMistakes.mistake: If someone behaves badly, the explanation is simply who they are.
commonMistakes.correction: That is the fundamental attribution error. It undercounts the situation: the same person behaves very differently in different contexts, as the wedding-toast example shows.

commonMistakes.mistake: If I say I believe something, my behavior will follow.
commonMistakes.correction: Attitudes are real, but they do not always predict action. Explicit and implicit attitudes can diverge, and situations intervene, as Mila's recycling example shows.

commonMistakes.mistake: The classic studies prove people are weak-willed.
commonMistakes.correction: They demonstrate the power of situations, not a verdict on human character. Later research also finds these effects vary across cultures and contexts, so the honest lesson is about context, not about weakness.

compareContrast.distinction: Conformity is adjusting to match a group's standards, often with no one commanding anything; obedience is complying with a direct command from authority. You conform to a clapping crowd; you obey a supervisor's instruction.
An attitude is an evaluation; behavior is an action. Attitudes often guide behavior but do not always predict it, because situations and implicit attitudes intervene.

A dispositional explanation credits or blames a person's traits; a situational explanation points to context, roles, and pressures. The fundamental attribution error is the habit of choosing the first when the second fits better.

keyTakeaway: Social psychology studies how other people — present, imagined, or symbolized — shape our thoughts, feelings, and behavior; its core lesson is that situations steer us powerfully, and its honest promise is that noticing that power is the first step to using it well.

questionBank.prompt: The working definition used in this lesson — social psychology as the study of how an individual's thoughts, feelings, and actions are affected by the actual, imagined, or symbolically represented presence of other people — is attributed to which psychologist?
options: Gordon Allport
Solomon Asch
Stanley Milgram
Philip Zimbardo
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary of Psychology carries this as the definition of social psychology as stated by Gordon W. Allport. Asch studied conformity, Milgram studied obedience, and Zimbardo ran the Stanford prison experiment — all famous researchers, but none of them authored the working definition this lesson uses.
questionBank.skill: Attributing the working definition of social psychology to its originator

questionBank.prompt: Which scenario is social psychology best suited to study?
options: How a person's heart rate changes during a morning run.
How a student's answer choices shift after hearing several classmates answer first.
Which brain regions activate during deep sleep.
How a child's height changes across the school years.
questionBank.explanation: Social psychology examines how other people affect thoughts, feelings, and behavior, so a student changing answers under the influence of classmates is squarely in its territory. Heart rate, sleep brain activity, and growth are physiology and development, not social influence.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the scope of social psychology

questionBank.prompt: Renata snaps at a client, and her coworker Omar thinks, "She is just rude." Omar has not learned that Renata received upsetting news minutes earlier. Which concept does Omar's thinking best illustrate?
options: Obedience to authority.
The attitude-behavior gap.
The fundamental attribution error.
Conformity to group norms.
questionBank.explanation: Omar explains Renata's behavior with a trait — rudeness — while ignoring the situation. That is the fundamental attribution error: overestimating personal character and underestimating context when explaining another person's behavior. Obedience, the attitude-behavior gap, and conformity do not fit the scenario.
questionBank.skill: Applying the fundamental attribution error to a new scenario

questionBank.prompt: Mila tells a survey she strongly supports recycling, yet when she is late for a train and no recycling bin is nearby, she drops a plastic bottle into the general trash. What does this episode best illustrate?
options: Obedience to a direct command.
The fundamental attribution error.
Conformity with a group's standards.
That attitudes do not always predict behavior.
questionBank.explanation: Mila's stated attitude is pro-recycling, but the situation — rushing, no bin in reach — produced different behavior. This is the honest note of the attitudes research: explicit attitudes can diverge from action. The episode involves no command, no misattribution of causes, and no group standard to match.
questionBank.skill: Applying the attitude-behavior distinction

questionBank.prompt: In the school play, a normally shy student is cast as a loud, commanding general. By the final rehearsal she is striding across the stage and bellowing her lines. Which explanation best fits the lesson's account of this change?
options: The power of the situation: the role, the script, and the stage expectations shaped her behavior.
Her attitude toward acting changed permanently and now controls her behavior in every setting.
She obeyed a direct command to change her underlying personality.
She committed the fundamental attribution error about herself.
questionBank.explanation: The lesson's core argument is that situations — roles, norms, scripts — shape behavior powerfully, which is exactly what Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment demonstrated with assigned roles. Option B overstates attitude-behavior consistency, C mistakes role-playing for obedience, and D applies the wrong concept: the fundamental attribution error is about explaining others, not about what the situation produced.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a role-based behavior change using the power of the situation
