title: Conformity
in30Seconds: Conformity is adjusting your opinions, judgments, or actions to match a group — the working definition used by the APA Dictionary of Psychology. People conform for two main reasons: to be accepted by the group (normative influence), and because the group may hold information they lack (informational influence). In Asch's 1950s line-judgment studies, roughly three-quarters of participants went along with an obviously wrong group answer at least once. Conformity is not always bad — but the pull is real, and noticing it is half the skill.
whyItMatters: Academically, conformity is a gateway into social psychology: classic research — Asch's line studies, Deutsch and Gerard's two-influence distinction — meets everyday life in a single concept. Practically, it explains real puzzles: why a show of hands feels different from a secret ballot, why a new hire copies the office's unspoken habits, why a crowd that seems to know the way usually gets followed. And it matters forward-looking: the same process that lets teams coordinate smoothly can quietly steer a person toward choices they would never make alone. Noticing when the group is pulling is a life skill — it protects judgment in meetings, friendships, and every group you will join.
learningObjectives: Define conformity using the working definition from the APA Dictionary of Psychology.
Distinguish normative influence from informational influence, using an original example of each.
Explain what Solomon Asch's line-judgment studies showed about group pressure, and why conformity rates vary.
Describe how group size, unanimity, and culture affect the strength of conformity.
Analyze a real-world situation to identify which type of social influence is operating and whether going along helps or harms.

collegeVersion.heading: What conformity is
collegeVersion.body: The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines conformity as the adjustment of one's opinions, judgments, or actions so they become more consistent with other people's views or with the normative standards of a group or situation. In plainer words: you change what you do, say, or believe so that it lines up with the group. Two details do real work: conformity covers actions and beliefs, not just visible behavior, and it includes outward going-along (compliance) as well as private acceptance. Original example: at a staff meeting, Tariq privately thinks the new filing system is worse than the old one, but when everyone else approves it he says "fine, sounds good." His outward behavior changed while his private belief did not — that still counts as conformity.

collegeVersion.heading: Why people conform: belonging and information
collegeVersion.body: Psychologists trace most conformity to two motives, a distinction attributed to Deutsch and Gerard (1955). The first is belonging. People go along with a group because they are concerned about what others think of them: they do not want to stand out or look out of step, and fitting in brings acceptance. The second is information. Other people often know things we do not, especially in new or unclear situations, so the group's behavior becomes evidence about what is correct. Original example of belonging: Amara, at a dinner with coworkers she barely knows, orders the restaurant's special like everyone else — even though she would have chosen the pasta. Original example of information: Kenji starts at a new gym and has no idea where weights belong after use, so on his first day he copies exactly how the regulars rack them. One motive is about being liked; the other is about being right.

collegeVersion.heading: Normative versus informational influence
collegeVersion.body: The two motives get formal names. Normative social influence is conformity driven by the desire to fit in and be accepted by the group — you go along because you care what the group thinks of you. Informational social influence is conformity driven by the belief that the group is competent and has the correct information, and it is strongest when the situation is ambiguous. The distinction is attributed to Deutsch and Gerard (1955). Original example of normative influence: at a concert, when everyone around you stands for the slow song, you stand too even though you would rather stay seated — not because standing is correct, but because being the only seated person in a standing crowd feels like a statement. Original example of informational influence: visiting an unfamiliar city, you see a long lunchtime line outside a small restaurant and join it, reasoning that locals know which place is worth waiting for.

collegeVersion.heading: The classic study: Asch's line judgments
collegeVersion.body: In the 1950s, Solomon Asch had participants judge which of three comparison lines matched a target line while a roomful of confederates — people working for the researcher — deliberately gave obviously wrong answers; about 76% of participants conformed at least once by giving the wrong answer too (Asch, 1956). The honest note: conformity rates vary. Replications since show that conformity depends on age, gender, and sociocultural background, with some evidence that overall rates have fallen since Asch's era (Bond & Smith, 1996; Larsen, 1990; Walker & Andrade, 1996). The judgment task was easy and unambiguous, which is why the conformity that occurred is read as social pressure rather than confusion.

collegeVersion.heading: What raises and lowers conformity
collegeVersion.body: Three factors appear again and again in the research. Group size: the larger the majority, the more likely an individual is to conform — but only up to a point. In Asch's procedure, conformity increased with majority size up to about seven people and then leveled off; Noba's summary of replications describes increases up to roughly five confederates. Unanimity: if even one other person disagrees with the majority, conformity rates drop dramatically — in Asch's studies, a single dissenter brought conformity down to near zero. Culture: the conformity effect appears in virtually every culture studied, but it is stronger in collectivist countries such as Japan and China, where group goals and harmony are valued highly, than in individualistic countries such as the United States (Bond & Smith, 1996). A related factor: people conform much more when responses are public than when they are private — the reason elections use secret ballots.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The honest note: conformity is not always bad. Following a group's norms is a large part of how groups coordinate — people queue in order, speak quietly in libraries, put litter in a container. Original example: a classroom norm of raising a hand before speaking makes the class run smoother, and the new student who copies it is learning the group's code, not being weak. The honest framing: conformity is the glue and sometimes the trap. The same mechanism that bonds groups can steer individuals into harm when the perceived norm is wrong. Research on descriptive norms — what people believe most others actually do — shows that misperceived norms shape real behavior: students who overestimate peers' drinking tend to drink more to match a norm that does not exist (Neighbors et al., 2007). Original example: Sana guesses that everyone in her class goes out four nights a week and pushes herself to match that imagined pace. The group was the glue; the imagined norm was the trap. Conformity itself is neither good nor bad — what matters is what the group is pulling you toward, and whether the group actually knows.

vocabulary.definition: The adjustment of one's opinions, judgments, or actions so they become more consistent with the opinions, judgments, or actions of other people or with the normative standards of a group or situation.
Conformity driven by the desire to fit in, be accepted, and avoid standing out; the group's pull toward belonging.
Conformity driven by treating the group's behavior as evidence about what is correct, especially when the situation is unclear.
A group's unwritten standard for how members should behave or what they should believe.
What most people in a situation actually do, which people use as a guide when they are unsure how to behave.
Going along with a request or demand without privately accepting it; a temporary outward form of conformity.
The tendency for a group majority to pull an individual's judgment toward its own, demonstrated in Solomon Asch's line-judgment studies.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Conformity is going along with the group — changing what you do, say, or believe so it matches everyone else. You do it for two reasons. Sometimes you want to be accepted, so you match the group to fit in; that is normative influence. Sometimes you genuinely do not know what is right, so you copy people who seem to; that is informational influence. It is one of the most ordinary things humans do. In a famous experiment from the 1950s, most people gave an obviously wrong answer at least once, just because everyone around them had. But conformity is not automatically bad: following the group can be smart when the group knows the way, and harmful when the group is wrong. The skill is noticing when it is happening.
eli10.analogy: Think of a standing ovation. One person rises and you stay seated, no problem. Two more stand and you start wondering if you missed something. By the time most of the hall is on its feet, staying seated feels like a public statement — so you stand too, even though you thought the show was only okay. That is conformity in miniature: the bigger and more united the crowd, the stronger the pull, and you often go along before you have decided to.
eli10.analogyLimits: A standing ovation is over in seconds, costs you nothing, and never changes what you privately believe. Real conformity is slower and quieter: it can shift your actual judgment, last for years, and operate without you noticing. And unlike an ovation, where everyone can see you, some of the strongest conformity happens in private, where nobody is watching you at all.

workedExample: Maya is in a study group preparing for a statistics exam. She works a practice problem and gets C. The other four students all got B. She rechecks her arithmetic — still C. But the group is confident and has been right all semester, so part of her assumes she must be missing something: that is informational influence, using the group as evidence. Another part of her simply does not want to be the only person who is wrong out loud in front of four people: that is normative influence, the pull to be accepted. Maya writes down B. Later, alone, she works the problem again and finds the step she had done correctly — C was right. Her behavior conformed while her belief never did, a textbook case of outward going-along without private acceptance, which is exactly what the working definition of conformity allows.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Only timid or weak-willed people conform."
commonMistakes.correction: Everyone conforms sometimes. In Asch's studies, roughly three-quarters of participants went along with an obviously wrong group answer at least once. Conformity is a normal response to being in a group, not a character flaw.

commonMistakes.mistake: "If I still privately disagree, it was not conformity."
commonMistakes.correction: Conformity includes temporary outward going-along as well as private acceptance, per the APA Dictionary's definition. Agreeing aloud while doubting inside — compliance — is still conformity.

commonMistakes.mistake: "The bigger the group, the more people conform, without limit."
commonMistakes.correction: Conformity rises with majority size only up to a point — roughly five to seven people — and then levels off. Adding more members does not keep increasing the pull.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Asch proved that people cave in almost every time."
commonMistakes.correction: About 76% conformed at least once, but that is not the same as conforming on every trial, and later research shows rates vary with age, background, and whether responses are public or private. One dissenter can drop conformity to near zero.

compareContrast.distinction: Both produce going along with the group, but normative influence is about belonging — fitting in and avoiding ridicule — while informational influence is about accuracy — treating the group as a source of correct information, especially when the situation is ambiguous. The distinction is attributed to Deutsch and Gerard (1955).

Conformity is the broad adjustment of opinions, judgments, or actions toward a group's standard, and it can include genuine private acceptance. Compliance is the narrower case: going along with a request or demand without privately accepting it.
People conform much more when their answers are given aloud in front of the group than when they respond privately — which is why elections use secret ballots to reduce the pressure of conformity.

keyTakeaway: Conformity is adjusting what you do, say, or believe to match a group — driven by the pull to belong and the pull to be right. It is neither good nor bad on its own; what matters is what the group is pulling you toward.

questionBank.prompt: According to the working definition used by the APA Dictionary of Psychology, what is conformity?
options: The adjustment of one's opinions, judgments, or actions so they become more consistent with the standards of a group or situation.
An automatic reflex in which people copy any nearby person's movements.
A personality trait that makes some people unusually agreeable.
Changing behavior only when an authority figure gives a direct order.
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary defines conformity as the adjustment of one's opinions, judgments, or actions so they become more consistent with the opinions, judgments, or actions of other people or the normative standards of a group. Option B describes automatic imitation, not conformity; C mistakes a situational process for a personality trait; and D describes obedience to authority, a different form of social influence.
questionBank.skill: Recalls the working definition of conformity and rejects the imitation, trait, and obedience look-alikes.

questionBank.prompt: In Solomon Asch's line-judgment studies from the 1950s, participants sometimes gave obviously wrong answers because confederates had given them first. Which statement about the results is accurate?
options: Participants conformed on every trial once the group had answered.
About three-quarters of participants conformed at least once by giving the wrong answer.
Participants conformed only when the correct answer was genuinely unclear.
Conformity occurred only when participants wrote their answers privately.
questionBank.explanation: Asch found that about 76% of participants conformed at least once, even though the line judgment was easy and unambiguous — which is why the effect is read as social pressure rather than confusion (options A and C are both wrong for this reason). Option D reverses the finding: conformity was more likely when answers were public, not private.
questionBank.skill: Checks understanding of Asch's core finding, including the 76% figure and why the easy task rules out ambiguity.

questionBank.prompt: On her first day at a new office, Priya sees everyone in the kitchen put used mugs in the left sink, although a sign above the right sink says "Mugs here." Unsure where the dishes actually go, she puts her mug in the left sink with everyone else's. Which type of social influence is mainly operating?
options: Obedience, because a posted sign issued an instruction.
Conversion, because she now privately believes the left sink is correct.
Informational influence, because she treats her coworkers' behavior as evidence of the correct practice.
Normative influence, because she wants to be accepted by her new coworkers.
questionBank.explanation: Priya is uncertain, and she uses the group's behavior as evidence about what is correct — the defining pattern of informational influence, which is strongest in ambiguous situations. Obedience requires a demand from an authority figure, which a sign does not make; conversion is private acceptance, which the scenario never establishes; and normative influence, about being accepted, is not the main motive here.
questionBank.skill: Applies the normative-versus-informational distinction to an original scenario with an ambiguous norm.

questionBank.prompt: A teacher asks the class to choose between two field-trip options by a show of hands. Dev prefers Option 2, but when nearly every hand goes up for Option 1, he raises his hand for Option 1 too. Based on the research in this lesson, how would a secret written ballot most likely change this situation?
options: It would not change anything, because conformity is automatic and identical whether responses are public or private.
It would increase conformity, because writing an answer is a stronger commitment than raising a hand.
It would make Dev more likely to conform, since the majority's choice would still be visible when the ballots are counted.
It would reduce conformity, because people conform much more when their responses are public than when they are private.
questionBank.explanation: The public-versus-private finding is the key: conformity is much more likely when responses are made aloud in front of others and much less likely when they are private — the reasoning behind secret ballots in elections. Option A denies the finding, B reverses the direction, and C confuses a private ballot with a public one, since individual choices are not visible during a secret vote.
questionBank.skill: Applies the public-versus-private responding finding to explain why secret ballots reduce conformity.

questionBank.prompt: Which situation best illustrates the honest note that conformity is not always bad?
options: A hiker on an unfamiliar trail follows the footsteps left by earlier hikers to find the way back to the parking lot.
A student changes a correct answer on an exam because the person next to her chose a different letter.
A driver runs a red light because the car in front did.
A concertgoer stands for the encore even though she privately thought the performance was mediocre.
questionBank.explanation: The hiker uses the group's behavior as information that genuinely helps — a case of informational conformity with a good outcome, illustrating that going along is not automatically harmful. Options B and C show conformity steering people toward harm, and D shows conformity with no benefit at all, so none of them supports the honest note.
questionBank.skill: Applies the honest note that conformity can be helpful, separating beneficial informational conformity from harmful or pointless examples.

title: Stress
in30Seconds: Stress is the body's response to demands or threats. The triggers — stressors — range from daily hassles to major life events to chronic strain. In a real emergency the alarm is useful: Walter Cannon named it the fight-or-flight response, and Hans Selye mapped its longer course as the general adaptation syndrome. The alarm gets expensive when it keeps ringing: chronic stress wears on the body. Not all stress is bad, though. Selye called the beneficial kind eustress. Stress is the body's alarm system — useful, and costly when overused.
whyItMatters: Stress is not a classroom abstraction; it is the body's oldest alarm system, and everyone lives with it. Academically, the topic connects psychology to biology: fight-or-flight and the general adaptation syndrome are the bridge between what you feel and what your body does. Practically, understanding stress changes how you read your own experience — a racing heart before a presentation runs on the same machinery that once fueled a sprint from a predator, and knowing that makes the feeling less mysterious. It also gives you a steadier frame for health claims: chronic stress is real, and so is the honest point that not all stress is harmful. How people manage stress belongs to the next topic; this lesson is the foundation it builds on.
learningObjectives: Define stress as the body's response to demands or threats, and attribute the working definition to Hans Selye.
Distinguish daily hassles, major life events, and chronic strain as types of stressors, with an original example of each.
Explain the fight-or-flight response, name Walter Cannon as the researcher who identified it, and analyze why the response often mismatches modern life.
Describe the three stages of Selye's general adaptation syndrome — alarm, resistance, and exhaustion.
Explain, factually, how chronic stress wears on the body, and distinguish eustress from distress with an original example.

collegeVersion.heading: What stress is
collegeVersion.body: The working definition is response-based: stress is the body's reaction to demands or threats. Hans Selye, the endocrinologist who pioneered stress research, defined stress as the response of the body to any demand, whether caused by pleasant or unpleasant conditions (Selye, 1976). The APA Dictionary of Psychology agrees: stress is the physiological or psychological response to internal or external stressors, touching nearly every body system. The word response is the heart of it — stress is what the body does about the event, not the event itself. Original example: Maya's phone buzzes with the acceptance email she has awaited for months; her heart pounds — the identical rush she felt last month when a stranger's car slid through the intersection in front of her. Good news and near-miss: one body, same alarm.

collegeVersion.heading: Stressors: what sets off the alarm
collegeVersion.body: A stressor is any event, force, or condition that results in physical or emotional stress. Stressors come in three families. Daily hassles are the minor irritations of ordinary life, and they build on one another, leaving people just as stressed as major events (Kanner, Coyne, Schaefer, & Lazarus, 1981). Original example: Priya's bus is late, her coffee lid pops off in her bag, and the office printer jams twice — nothing catastrophic, everything cumulative. Major life events are changes that demand significant readjustment, from moving house to a new job to a divorce (Holmes & Rahe, 1967). Original example: Marta and her partner move to a new city the same month both start new jobs — a chosen move, and still a stretch of stress. Chronic strain is the third family: conditions that persist over an extended period — long-term unemployment, unrelenting caregiving. Original example: Deniz has commuted three hours a day for two years to a warehouse job he cannot afford to leave.

collegeVersion.heading: The stress response: fight-or-flight
collegeVersion.body: Walter Cannon, a Harvard physiologist, first articulated and named the body's immediate reaction to a perceived threat: the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932). Faced with danger, the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal glands flood the body with epinephrine and norepinephrine: the heart speeds up, breathing quickens, pupils dilate, blood flows to the muscles, and digestion slows. The point is energy mobilization — the body prepares to fight or flee. Original example: Nia is crossing the street when a car runs the red light and swerves toward her; within a second her heart pounds and her breath shortens as she jumps back onto the curb. The honest note: this machinery is ancient, tuned for physical emergencies like predators, falls, and fights. Most modern stressors — a deadline, an argument, an inbox — do not call for fighting or fleeing, so the alarm rings with no physical action to follow.

collegeVersion.heading: The general adaptation syndrome: Selye's three stages
collegeVersion.body: Selye asked what happens when stress does not end quickly. His answer, the general adaptation syndrome (GAS), describes three stages of responding to prolonged stress (Selye, 1936; 1976). The alarm reaction is the body's immediate mobilization on facing a threat — roughly the fight-or-flight response. Original example: a lifeguard hears a scream from the pool and is instantly alert, heart racing. The stage of resistance follows if the stressor continues: the initial shock wears off, the body adapts and keeps functioning, yet remains on alert, ready to respond with less intensity. Original example: by the second week of final exams, the first-day panic has faded, but the student sleeps lightly and stays keyed up. Exhaustion arrives if the stressor drags on long enough: adaptation fails, resources are depleted, and the body's resistance breaks down — illness and disease become more likely. Original example: after five months of caring for a sick parent, Rosa feels wrung out, sleeps poorly, and catches every cold that passes through her household.

collegeVersion.heading: Stress and health: when the alarm keeps ringing
collegeVersion.body: The stress response is built for short emergencies, not for years of low-grade ringing. When the reactions that compose it are chronic, or frequently exceed normal ranges, they produce cumulative wear and tear on the body (McEwen, 1998). The mechanisms are concrete: sustained elevated levels of the stress hormone cortisol can weaken immune system functioning, leaving a person more open to infection and disease, and blood pressure that stays high under prolonged strain can take a toll on the heart. Original example: a bakery owner running a six-day-a-week shop for years is winded on the stairs and catches every flu his staff brings in — the bill for an alarm that has not fully stopped ringing since he opened. What people do about chronic stress — coping — is its own topic; this lesson only describes what the alarm does.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note: eustress, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Not all stress is bad. Selye pointed out that stress can be a positive, motivating force, and he gave the good kind a name: eustress, from the Greek eu, meaning good (Selye, 1974). The APA Dictionary defines eustress as the positive stress response that comes from challenging but attainable and worthwhile tasks, generating fulfillment and high performance. Original example: a violinist feels a flutter of nerves before her first solo recital and uses the extra energy to play with more focus and finish stronger than in rehearsal. The harmful kind, distress, overwhelms. That leads to the honest framing of this lesson: stress is the body's alarm system. It is useful because it mobilizes you in genuine emergencies, and expensive because every alarm costs something — the bill comes due when it rings too often or too long. Stress is not the enemy. It is a tool with running costs.

vocabulary.definition: The body's physiological and psychological response to demands or threats — the working definition, attributed to Hans Selye, covers any demand, pleasant or unpleasant.
Any event, force, or condition that results in physical or emotional stress; stressors include daily hassles, major life events, and chronic strain.
The minor irritations and annoyances of everyday life that build on one another and can leave people just as stressed as major events.
A stressor that persists over an extended period, such as long-term unemployment or unrelenting caregiving demands.
The rapid, whole-body arousal pattern first articulated and named by Walter Cannon, in which the sympathetic nervous system mobilizes the body to fight a threat or flee from it.
Hans Selye's three-stage account of the body's response to prolonged stress: alarm reaction, stage of resistance, and stage of exhaustion.
The beneficial kind of stress, named by Selye, arising from challenging but attainable tasks and associated with fulfillment and high performance.
The harmful kind of stress, in which demands overwhelm the body's ability to adapt and performance, well-being, and health decline.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Stress is the body's alarm system, and the alarm does one job: it tells you something demands your attention. When it sounds, your heart speeds up, your breath quickens, and your muscles tense — that rush is fuel, and it is genuinely useful when the danger is real. The catch is that the alarm was designed for a world of immediate physical dangers: predators, falls, fights. Modern life sets it off with deadlines, arguments, and inboxes — situations where neither fighting nor fleeing helps, so the fuel gets spent on nothing. Ring the alarm constantly and it wears on the body, the way a doorbell that never stops eventually wears on the house. And the alarm is not always bad news: eustress is the good kind, the buzz from challenges you chose, which sharpens you instead of draining you.
eli10.analogy: Think of a smoke detector. A working one sits quietly for years, then screams the instant smoke appears — that is its job, and a screaming detector in a real fire is a lifesaver. Stress is the body's smoke detector: it senses a demand or threat and raises the alarm with a burst of energy and alertness. A home needs its detector; a body needs its alarm.
eli10.analogyLimits: A smoke detector can be silenced with a button or have its battery removed; the body's stress alarm cannot be switched off at will — once a threat is perceived, the response runs on its own. A detector signals one clear danger, while stress responds to anything appraised as demanding, pleasant or unpleasant. And a detector that goes off constantly is merely annoying, while a constantly ringing stress alarm does measurable wear on the body. The detector is also a device you can calibrate; the body's alarm is largely automatic, which is why understanding it matters.

workedExample: Leo, a night-shift nurse, hears a crash from the waiting room at 2 a.m. Instantly his heart pounds and his breath shortens — the fight-or-flight response Walter Cannon described, mobilizing energy before Leo has even decided what to do. The crash was a vending machine tipping over; no one is hurt, and the arousal fades within minutes: an alarm that rang, did its job, and stopped. Leo's other stressor does not stop. For a year, his mother's care has fallen on him, and the demands are unrelenting. Early on, the constant worry kept him wired — an alarm reaction that never quite switched off. Over the months his body adapted, sleeping lightly and staying on edge — Selye's stage of resistance. Lately he wakes exhausted, catches every cold that moves through the ward, and snaps at colleagues; his resources are running down, the stage of exhaustion. The same alarm that saved the vending-machine moment is wearing him out by never fully silencing. The lesson is not that stress is bad. It is that the alarm is useful in emergencies and expensive when it never stops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stress is just a feeling of being overwhelmed or anxious.
commonMistakes.correction: The feeling is only the part you notice. Stress is a whole-body response — physiological and psychological — involving changes in nearly every system of the body, as the APA Dictionary describes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only bad events cause stress.
commonMistakes.correction: Selye's definition covers any demand, pleasant or unpleasant. A wedding, a promotion, or a long-awaited move can trigger the same response as a setback — which is exactly why the body, not the event's label, defines stress.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fight-or-flight means you literally fight or run away every time.
commonMistakes.correction: It is the body's arousal pattern — heart, breath, muscles — preparing for physical action. Most modern stressors call for neither fighting nor fleeing, so the response fires with no physical action to match.

commonMistakes.mistake: All stress is harmful and should be avoided.
commonMistakes.correction: Eustress, from challenging but attainable tasks, is beneficial and energizing. The wear-and-tear story belongs to chronic stress — the alarm ringing too often or too long — not to stress itself.

compareContrast.distinction: Both are stress, but eustress comes from challenging yet attainable demands and fuels fulfillment and performance, while distress overwhelms the body's capacity to adapt and drains performance and health.

Acute stressors are brief focal events, like a near-miss on the street; chronic stressors persist over a long period, like a years-long grinding commute, and it is the chronic kind that produces cumulative wear and tear.

compareContrast.b: The alarm reaction of the GAS
compareContrast.distinction: Both describe the body's immediate mobilization in the face of a threat, but fight-or-flight names the sympathetic arousal itself, while the alarm reaction is the opening stage of Selye's longer three-stage sequence of responding to prolonged stress.

keyTakeaway: Stress is the body's alarm system: a useful, whole-body response to demands and threats that becomes expensive when it rings too often or too long — and, as Selye's eustress shows, not every alarm is bad news.

questionBank.prompt: A psychology text says stress is the body's response to any demand, whether pleasant or unpleasant. Which researcher is the source of this working definition?
options: Walter Cannon
Richard Lazarus
Hans Selye
Sigmund Freud
questionBank.explanation: The response-based definition comes from Hans Selye, the endocrinologist who defined stress as the response of the body to any demand (Selye, 1976), as OpenStax Psychology 2e reports; the APA Dictionary also credits Selye with first describing stress. Walter Cannon named the fight-or-flight response, not the definition of stress itself; Freud and Lazarus are not the source of this definition.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the researcher behind the working definition of stress

questionBank.prompt: Which researcher first articulated and named the fight-or-flight response?
options: Hans Selye
John Watson
William James
Walter Cannon
questionBank.explanation: Walter Cannon, a Harvard physiologist, first articulated and named the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932), per OpenStax Psychology 2e, and the APA Dictionary's entry records that it was first described by Cannon. Selye developed the general adaptation syndrome and the eustress concept; Watson is associated with behaviorism and James with early American psychology, and neither named this response.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the attribution of the fight-or-flight response

questionBank.prompt: Priya's morning is a string of small frustrations: the bus is late, her coffee lid pops off in her bag, and the office printer jams twice before her first meeting. Which term best describes these stressors?
options: Daily hassles
Major life events
Chronic strain
Eustress
questionBank.explanation: Daily hassles are the minor irritations and annoyances of ordinary life that build on one another and can leave people just as stressed as major events (Kanner et al., 1981), as OpenStax Psychology 2e describes. A late bus and a jammed printer are irritations, not life changes; nothing here persists over a long period, so chronic strain does not fit; and eustress is beneficial stress, not frustration.
questionBank.skill: Classifying stressors by type in an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: Rosa has cared for her sick mother for five months. The first weeks left her wired and sleepless; now the initial shock has faded and she functions — but she stays on edge, sleeps lightly, and feels constantly keyed up. According to Selye's general adaptation syndrome, which stage is Rosa in?
options: The alarm reaction
The stage of resistance
The stage of exhaustion
The fight-or-flight response
questionBank.explanation: The stage of resistance is when the initial shock of the alarm reaction wears off and the body adapts to the stressor while remaining on alert at a reduced intensity (Selye, 1936; 1976) — Rosa's wired-and-sleepless first weeks were the alarm reaction, and her current adapted-but-on-edge state is resistance. Exhaustion is the later stage when adaptation fails and resources are depleted; fight-or-flight is the immediate arousal pattern, not one of the three GAS stages.
questionBank.skill: Applying the stages of the general adaptation syndrome to a scenario

questionBank.prompt: Maya feels a flutter of nerves before her first solo recital, and the extra energy helps her play with more focus and finish stronger than in rehearsal. Which concept best describes her experience?
options: Eustress
Distress
Chronic stress
The exhaustion stage
questionBank.explanation: Eustress is the positive stress response from challenging but attainable and worthwhile tasks, generating fulfillment and high performance; Selye coined the term, and the APA Dictionary defines it that way. Distress is the overwhelming kind of stress, chronic stress persists over time, and the exhaustion stage is the GAS stage of depleted adaptation — none of them fits a nervous-but-focused performance that goes well.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing eustress in an original scenario

provenance.transformation: The working definition of stress was verified against OpenStax Psychology 2e Section 14.1 (read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL) and the APA Dictionary of Psychology entries for stress, stressor, fight-or-flight response, general adaptation syndrome, and eustress (read via the dictionary's public content API). Stressor types and the Holmes-Rahe/Kanner background were verified against Section 14.2; the chronic-stress wear-and-tear facts against Section 14.3. Attribution claims (Selye for the definition, GAS, and eustress; Cannon for fight-or-flight) follow the sources. The mismatch-between-alarm-and-modern-life point is presented as an honest interpretive framing, not a research statistic. All examples, scenarios, and practice questions are original to this lesson.

title: Coping
in30Seconds: Coping is the effort to manage stress: the mental and behavioral moves people use to handle a situation's demands and the feelings those demands create. Psychologists sort coping into two families, a distinction introduced by Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman: problem-focused coping changes the problem, emotion-focused coping changes the feeling. Planning, seeking support, reframing, distraction, and avoidance are familiar moves, and avoidance helps only in the short term. What works depends on the fit between the move and the situation. Coping manages stress — it does not eliminate it.
whyItMatters: Coping is where the science of stress meets ordinary life. Everyone faces deadlines, losses, conflicts, and changes, and the strategies people reach for shape how those demands land. Academically, the problem-focused and emotion-focused distinction is one of the most influential ideas in stress research, and it reappears across psychology courses, from health psychology to clinical foundations. Practically, knowing the difference between changing a problem and changing a feeling gives you a clearer read on your own habits — and more options when a strategy stops working. The honest notes matter too: there is no one right way, and coping manages stress rather than erasing it. Other people are part of the toolkit: social support helps people cope.
learningObjectives: Define coping as the mental and behavioral efforts people use to manage stress and its demands, and attribute the problem-focused versus emotion-focused distinction to Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman.
Distinguish problem-focused coping from emotion-focused coping — changing the problem versus changing the feeling — with an original example of each.
Identify and explain five common coping strategies — planning, seeking support, reframing, distraction, and avoidance — and explain why avoidance helps only in the short term.
Explain how the fit between a coping strategy and the situation affects whether coping works, using an original example.
Describe how social support helps people cope, and evaluate the honest framing that coping manages stress rather than eliminating it.

collegeVersion.heading: What coping is
collegeVersion.body: Coping is what people do about stress. The working definition used in this lesson: coping is the mental and behavioral efforts a person uses to manage stress and its demands. OpenStax Psychology 2e puts it as mental and behavioral efforts we use to deal with problems relating to stress, and the APA Dictionary of Psychology describes coping as the use of cognitive and behavioral strategies to manage the demands of a situation when these are appraised as taxing or exceeding one's resources — or to reduce the negative emotions and conflict caused by stress. Two parts of that definition do the work. First, coping is effort: it is something a person does, not something that happens to them. Second, coping targets both the demand itself and the feelings it creates. Original example: when the repair bill for his van arrives, Tomás calls three garages for quotes and sets up a payment plan — efforts aimed at the demand. He also tells himself the van is safe and the bill is a one-time hit — an effort aimed at the feeling. Both are coping.

collegeVersion.heading: The two families: problem-focused and emotion-focused
collegeVersion.body: Psychologists usually sort coping into two families, a distinction Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman introduced in 1984. Problem-focused coping attempts to manage or alter the problem that is causing the stress — the stressor itself. Emotion-focused coping attempts to change or reduce the negative emotions associated with stress. The difference is the target: change the problem, or change the feeling. Original example: Priya's landlord raises her rent. Problem-focused moves: she researches comparable apartments, writes a polite letter asking for a smaller increase, and tours cheaper units. Emotion-focused moves: she vents to her sister, reminds herself the family has managed tighter years, and cooks a favorite meal to settle her nerves. She is coping either way — the two families just aim at different targets. As OpenStax notes, many stressors elicit both kinds, often at the same time.

collegeVersion.heading: Five familiar strategies
collegeVersion.body: Within those two families sit the moves people actually make. Planning is problem-focused: mapping concrete steps to change the situation. Original example: a graduate student facing a thesis deadline breaks the remaining work into a week-by-week plan with a daily writing target. Seeking support means turning to other people for practical help, advice, or comfort. Original example: a new parent asks their sibling to cover one night shift and talks through feeding worries with a friend. Reframing is emotion-focused: construing the stressor differently without changing its objective level of threat. Original example: a nurse assigned to a less convenient shift tells herself the new hours let her attend her daughter's evening matches — the schedule is unchanged, the meaning is different. Distraction is emotion-focused: temporarily turning attention away from the stressor. Original example: a firefighter awaiting the result of a certification appeal spends the evening rewatching a favorite series instead of refreshing the email. Avoidance means disengaging from the stressor and averting attention from it — skipping the exam, ignoring the bill, withdrawing from the argument. The honest note: avoidance can reduce stress in the short term and keep anxiety from becoming overwhelming, but it does not address the problem, so the stressor tends to return, often bigger.

collegeVersion.heading: What makes coping work: the fit
collegeVersion.body: Coping is not a menu where some items are always right. What makes a strategy work is the fit between the strategy and the situation. Lazarus and Folkman proposed that problem-focused coping is used primarily when a person appraises the stressor as within their capacity to change, while emotion-focused coping predominates when the stressor is appraised as beyond their control — and OpenStax adds that emotion-focused coping is more effective for uncontrollable stressors. Original example: a burst pipe under the sink is changeable — a call to a plumber fits, and telling yourself the water is fine does not. A loved one's serious illness is not changeable by effort — accepting help and regulating grief fits, and insisting on fixing it does not. Neither family is good or bad in general. The situation decides.

collegeVersion.heading: Social support: people help people cope
collegeVersion.body: Social support is the help and comfort people get from their social network — family, friends, neighbors, colleagues. It takes three common forms: practical help like chores or money, advice and guidance, and emotional support that makes a person feel valued, accepted, and understood. The one-line summary: people help people cope. Support is both a coping strategy people reach for and a resource that cushions stress in general; Noba's health psychologists count social relationships among the factors that protect health. Original example: when Mei's mother is hospitalized, her neighbor mows the lawn, her cousin sends a meal, and her best friend calls every evening just to listen — three different kinds of support, all lightening the load.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note: no one right way — coping manages, not eliminates
collegeVersion.body: Two honest notes close the lesson. First, there is no one right way to cope. Strategies that fit one person's situation may not fit another's, and what works can change as the situation changes. The fit between strategy and situation is the closest thing to a rule. Second, coping is stress management, not stress elimination. It reduces the weight of demands and regulates emotions; it does not make stressors vanish. A student who plans, seeks support, and reframes an exam still has to take the exam. That is not a failure of coping — it is what coping is.

vocabulary.definition: The mental and behavioral efforts a person makes to manage the demands of stress and the emotions those demands create.
A stress-management approach that aims to change, reduce, or remove the source of the stress itself, such as fixing, negotiating, or planning around the problem.
A stress-management approach that aims to regulate the emotional response to stress rather than changing the stressor that triggered it.
An emotion-focused strategy that changes how a stressor is interpreted — its meaning — without changing the stressor itself.
A coping strategy that disengages from the stressor and turns attention away from it, giving short-term relief without addressing the underlying problem.
The practical help, advice, and emotional comfort that people receive from family, friends, and other members of their social network.
A person's belief about how much influence they have over a stressful situation, which helps determine which coping approach fits.
An event, condition, or demand that a person appraises as taxing or exceeding their resources and that triggers the stress response.
An emotion-focused strategy that temporarily turns attention away from the stressor to give the person a mental break from it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Coping is anything you do, on purpose, to carry stress better. Picture stress as weight on your shoulders. Problem-focused coping takes some of the weight off — you fix the leak, finish the task, ask for the raise. Emotion-focused coping changes how the weight feels — you slow your breathing, tell yourself a different story about it, or let someone help you carry it. Planning, seeking support, reframing, and distraction are all ways people lighten the load, and each fits some moments better than others. Avoidance is the odd one: it feels like relief for an hour, then the weight comes back exactly where it was. The rule of thumb: if you can change the thing, change it; if you cannot, change how you carry it. And no single strategy is right for everyone — fit matters more than fashion. Coping does not make the weight disappear. It makes the weight carryable.
eli10.analogy: Think of coping as steering a kayak through rough water. The waves are the stressors: you cannot make the water calm, but you can paddle to change your course, brace and lean to keep from capsizing, or angle toward shore to rest. Problem-focused coping is the paddling that changes where the boat goes. Emotion-focused coping is the bracing and steady breathing that keeps you upright while the waves hit. A paddler who only braces gets nowhere; a paddler who only charges into every wave wears out. Skilled paddling is mostly matching the move to the water.
eli10.analogyLimits: The kayak image leaves three things out. Waves are impersonal and predictable in a way stressors are not: people can often change the source of stress itself — negotiate, fix, quit, apologize — which no paddler can do to weather. Coping is also usually social, and the kayak is a solo boat: other people help carry the load in ways the image cannot show. And a kayaker wants to leave the water entirely, but the goal of coping is not a stress-free life; it is managing the stress that remains.

workedExample: Nadia runs a small catering kitchen. A week before her biggest wedding order, her walk-in cooler fails and the supplier says the replacement part takes ten days. The stress is immediate and physical. Her problem-focused moves: she calls two refrigeration companies for emergency repair quotes, rents a backup cold-storage unit for the week, and rearranges her prep schedule around the delivery. Her emotion-focused moves: she calls her sister to vent and to ask for help covering the Saturday shift, and she reframes the situation — a cooler failure now, she tells herself, is better than one discovered the morning of the event. She briefly considers canceling the wedding order — pure avoidance, tempting for an hour — and rejects it because the problem would return with interest. The mix works because the failure is fixable, so action fits, and the feelings needed handling too.

commonMistakes.mistake: Coping means making the problem go away.
commonMistakes.correction: Coping manages the demands and the emotions; many stressors — illness, loss, a decision already made — cannot be eliminated, and coping still happens there.

commonMistakes.mistake: Emotion-focused coping is the weak option; problem-focused is the real coping.
commonMistakes.correction: For stressors a person cannot change, emotion-focused coping is the effective choice. The fit between strategy and situation decides, not the family.

commonMistakes.mistake: Avoidance is never useful.
commonMistakes.correction: Avoidance can reduce stress in the short term and keep anxiety from becoming overwhelming, but it leaves the problem untouched, so it fails as a long-term strategy.

commonMistakes.mistake: There is one best way to cope.
commonMistakes.correction: No single strategy fits every person or situation; what works depends on the stressor, the person, and the context, and it can change over time.

compareContrast.distinction: Both are coping, but they target different things: problem-focused coping aims to change or remove the stressor itself, while emotion-focused coping aims to regulate the emotional reaction to it. Lazarus and Folkman drew the line in 1984.

Both belong to the emotion-focused family, but reframing stays engaged with the stressor and changes its meaning, while avoidance disengages from the stressor and turns attention away without changing its meaning.

Support adds other people's resources — practical help, advice, emotional comfort — to a person's own efforts; coping alone relies only on what the individual can muster. Support is a strategy and a resource at once.

keyTakeaway: Coping is the effort to manage stress: change what can be changed, regulate what cannot, and let other people help — and no single strategy fits every situation.

questionBank.prompt: Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman are known in stress research for which contribution?
options: Naming the fight-or-flight response
Distinguishing problem-focused from emotion-focused coping
Describing the general adaptation syndrome
Developing the learned helplessness model
questionBank.explanation: Lazarus and Folkman (1984) distinguished two fundamental kinds of coping — problem-focused coping, which manages or alters the stressor, and emotion-focused coping, which changes or reduces the negative emotions associated with stress (OpenStax Psychology 2e, 14.4; APA Dictionary entries for both terms carry the same 1984 attribution). Cannon named fight-or-flight, Selye described the general adaptation syndrome, and learned helplessness belongs to Seligman — none of them is this distinction's source.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the attribution of the problem-focused/emotion-focused distinction

questionBank.prompt: Marcus's car breaks down a week before an important road trip. He calls three mechanics for quotes, books the cheapest repair, and rearranges his schedule around the workshop. Which coping approach is Marcus using?
options: Emotion-focused coping
Avoidance
Reframing
Problem-focused coping
questionBank.explanation: Marcus is trying to manage or alter the stressor itself — the broken car — by generating options, comparing them, and acting, which is the signature of problem-focused coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984; OpenStax 14.4; APA Dictionary). Emotion-focused coping would regulate his feelings about the breakdown, avoidance would mean ignoring the car, and reframing would change how he interprets the event — none matches his actions.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a strategy as problem-focused in an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: Lena learns her application for a dream job was rejected. She cannot change the decision, so she tells herself the rejection frees her to apply for a better-matched role next cycle, and she books a long-planned hiking weekend to lift her mood. Which pair of strategies is Lena using?
options: Reframing and distraction
Planning and avoidance
Seeking support and planning
Avoidance and reframing
questionBank.explanation: Reframing (reappraisal) construes the stressor differently without changing its objective threat — Lena recasts the rejection as an opening — and distraction temporarily turns attention away, as the hiking weekend does (OpenStax 14.4; APA Dictionary's emotion-focused coping entry lists positive reframing and avoidance techniques). She does not plan a concrete change (the decision is fixed), avoid the news entirely, or seek support here, so the other pairs do not fit.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing reframing and distraction in an original scenario

questionBank.prompt: Danilo's landlord announces rent will rise in two months, and Danilo cannot afford the new amount. He can look for a cheaper apartment, negotiate a smaller increase, or move in with his brother. Which coping approach fits his situation best?
options: Avoidance, because the rise is inevitable
Emotion-focused coping only, because feelings matter most
Problem-focused coping, because the stressor is changeable
Distraction, because the move is far away
questionBank.explanation: The rent rise is a stressor Danilo can influence, and problem-focused coping is used primarily when a person appraises a stressor as within their capacity to change — searching, negotiating, and moving are exactly the instrumental actions it favors (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984; OpenStax 14.4; APA Dictionary). Avoidance leaves the problem to grow, emotion-focused coping alone would not address the changeable situation, and distraction is a temporary break, not a fit for a fixable problem.
questionBank.skill: Judging strategy-situation fit for a changeable stressor

questionBank.prompt: Rosa's father has a serious illness that treatment cannot reverse. Her sister urges her to 'fix it,' but no fix exists. Which honest conclusion about coping fits Rosa's situation?
options: Emotion-focused coping — accepting support and regulating grief — fits, because the stressor cannot be changed
Avoidance is the only honest option
Problem-focused coping will change the outcome if she tries hard enough
Coping has failed because the stressor remains
questionBank.explanation: For stressors appraised as beyond a person's capacity to change, emotion-focused coping is the effective choice — accepting help, regulating grief, reframing the situation (Lazarus & Folkman; OpenStax 14.4: emotion-focused coping is more effective in dealing with uncontrollable stressors; APA Dictionary). Avoidance is not the only option, problem-focused coping cannot change an unchangeable outcome, and a stressor that remains is not evidence that coping failed — coping manages stress rather than eliminating it.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating the honest framing of coping against an uncontrollable stressor

Reframing
Problem-focused coping
quickCheck.explanation: Marcus is trying to manage or alter the stressor itself — the broken car — by generating options, comparing them, and acting, which is the signature of problem-focused coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984; OpenStax 14.4; APA Dictionary). Emotion-focused coping would regulate his feelings about the breakdown, avoidance would mean ignoring the car, and reframing would change how he interprets the event — none matches his actions.
quickCheck.skill: Classifying a strategy as problem-focused in an original scenario

quickCheck.prompt: Lena learns her application for a dream job was rejected. She cannot change the decision, so she tells herself the rejection frees her to apply for a better-matched role next cycle, and she books a long-planned hiking weekend to lift her mood. Which pair of strategies is Lena using?
options: Reframing and distraction
Planning and avoidance
Seeking support and planning
Avoidance and reframing
quickCheck.explanation: Reframing (reappraisal) construes the stressor differently without changing its objective threat — Lena recasts the rejection as an opening — and distraction temporarily turns attention away, as the hiking weekend does (OpenStax 14.4; APA Dictionary's emotion-focused coping entry lists positive reframing and avoidance techniques). She does not plan a concrete change (the decision is fixed), avoid the news entirely, or seek support here, so the other pairs do not fit.
quickCheck.skill: Recognizing reframing and distraction in an original scenario

title: Psychological Disorders
in30Seconds: A psychological disorder is a pattern of thinking, feeling, or behaving that causes distress or impaired functioning — the working definition this lesson uses, close to how MedlinePlus and the DSM describe mental disorders. Where the line falls is debated, and experts keep refining the manual they use. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association, is the main classification tool in the United States — a tool, not a truth machine. Stigma, misunderstanding that harms people, is a real problem. This lesson is education, not diagnosis.
whyItMatters: Mental health is not a niche topic: more than one in five U.S. adults live with a mental illness in a given year, so most people know someone touched by these conditions — or are that someone themselves. Academically, psychological disorders sit where biology, thought, and culture meet; the same mind that learns and remembers can also suffer. Practically, this lesson gives you an accurate frame for what a diagnosis is and is not, so you can talk about mental health without fear-mongering, spot stigma when you see it, and read health claims more carefully. It also lays the groundwork for the next topic in this sequence: how treatment works.
learningObjectives: Define psychological disorder using the working definition — a pattern of thinking, feeling, or behaving that causes distress or impaired functioning — and name the sources that anchor it.
Explain the medical model's core idea in one line: psychological disorders treated as health conditions, analogous to biological problems.
Distinguish the anxiety, mood, psychotic, and personality categories of disorders, each with an original fictional example.
Describe the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders — what it is, who publishes it, and why it is a tool rather than a truth machine.
Analyze how stigma operates and why misunderstanding harms people with psychological disorders.
Apply the honest framing that a diagnosis describes a pattern of symptoms and is not a verdict on a person.

collegeVersion.heading: What counts as a psychological disorder
collegeVersion.body: The working definition used in this lesson: a psychological disorder is a pattern of thinking, feeling, or behaving that causes distress or impaired functioning. It is not invented here. MedlinePlus describes mental disorders as conditions that affect thinking, feeling, mood, and behavior and can impair the ability to function each day; the DSM-5 definition quoted in OpenStax adds significant distress in social, occupational, or other important activities. Both agree on the spine: distress, impaired functioning, or both. Original example: Amir, a fictional student, has slept badly for three months, stopped answering calls from friends, and watched his grades collapse. Thinking (constant dread), feeling (misery), behaving (withdrawal): real distress and impaired functioning — it meets the working definition. The honest note: definitions are debated. Experts struggle to agree on which thoughts, feelings, and behaviors truly indicate psychopathology — the study of psychological disorders, their symptoms, causes, and treatment — and uncomfortable states like first-date nerves can fall in the normal range.

collegeVersion.heading: The medical model: disorders as health conditions
collegeVersion.body: The medical model is one influential way of thinking about psychological disorders, and it fits in one line: mental and emotional problems are analogous to biological problems — with detectable causes and specific treatments (APA Dictionary of Psychology). Stated simply, the model treats a psychological disorder as a health condition to be understood, named, and addressed — not as a moral failing or weak character. The honest limits matter: the APA Dictionary's mental disorder entry lists physiological, genetic, chemical, social, and other factors among the causes, so biology, psychology, and life experience all contribute; the model is a starting point, not the whole story. Original example: when a doctor says a patient has diabetes, no one hears a character judgment; the medical model holds that a depression diagnosis deserves the same treatment.

collegeVersion.heading: Four categories, four original examples
collegeVersion.body: Anxiety disorders are characterized by excessive and persistent fear and anxiety plus related behavioral disturbances (APA, 2013). Original example: Hana, a fictional graduate, feels crushing dread at the thought of attending her own graduation and avoids crowded places now. Mood disorders are characterized by severe disturbances in mood and emotions — most often depression, but also mania and elation. Original example: Marcus, a fictional mechanic, spends weeks feeling hollow and uninterested in the engine projects he once loved. Psychotic disorders, such as schizophrenia, involve major disturbances in thought, perception, emotion, and behavior, including hallucinations and delusions. Original example: Elena, a fictional librarian, hears voices no one else hears and believes strangers are plotting against her. One myth cleared: schizophrenia is not split personality (OpenStax). Personality disorders involve a personality style that differs markedly from cultural expectations, is pervasive and inflexible, and causes distress or impairment. Original example: Dev, a fictional bookkeeper, has for years read friendly remarks as hidden attacks and pushed people away before they could get close. These four families are a map, not a menu: real people rarely fit one neat box, and disorders often co-occur — comorbidity is common.

collegeVersion.heading: The DSM: a tool, not a truth machine
collegeVersion.body: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders — the DSM — is the classification system used by most mental health professionals in the United States, published by the American Psychiatric Association. The first edition appeared in 1952; DSM-5 followed in 2013 and its text revision, DSM-5-TR, in 2022 (APA Dictionary). The manual exists so professionals share a common language: a diagnosis labels a set of symptoms, supporting communication and, ultimately, treatment decisions. The honest note: the DSM is a tool, not a truth machine. Its categories are expert judgments that have changed — the first two editions listed homosexuality as a disorder until the APA voted to remove it in 1973 (OpenStax) — and researchers continue to critique the overlap between diagnoses. A manual written, revised, and used by people: useful, and worth treating as such.

collegeVersion.heading: Stigma: when misunderstanding harms
collegeVersion.body: The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines stigma as the negative social attitude attached to a characteristic of an individual that may be regarded as a mental, physical, or social deficiency; it implies social disapproval and can lead unfairly to discrimination against and exclusion of the individual. In plainer words: misunderstanding psychological disorders causes real harm. Original example: at a fictional office, a manager quietly moves a colleague who once mentioned a depression diagnosis off a major project, 'just to be safe' — although her work has always been on time. No evidence, no missed deadline — a label, and a quiet exclusion: stigma in action. The honest note is simple: misunderstanding harms people. A diagnosis describes a pattern; it is not a summary of a person's worth, and the person behind the label is the same colleague, neighbor, or friend as before.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest note: education, not diagnosis
collegeVersion.body: This lesson is education, not diagnosis. Reading descriptions of symptom patterns does not qualify anyone to diagnose; only trained professionals, comparing a person's experience against established criteria, can do that. The categories here are for orientation, the way learning the names of constellations helps you look at the sky without claiming to navigate by them. The honest framing that closes the lesson: a diagnosis is a description, not a verdict. It names a pattern of suffering so it can be talked about, studied, and addressed; it does not define who a person is, what they are capable of, or what their future holds. If you or someone you care about is struggling, the right next step is a conversation with a qualified professional — the subject of the next topic in this sequence.

vocabulary.definition: A pattern of thinking, feeling, or behaving that causes distress or impaired functioning; the working definition used in this lesson, anchored in how MedlinePlus and the DSM describe mental disorders.
The study of psychological disorders, including their symptoms, their causes, and their treatment, per OpenStax Psychology 2e.
The concept, defined in the APA Dictionary, that mental and emotional problems are analogous to biological problems, with detectable causes and specific treatments.

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, the classification system used by most mental health professionals in the United States and published by the American Psychiatric Association.
A category characterized by excessive and persistent fear and anxiety plus related disturbances in behavior, such as avoidance.
A category characterized by severe disturbances in mood and emotions, ranging from the extreme sadness of depression to the extreme elation of mania.
A category, including schizophrenia, marked by major disturbances in thought, perception, emotion, and behavior, such as hallucinations and delusions.
Long-standing, pervasive, and inflexible personality styles that differ markedly from cultural expectations and cause distress or impairment.
The negative social attitude attached to a characteristic, implying social disapproval and leading unfairly to discrimination against and exclusion of the individual, per the APA Dictionary.
The co-occurrence of two or more disorders in the same person, which research shows is common among psychological disorders.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of the mind as machinery for thinking, feeling, and behaving. A psychological disorder is when that machinery goes off course in a way that hurts the person — causing distress — and gets in the way of daily life — impairing functioning. Where exactly 'off course' begins is a judgment experts debate, so definitions are honest approximations, not engraved truths. The DSM is the big manual experts use to describe and compare disorders, and it gets revised because expert judgment improves and changes. One more thing matters: a person with a disorder is a person first, and the cruelest part of these conditions is often the misunderstanding around them — stigma that makes people ashamed to ask for help. This lesson teaches you to see clearly; it does not teach you to diagnose.
eli10.analogy: A diagnosis is like a label on a jar: the label tells you what is inside — a pattern of symptoms — not what the jar is worth. Stigma is what happens when people judge the jar by a rumor about the label instead of by the person holding it.
eli10.analogyLimits: The comparison breaks down because a jar's label is fixed and simple, while a diagnosis is a professional judgment that can be revised, debated, and even changed by new editions of the manual. A jar has no feelings and no story; a person does, so a label can never capture a whole life. And a jar's label is applied by a machine, while a diagnosis is made by trained people who must weigh evidence with care.

workedExample: Consider Tomás, a fictional barista. For two months, his chest tightens whenever a line forms at the counter, he dreads opening the shop, and last week he called in sick to avoid a busy Saturday. Walk through the working definition: his pattern involves feeling (fear), thinking (dread of the line), and behaving (avoidance), and it is causing distress and impairing his work — so the pattern meets the lesson's working definition of a psychological disorder. Which family? Persistent, excessive fear and avoidance fit the description of the anxiety disorders. Now the honest framing: even this careful walkthrough does not diagnose Tomás — a professional comparing his experience against the DSM's criteria would make that call. What this lesson contributes is the accurate vocabulary to describe the pattern, and the reminder that Tomás is a person with a condition, not a case file.

commonMistakes.mistake: A psychological disorder is just being unusual or different from other people.
commonMistakes.correction: Unusual alone does not make a disorder. The working definition requires distress or impaired functioning, and where the line falls is debated — first-date nerves are uncomfortable but normal, while a pattern that disrupts daily life meets the test.

commonMistakes.mistake: The DSM is a complete, unchanging list of all mental illnesses, straight from nature.
commonMistakes.correction: The DSM is a classification tool written by experts and published by the American Psychiatric Association. Its categories have changed over time — homosexuality was removed in 1973 — so it is best treated as a useful tool, not a truth machine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Schizophrenia means split personality.
commonMistakes.correction: It does not. As OpenStax stresses, schizophrenia involves major disturbances in thought, perception, emotion, and behavior, including hallucinations and delusions; split personality is a different, dissociative condition.

commonMistakes.mistake: After reading this lesson, I can diagnose someone from their symptoms.
commonMistakes.correction: This lesson is education, not diagnosis. Only qualified professionals, comparing a person's experience against established criteria, can diagnose — and the honest next step for someone struggling is a conversation with a professional.

commonMistakes.mistake: People with psychological disorders are dangerous, and it is their own fault.
commonMistakes.correction: Stigma works exactly this way: a negative attitude attached to a label, leading to unfair treatment. Disorders are health conditions to be understood and addressed, not character verdicts, and misunderstanding — not the person — is the problem.

compareContrast.a: Ordinary distress, like first-date nerves or homesickness
compareContrast.distinction: Both involve uncomfortable feelings, but a disorder is a pattern that causes significant distress or impaired functioning, while ordinary distress falls in the normal range — and experts debate exactly where the line sits.

The medical model treats disorders as health conditions analogous to biological problems, with detectable causes and specific treatments; a broader view, reflected in the APA Dictionary's mental disorder entry, adds psychological and social factors to the mix.
A diagnosis labels a pattern of symptoms so professionals share a common language; it describes a condition the person has, while a verdict would judge the person's worth — which no diagnosis does.

keyTakeaway: A psychological disorder is a pattern of thinking, feeling, or behaving that causes distress or impaired functioning — a description of a condition, not a verdict on a person, and a topic that calls for understanding rather than stigma.
