title: Classical Greece
in30Seconds: Classical Greece is the world of the Greek city-states in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, roughly from the end of the Persian Wars (479 BCE) to the death of Alexander the Great (323 BCE). Its independent poleis included democratic Athens and militarized Sparta. Athens ran a direct democracy — but only for adult male citizens, excluding women, enslaved people, and foreigners. The era's philosophy, drama, and history-writing shaped later Western thought, and Alexander's conquests spread Greek culture across the Near East.
whyItMatters: Classical Greece is a reference point for later Western politics, philosophy, science, and art, so college courses across the humanities keep returning to it. Understanding it well means holding two things at once: crediting genuine innovations — direct democracy, systematic philosophy, critical history-writing, monumental architecture — while being honest that Athenian democracy excluded most of the people who lived there, and that equally sophisticated civilizations flourished at the same time in Persia, India, and China. That double vision is exactly the historical skill instructors want: distinguishing real achievement from myth, and describing a society's ideals and its exclusions in the same breath rather than choosing one.
learningObjectives: Define the polis and describe the political contrast between Athens and Sparta.
Explain how Athenian direct democracy worked and identify who it excluded.
Place the Greco-Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War in sequence with approximate dates and outcomes.
Identify the major figures of Classical Greek philosophy, history-writing, and drama.
Explain how the Hellenistic era spread Greek culture after Alexander the Great, and evaluate Greek achievement without triumphalism.

collegeVersion.heading: The polis and the world of city-states
collegeVersion.body: The Greek world of the Classical period — conventionally the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, from the end of the Persian Wars (479 BCE) to the death of Alexander the Great (323 BCE) — was not a single country. It was a patchwork of hundreds of independent city-states, each called a polis. A polis typically grew up around a fortified hill, or acropolis, where inhabitants could shelter in danger, and each had its own government, laws, and religious cults. Greeks shared a language, gods, and festivals, and thought of themselves as a common people distinct from non-Greek 'barbarians,' but they rarely united politically, and the poleis competed and warred with one another as often as they cooperated. This is why 'ancient Greece' names a culture rather than a state, and why its politics is best studied one city at a time. The two most influential — because they are the best documented and because they became rivals — were Athens and Sparta, and their differences show how much variation the polis system contained.

collegeVersion.heading: Athens and Sparta: democracy and oligarchy
collegeVersion.body: Sparta was an oligarchy: real power lay with a small class of full citizens, the soldier-citizens, and the state was organized around military strength. Sparta was headed by two hereditary kings and governed with a council of elders and assemblies, but participation was narrow, and its economy depended on a large subjugated population of helots who farmed the land. Spartan boys were taken from their families at about age seven and raised by the state for a lifetime of military service. Athens took a different path. Over the sixth and fifth centuries it developed a democracy — literally 'rule by the people' (demos) — in which all adult male citizens could take part in government directly. The foundations were laid by the reforms of Cleisthenes around 508 BCE, which reorganized citizens by locality into demes and ten tribes, weakening the old aristocratic clans, and created a Council of 500 (the boule) in which citizens had an equal right to speak. Neither system was 'better' in the abstract; they were different answers to how a polis should be governed, and much of Classical history is the story of their rivalry.

collegeVersion.heading: How Athenian democracy worked — and whom it excluded
collegeVersion.body: Athenian democracy was direct, not representative: citizens did not elect legislators to act for them but gathered in person in the Assembly to debate and vote on laws, war, and public spending, with a majority of those present deciding. Many offices were filled by lot rather than election, on the principle that ordinary citizens could govern. This was a genuine innovation, and it is a real ancestor of later democratic thought. But it is essential to be exact about its limits. Full political participation was reserved for adult male citizens — a body of perhaps thirty to forty thousand men in the Classical period. Women of citizen families had no vote and little public role, though they could serve as priestesses. Enslaved people, who made up a large part of the population, had no political rights at all. And metics — free foreigners living in Athens, including many long-settled merchants and craftsmen — were excluded from citizenship no matter how long they stayed. Athenian democracy was therefore direct and, for its citizens, remarkably participatory, but it was far from universal: most adults in Athens could not vote. Describing both the innovation and the exclusion is not a contradiction; it is the accurate picture.

collegeVersion.heading: Two defining wars
collegeVersion.body: Two conflicts frame the period. First came the Greco-Persian Wars, when the vast Persian (Achaemenid) Empire tried to bring the mainland Greeks under its control. The Athenians turned back a Persian invasion at Marathon in 490 BCE; a decade later a small Spartan-led force made its famous stand at Thermopylae while the Greek fleet destroyed the Persian navy at Salamis (both 480 BCE), and the following year the Greeks won decisively on land at Plataea (479 BCE). (OpenStax dates the wars as a whole to 492-449 BCE.) After the victory, Athens organized the Delian League in 477 BCE, an alliance that it gradually turned into an empire. That growing power alarmed Sparta, and the two led opposing coalitions into the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE). Pericles, the leading Athenian statesman of the era, died in 429 BCE during a plague that ravaged the crowded city early in the war. A truce, the Peace of Nicias, paused the fighting in 421 BCE, but the war resumed and finally ended in 404 BCE when a defeated Athens surrendered to Sparta. Athens lost its empire, and no single polis held lasting dominance afterward.

collegeVersion.heading: Culture, Alexander, and the Hellenistic spread
collegeVersion.body: The same century produced an extraordinary cultural record. In philosophy, Socrates (c. 470-399 BCE) pressed Athenians to examine their assumptions and was tried and executed by the city in 399 BCE; his student Plato (c. 428-348 BCE) founded the Academy, and Plato's student Aristotle (384-322 BCE) wrote across logic, biology, ethics, and politics and later tutored Alexander. Greeks also invented critical history-writing: Herodotus, later called the 'Father of History,' chronicled the Persian Wars, and Thucydides wrote a sharply analytical account of the Peloponnesian War he had lived through. Drama flourished in the forms of tragedy and comedy, and Athens rebuilt its Acropolis — crowned by the Parthenon — under Pericles. Political independence, however, was ending. By 338 BCE the kingdom of Macedon under Philip II dominated Greece, and his son Alexander the Great (356-323 BCE) conquered the Persian Empire, winning at Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (330 BCE) and pushing into central Asia and India before dying at Babylon in 323 BCE. His death opened the Hellenistic period (323-31 BCE), in which Greek language and culture blended with local traditions across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East. New Greek cities such as Alexandria in Egypt became centers of learning, and philosophies like Stoicism and Epicureanism spread. All of this deserves credit without triumphalism: at the very same time, Achaemenid Persia, the Maurya empire in India, and the states of Zhou-era China were building equally sophisticated societies, and the Greek story is one among several, not the single source of civilization.

vocabulary.definition: An independent, self-governing Greek city-state, usually centered on a fortified hill (acropolis), with its own government, laws, and religious cults.
A system in which citizens themselves debate and vote on laws and policy in person, rather than electing representatives to decide for them.
Rule by a small group; in Sparta, political power was held by a narrow class of full soldier-citizens rather than by the people at large.
A free foreign-born resident of Athens who could live and work in the city but was barred from citizenship and the vote.
The Athenian Council of 500, created by Cleisthenes' reforms, which prepared business for the Assembly and gave citizens an equal right to speak.
An alliance of Greek city-states formed in 477 BCE and led by Athens after the Persian Wars, which Athens gradually turned into an empire.
The era from Alexander the Great's death (323 BCE) to the Roman conquest of the last Greek kingdom (31 BCE), when Greek culture spread across the Near East.
A large subjugated population in Sparta who farmed the land for the citizen class and had no political rights, underpinning Sparta's military society.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Ancient Greece was not one country. It was hundreds of separate towns-with-their-own-rules called city-states, and they often argued and fought. Athens let its adult male citizens vote directly on everything, all together, which was a big new idea — but women, enslaved people, and people born elsewhere were not allowed to vote, so most people there had no say. Sparta was run by a small group and trained its boys to be soldiers from age seven. The Greeks fought off the huge Persian Empire, then Athens and Sparta fought each other for almost thirty years and Sparta won. Greek thinkers, playwrights, and history-writers from this time still get read today. Later a king named Alexander conquered a giant empire and spread Greek language and ideas far to the east.
eli10.analogy: Think of Classical Greece like a league of separate small towns that all speak the same language and cheer at the same festivals but each have their own mayor and rulebook — sometimes teaming up against an outside threat, often feuding with each other.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy is loose: modern towns sit inside one country with shared national laws, while each polis was fully sovereign, could wage its own wars, and answered to no higher Greek government. And a friendly sports league understates how deadly the rivalries became — the Peloponnesian War lasted a generation and ended one city's power for good.

workedExample: Imagine you want to place Athens' three big moments in order and say who was in and out of power. Start with democracy: Cleisthenes' reforms around 508 BCE set up the Assembly and the Council of 500, so by the early fifth century adult male citizens governed directly. Next, external threat: the Persian Wars peak in 490 BCE (Marathon) and 480-479 BCE (Salamis and Plataea), and Athens' leadership of the resulting Delian League (477 BCE) grows into an empire. Then, internal war: that empire frightens Sparta, and the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) ends with Athens' surrender. Now ask the exclusion question at any point: could a metic merchant or a citizen's wife vote? No — only adult male citizens could. Laying the events on a timeline and separately checking who held rights keeps the achievement and its limits both in view.

commonMistakes.mistake: Talking about 'ancient Greece' as if it were a single unified country or empire.
commonMistakes.correction: It was a culture shared across hundreds of independent poleis. They shared language and gods but had separate governments and frequently fought one another.

commonMistakes.mistake: Describing Athenian democracy as if everyone could vote.
commonMistakes.correction: Only adult male citizens could participate. Women, enslaved people, and metics (free foreigners) were all excluded, so most adults in Athens had no vote.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the Persian Wars with the Peloponnesian War, or reversing who fought whom.
commonMistakes.correction: In the Persian Wars the Greek city-states resisted the Persian Empire; in the Peloponnesian War Athens and Sparta fought each other. Sparta won the latter, in 404 BCE.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Greece was uniquely advanced and the sole origin of civilization.
commonMistakes.correction: Avoid triumphalism. Persia, Maurya India, and Zhou-era China were equally sophisticated at the same time; Greek contributions are one important thread, not the whole story.

compareContrast.distinction: Athens was a direct democracy in which adult male citizens voted in person; Sparta was a militarized oligarchy run by a small class of soldier-citizens and two kings.
The Persian Wars (early fifth century BCE) pitted allied Greek poleis against the Persian Empire; the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) was Greek-against-Greek, Athens versus Sparta.
The Classical period (to 323 BCE) centers on independent poleis like Athens; the Hellenistic period (323-31 BCE) follows Alexander, spreading Greek culture across large kingdoms in the Near East.

keyTakeaway: Classical Greece was a world of independent city-states whose achievements in democracy, philosophy, and the arts were real and lasting — but Athenian democracy reached only adult male citizens, and equally sophisticated civilizations thrived elsewhere at the same time, so the era deserves credit without triumphalism.

questionBank.prompt: In the Greek world of the Classical period, what was a polis?
options: A large regional empire ruled by a single hereditary monarch
An independent, self-governing city-state
A pan-Hellenic parliament that governed all Greeks together
A four-yearly religious festival held at Olympia
questionBank.explanation: A polis was an independent, self-governing city-state, usually centered on an acropolis, with its own government and cults. Option A is wrong because the poleis were not unified under one monarch. Option C is wrong because the Greeks had no common government — that is the whole point of the city-state system. Option D describes the Olympic festival, not a polis.
questionBank.skill: Defining the polis

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures the political contrast between Athens and Sparta in the Classical period?
options: Both were direct democracies open to all residents, including women and enslaved people
Athens was ruled by two hereditary kings, while Sparta was governed by a mass citizen assembly
Athens was a democracy in which adult male citizens participated directly, while Sparta was an oligarchy dominated by an elite of soldier-citizens
Sparta was a democracy and Athens an empire with no citizen government at all
questionBank.explanation: Athens developed direct democracy for its adult male citizens; Sparta was an oligarchy centered on its soldier-citizen class and headed by two kings. Option A is false — neither was open to women or enslaved people, and Sparta was not a democracy. Option B reverses the two cities (the two kings were Spartan). Option D is simply inverted.
questionBank.skill: Contrasting Athenian democracy and Spartan oligarchy

questionBank.prompt: Four adults live in democratic Athens: a native adult male citizen, a citizen's wife, an enslaved worker, and a metic (a free foreign-born merchant). Under the rules of Athenian democracy, who could vote in the Assembly?
options: All four, because Athens was a direct democracy
The citizen and his wife, but not the enslaved worker or the metic
The citizen and the metic, since both were free adults
Only the native adult male citizen
questionBank.explanation: Athenian democracy limited political participation to adult male citizens, so only that one person could vote. Option A ignores the exclusions. Option B is wrong because women, even of citizen families, could not vote. Option C is wrong because metics were barred from citizenship and the vote no matter how long they lived in Athens.
questionBank.skill: Applying the exclusions of Athenian democracy to a case

questionBank.prompt: How did the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) end?
options: Athens surrendered to Sparta, which won the war
Athens defeated Sparta and absorbed it into the Athenian empire
The Persian Empire conquered both Athens and Sparta
The two sides signed a lasting peace that left Athens the dominant power
questionBank.explanation: The war ended in 404 BCE with Athens' surrender to Sparta. Option B reverses the outcome. Option C is wrong — the Persian Wars were an earlier, separate conflict against Persia, not the end of the Peloponnesian War. Option D is wrong because the Peace of Nicias (421 BCE) was only a temporary pause, after which the war resumed and Athens lost.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the outcome of the Peloponnesian War

questionBank.prompt: Which event conventionally marks the beginning of the Hellenistic period, when Greek culture spread widely across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East?
options: The Athenian victory over Persia at the Battle of Marathon
The reforms of Cleisthenes that founded Athenian democracy
The death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE
The outbreak of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta
questionBank.explanation: The Hellenistic period is conventionally dated from Alexander the Great's death in 323 BCE to the Roman conquest of the last Greek kingdom in 31 BCE. Options A (490 BCE) and B (c. 508 BCE) belong to the earlier Classical period, and option D (431 BCE) is the start of an intra-Greek war, not the Hellenistic era.

quickCheck.prompt: In the Greek world of the Classical period, what was a polis?
options: A large regional empire ruled by a single hereditary monarch
An independent, self-governing city-state
A pan-Hellenic parliament that governed all Greeks together
A four-yearly religious festival held at Olympia
quickCheck.explanation: A polis was an independent, self-governing city-state, usually centered on an acropolis, with its own government and cults. Option A is wrong because the poleis were not unified under one monarch. Option C is wrong because the Greeks had no common government — that is the whole point of the city-state system. Option D describes the Olympic festival, not a polis.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement best captures the political contrast between Athens and Sparta in the Classical period?
options: Both were direct democracies open to all residents, including women and enslaved people
Athens was ruled by two hereditary kings, while Sparta was governed by a mass citizen assembly
Athens was a democracy in which adult male citizens participated directly, while Sparta was an oligarchy dominated by an elite of soldier-citizens
Sparta was a democracy and Athens an empire with no citizen government at all
quickCheck.explanation: Athens developed direct democracy for its adult male citizens; Sparta was an oligarchy centered on its soldier-citizen class and headed by two kings. Option A is false — neither was open to women or enslaved people, and Sparta was not a democracy. Option B reverses the two cities (the two kings were Spartan). Option D is simply inverted.

quickCheck.prompt: Four adults live in democratic Athens: a native adult male citizen, a citizen's wife, an enslaved worker, and a metic (a free foreign-born merchant). Under the rules of Athenian democracy, who could vote in the Assembly?
options: All four, because Athens was a direct democracy
The citizen and his wife, but not the enslaved worker or the metic
The citizen and the metic, since both were free adults
Only the native adult male citizen
quickCheck.explanation: Athenian democracy limited political participation to adult male citizens, so only that one person could vote. Option A ignores the exclusions. Option B is wrong because women, even of citizen families, could not vote. Option C is wrong because metics were barred from citizenship and the vote no matter how long they lived in Athens.

title: The Roman World
in30Seconds: The Roman world began as a republic, founded by tradition in 509 BCE after Romans expelled their last king. A mixed government of the Senate, elected consuls, and popular assemblies balanced power, though patricians and plebeians long struggled over rights. Rome conquered the Mediterranean, defeating Carthage in the Punic Wars, on an economy that leaned heavily on enslaved labor. Civil wars ended the Republic: Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE, and Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BCE, beginning centuries of empire, law, engineering, and the spread of Christianity.
whyItMatters: Rome is one of history's most influential states, and courses in history, political science, law, and the humanities return to it constantly. Its republican institutions — divided powers, elected magistrates, and checks such as the tribunes' veto — shaped later constitutional thinking, including that of the framers of the United States. Roman law, roads, aqueducts, and concrete still underlie European infrastructure and legal traditions, and Christianity spread through the empire to become a world religion. Studying Rome well means holding achievement and injustice together: real engineering and legal innovation alongside conquest and a society in which enslaved people were central. That double vision — crediting what Rome built while naming its brutality honestly — is exactly the historical skill instructors want.
learningObjectives: Describe how the Roman Republic was organized and how its mixed constitution balanced the Senate, consuls, and assemblies.
Explain the Conflict of the Orders between patricians and plebeians and the reforms it produced, including the Twelve Tables and the tribunes.
Outline Rome's Mediterranean expansion, including the Punic Wars against Carthage, and the central role of enslaved labor.
Trace the crisis of the Republic and the transition to empire under Julius Caesar and Augustus, with accurate dates.
Explain the Pax Romana and Rome's contributions in law, engineering, and the spread of Christianity.
Distinguish the traditional 476 CE end of the Western Roman Empire from the survival of the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire to 1453.

collegeVersion.heading: From kings to a republic: the mixed constitution
collegeVersion.body: By tradition, Romans overthrew their monarchy and declared a republic in 509 BCE, after expelling their last king. A republic is a state without a monarch, in which officials are chosen and power is shared rather than held for life by one person. Rome's government mixed several bodies so that no individual could dominate. At its center was the Senate, a council of experienced aristocrats that guided policy, finance, and foreign affairs. Executive power lay with two consuls elected each year; because there were two and they served only twelve months, each could check the other, and neither could settle into permanent rule. Popular assemblies of citizens passed laws and elected magistrates. In a genuine emergency the state could appoint a single dictator with sweeping authority, but only for a strictly limited term. Later thinkers admired this balance of one-man, few, and many elements — consuls, Senate, and assemblies — as a 'mixed constitution' that distributed power. It was never a modern democracy: wealth and birth weighted the assemblies, and real influence concentrated in a narrow elite. But the principles of elected, term-limited magistrates and institutional checks were a durable Roman contribution to later political thought.

collegeVersion.heading: Patricians, plebeians, and the Conflict of the Orders
collegeVersion.body: Early Roman society was split between patricians, an aristocratic elite who monopolized office and priesthood, and plebeians, the common citizens who farmed, traded, and fought in the army. For roughly two centuries the plebeians pressed for legal and political equality in a long struggle historians call the Conflict of the Orders. Their leverage was collective: because plebeians filled the legions, they could withdraw and refuse to serve. Several reforms followed. Around 450 BCE Rome published the Twelve Tables, its first written law code, so that legal rules were public rather than known only to patrician judges. Plebeians gained their own officials, the tribunes of the plebs, who could veto actions harmful to plebeians and so provided a real check on patrician power. After 367 BCE one of the two consuls was required to be a plebeian, and by 287 BCE the plebeian assembly could pass laws binding on all citizens. The result was not equality of wealth — a small circle of families still dominated — but the plebeians had won legal protections and a share of political power through sustained, mostly non-violent pressure.

collegeVersion.heading: Expansion, the Punic Wars, and enslavement
collegeVersion.body: Over the third and second centuries BCE Rome expanded from central Italy to command the whole Mediterranean. Its greatest rival was Carthage, a wealthy North African trading power, and the two fought three Punic Wars. In the First Punic War (264-241 BCE) Rome won and annexed Sicily. In the Second (218-201 BCE), the Carthaginian general Hannibal invaded Italy with war elephants and won stunning victories, but Rome recovered and defeated him at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE. In the Third (149-146 BCE) Rome destroyed the city of Carthage entirely. Victory made Rome the Mediterranean's dominant power, but conquest also transformed its society. Wars produced enormous numbers of captives, and enslavement was central to the Roman economy: enslaved people worked large agricultural estates, mines, and households, and had no legal freedom. Stating this plainly is part of an honest account — Rome's prosperity and public works rested substantially on coerced, unfree labor, and the wealth pouring in from conquest also widened the gap between rich and poor citizens, feeding the crisis to come.

collegeVersion.heading: Crisis of the Republic: from Caesar to Augustus
collegeVersion.body: The strains of empire eventually broke the Republic. Reformers such as the brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus tried to redistribute land to poorer citizens in the late second century BCE and were killed by senators, showing how political disputes were turning violent. Ambitious generals, whose troops were loyal to them rather than to the state, then fought for supremacy: Marius and Sulla marched armies on Rome, and Sulla made himself dictator. In 60 BCE Julius Caesar joined Pompey and Crassus in the First Triumvirate, an informal power-sharing pact. Caesar crossed the Rubicon River with his legions in 49 BCE, won the resulting civil war, and had himself named dictator for life. Fearing a return to monarchy, a group of senators assassinated him on 15 March 44 BCE. His heir Octavian, with Mark Antony and Lepidus, formed the Second Triumvirate, then turned on Antony and Cleopatra and defeated them at the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE Octavian claimed to 'restore' the Republic while in fact keeping supreme power; the Senate gave him the honorific Augustus. He was, in effect, the first Roman emperor, and the Republic was over.

collegeVersion.heading: The Empire: Pax Romana, law, engineering, and Christianity
collegeVersion.body: Augustus's settlement opened the imperial era and about two centuries of relative internal peace, the Pax Romana, conventionally running from his reign (27 BCE) to the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE. Stability let trade, cities, and culture flourish across a vast, connected realm. Rome's practical achievements were remarkable: a network of tens of thousands of miles of roads, aqueducts that carried water by gravity across valleys on arches into cities, and the use of concrete and the arch to build durable structures on a huge scale. Roman law — from the Twelve Tables through centuries of jurists, later codified in the East as the Code of Justinian in the sixth century — became a foundation of European legal systems. Christianity emerged in the empire's eastern provinces in the first century CE. Christians were periodically persecuted, notably under Nero in 64 CE and Diocletian in 303-311, but the emperor Constantine's Edict of Milan in 313 CE legalized the faith, and in 380 CE the emperor Theodosius I made Christianity the official religion of the empire, spreading it far beyond its origins.

collegeVersion.heading: Division and the two 'falls': 476 in the west, 1453 in the east
collegeVersion.body: Rome's later centuries brought civil war, invasion, and pressure on the frontiers, and the empire was increasingly governed as two halves, west and east. When Theodosius I died in 395 CE, the empire was divided permanently between his two sons and never reunited. The western half weakened as Germanic peoples settled within its borders, and by tradition the Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE, when a Germanic general, Odoacer, deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and made himself King of Italy. Historians stress there was no single dramatic 'fall': Roman authority faded gradually, and Roman culture, law, and Christianity persisted in the successor kingdoms. Crucially, only the western empire ended in the fifth century. The eastern half, centered on Constantinople and known to historians as the Byzantine Empire, continued to call itself Roman and endured for nearly another thousand years. It preserved Roman law and Greek learning, reached a height under Justinian (reigned 527-565), and finally fell in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks under Mehmed II captured Constantinople. So the common phrase 'the fall of Rome' is really two very different events, a millennium apart.

vocabulary.definition: A form of government without a monarch, in which officials are elected and power is shared among institutions rather than held for life by one ruler; Rome's from 509 BCE to the rise of Augustus.
The council of experienced Roman aristocrats that advised on and guided policy, finance, and foreign affairs; the most prestigious governing body of the Republic and, in reduced form, the Empire.

One of two chief magistrates elected annually to lead the Roman Republic; the pair shared executive and military authority and could check each other, and their one-year term prevented permanent personal rule.
An elected official who represented the common citizens and could veto state actions harmful to them, a protection won by the plebeians during the Conflict of the Orders.
Rome's first written law code, published around 450 BCE, which made basic legal rules public instead of leaving them in the hands of patrician judges.
Three wars between Rome and Carthage (264-241, 218-201, and 149-146 BCE) that ended with Rome destroying Carthage and dominating the western Mediterranean.
The roughly two-century span of relative internal peace and stability across the empire, conventionally from Augustus (27 BCE) to the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE.
The name historians give the eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, which continued to call itself Roman and survived nearly a thousand years after the west, until 1453.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Rome started as a republic, which means no king. Instead, elected officials shared power, and special officials called tribunes could block laws that hurt ordinary people. Rome grew huge by winning wars, including against a rival city called Carthage, and much of its work was done by enslaved people who had no freedom. After a lot of fighting among powerful generals, a leader named Julius Caesar was killed in 44 BCE, and soon after, his adopted son Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BCE. For a long time the empire was mostly peaceful, and Romans built amazing roads, water bridges, and buildings, wrote laws still used as models, and Christianity spread across their lands. Later the empire split into a western and an eastern half. The western half ended in the year 476, but the eastern half kept going for almost another thousand years until 1453.
eli10.analogy: Think of the Roman Republic like a student council with two co-presidents who swap out every year and a rule that lets class representatives veto anything unfair to students, instead of one principal deciding everything forever.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy is loose in important ways. A student council is small, voluntary, and answers to a school; Rome was a sovereign state that waged wars, ruled millions, and depended on enslaved labor a school never would. And unlike a council that keeps meeting, Rome's Republic collapsed into one-man rule under the emperors, so the 'co-presidents' eventually vanished.

workedExample: Suppose a question asks you to place Rome's turning points in order and separate the Republic from the Empire. Start at 509 BCE: the Republic is founded, run by the Senate, two yearly consuls, and assemblies. Next, expansion — the Punic Wars against Carthage (264-241, 218-201, 149-146 BCE) make Rome the Mediterranean power. Then the crisis: Julius Caesar is assassinated in 44 BCE, still a dictator, never an 'emperor.' The Empire proper begins in 27 BCE when Augustus takes power. Finally the 'fall': the Western Roman Empire ends by tradition in 476 CE, but the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire continues until 1453. Laying dates on a timeline, and asking at each point 'republic or empire?', keeps the two eras and the two very different 'falls' straight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Rome was always ruled by emperors.
commonMistakes.correction: For its first roughly five centuries (509 BCE onward) Rome was a republic governed by the Senate, elected consuls, and assemblies. Emperors began only with Augustus in 27 BCE, after civil wars destroyed the Republic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing the whole Roman Empire 'fell' in 476 CE.
commonMistakes.correction: Only the Western Roman Empire is traditionally dated to 476 CE. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, centered on Constantinople, continued for nearly another thousand years and fell in 1453.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the Punic Wars with Rome's civil wars.
commonMistakes.correction: The Punic Wars (264-146 BCE) were fought against the foreign power Carthage. The civil wars of the first century BCE, such as those of Caesar, Pompey, and Octavian, were Romans fighting other Romans for control of the state.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picturing Roman prosperity and public works without enslavement.
commonMistakes.correction: Enslavement was central to Roman society. Conquest produced large numbers of captives who were forced to labor on estates, in mines, and in households, and much of Rome's wealth and building rested on this unfree labor.

compareContrast.distinction: The Republic (from 509 BCE) shared power among the Senate, two annually elected consuls, and assemblies; the Empire (from 27 BCE) concentrated supreme power in one emperor, beginning with Augustus.

Patricians were the aristocratic elite who first monopolized office and priesthood; plebeians were the common citizens who, through the Conflict of the Orders, won written law, tribunes, and a share of political power.
The west, ruled from Italy, is traditionally dated to have ended in 476 CE; the east, ruled from Constantinople, called itself Roman and survived until 1453.

keyTakeaway: Rome went from a republic of shared, checked power (509 BCE) to rule by emperors under Augustus (27 BCE), built lasting law and engineering on an economy centered on enslaved labor, and did not end all at once — the Western Empire is dated to 476 CE, but the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453.

44 BCE
27 BCE

questionBank.prompt: Which feature best captures how the Roman Republic tried to prevent any single person or group from dominating the state?

One assembly decided everything by direct majority vote of all inhabitants, including women and enslaved people.
Power was divided among the Senate, two annually elected consuls, and popular assemblies, with tribunes able to veto acts harmful to the plebeians.
A council of priests appointed every official and could overturn any law it disliked.

The Senate
The emergency dictatorship
The tribune of the plebs

The Roman Empire never divided and continued unbroken until 1453.

questionBank.explanation: The empire had split into western and eastern halves; the west traditionally ended in 476 CE when Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, while the east (the Byzantine Empire) survived until Constantinople fell in 1453. title: Major World Religions
in30Seconds: Historians study religions descriptively: they record when and where a tradition formed, what it teaches, its sacred texts, and how many people follow it, without judging whether any of its claims are true. By adherents, the five largest traditions are Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Judaism. Others, including Sikhism, Jainism, Chinese and Indigenous traditions, and the growing religiously unaffiliated, round out a diverse global picture that survey data help us measure.
whyItMatters: Nearly every field a college student enters, from history and literature to medicine, law, and international relations, involves people whose lives are shaped by religion. Being able to describe the major traditions accurately and even-handedly, without endorsing or dismissing any of them, is a basic literacy for reading the past and working across cultures. This overview also teaches a transferable habit of mind: separating what can be documented, such as when a tradition formed and how many follow it, from questions of belief that evidence cannot settle. That discipline protects you from both stereotype and false certainty.
learningObjectives: Explain how a historian describes a religion without making or evaluating a truth claim.
Identify the origins, core ideas, and principal sacred texts of Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Judaism.
Distinguish universalizing religions from ethnic religions and give examples of each.
Interpret dated, attributed adherent figures and explain why such counts are estimates.
Name major traditions beyond the largest five, including the religiously unaffiliated.

collegeVersion.heading: Studying religion as a historian
collegeVersion.body: A historian approaches religion the way any other human phenomenon is approached: as something people do, build, write down, and pass on. The historian's questions are descriptive and evidentiary. Where and when did a tradition take shape? Who, if anyone, is regarded as its founder, and in what period? What does it teach, and which texts does it hold sacred? How many people follow it today, and where do they live? Crucially, the historian does not ask whether a religion's claims about God, the cosmos, or salvation are true. Those are questions of faith and philosophy that documentary evidence cannot settle, and treating them as history would mean privileging one tradition over another. So a careful writer states what a tradition holds ('Muslims regard the Qur'an as the word of God revealed to Muhammad') rather than asserting the claim as fact. This even-handed stance is not indifference; it is precision. It lets us compare traditions fairly and describe each with the same seriousness and respect.

collegeVersion.heading: The five largest traditions
collegeVersion.body: By number of adherents, five traditions dominate the global picture. Hinduism has no single founder; it grew out of the Vedic religious traditions of the Indian subcontinent over the second and first millennia BCE, and its foundational texts include the Vedas and Upanishads. Its ideas commonly include dharma (moral and cosmic order), karma (action and consequence), and rebirth. Buddhism traces to Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha, traditionally placed in the sixth to fifth century BCE in South Asia, though some modern scholars date his life somewhat later; its teachings center on the causes of suffering and a path beyond it, and its scriptures include the Tripitaka (Pali Canon). Judaism formed among the ancient Israelites in the southern Levant during the first and second millennia BCE; it centers on a covenant with one God, and its scripture is the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), whose first section is the Torah. Christianity began in the first century CE in Roman Judea, rooted in the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians hold to be the Son of God; its scripture is the Bible, comprising the Old and New Testaments. Islam arose in the seventh century CE on the Arabian Peninsula, associated with the Prophet Muhammad; its scripture is the Qur'an, and the Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, is a foundational event. Christianity, Islam, and Judaism are often grouped as the Abrahamic traditions because each looks back to the figure of Abraham.

collegeVersion.heading: Beyond the five: other traditions and the unaffiliated
collegeVersion.body: The largest five do not exhaust the map. Sikhism originated in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late fifteenth to early sixteenth century CE, associated with Guru Nanak (1469-1539), and its scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib. Jainism is an ancient tradition of the Indian subcontinent emphasizing non-violence (ahimsa), associated in its classical form with Mahavira. In China, Daoist and Confucian traditions, together with widespread folk practice, have shaped religious life for more than two millennia. Across every continent, Indigenous and folk religions remain tied to particular peoples and places. Finally, a large and growing share of people are religiously unaffiliated, sometimes called 'nones.' This is not itself a religion but a category that includes atheists, agnostics, and people with no particular affiliation; some still hold spiritual beliefs. Pew Research Center estimated that in 2020 the unaffiliated made up about 24.2 percent of the world's population, the third-largest group after Christians and Muslims.

collegeVersion.heading: Universalizing versus ethnic religions
collegeVersion.body: Scholars of religion and geography often sort traditions into two broad kinds. A universalizing religion presents its message as meant for everyone and actively invites members from any background, often through missionary activity, trade, and conversion; Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism are the classic examples, and their followers are spread widely across the globe. An ethnic religion is bound up with a particular people, culture, or homeland and generally does not seek converts; membership usually comes through birth and community rather than recruitment. Judaism, Hinduism, and many folk and Indigenous religions fit this pattern, and their adherents tend to be concentrated in specific regions. The distinction is a useful generalization, not an iron law: traditions can carry features of both, and individual communities vary. Used carefully, though, it explains a great deal about why some traditions are dispersed worldwide while others remain rooted in one place.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading the numbers with care
collegeVersion.body: Adherent figures are estimates, not a census of belief, so they should always be dated and attributed. According to Pew Research Center estimates for 2020, published in June 2025, Christians numbered about 2.3 billion (28.8 percent of the world population), Muslims about 2.0 billion (25.6 percent), the religiously unaffiliated about 1.9 billion (24.2 percent), Hindus about 1.2 billion (14.9 percent), Buddhists about 324 million (4.1 percent), adherents of other religions about 377 million (2.2 percent), and Jews about 14.8 million (0.2 percent). The same study found that between 2010 and 2020 Muslims were the fastest-growing major group, increasing by about 347 million, while Buddhists were the only major group with fewer people at the end of the decade than at the start. Numbers like these come from combining censuses, surveys, and population registers, and different organizations define categories differently, so counts vary between sources. Citing the survey and the year is what keeps a factual statement honest.

vocabulary.definition: A person counted as belonging to or following a particular religion in a survey or estimate.
A religion that presents its message as intended for all people and actively welcomes converts from any background.
A religion tied to a specific people, culture, or place, typically joined by birth and community rather than by conversion.
Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, grouped together because each traces its heritage to the figure of Abraham and worships one God.
The belief in a single God, as in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
A writing a tradition regards as authoritative or holy, such as the Vedas, the Tanakh, the Bible, or the Qur'an.
People who report no particular religion, including atheists and agnostics; a demographic category rather than a single religion.
The study of the size, distribution, and change over time of religious populations.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine you are making a fair guidebook to the world's religions. Your job is not to say which one is right. Your job is to write down, for each tradition, where and when it started, what its followers believe, which book they treasure, and how many people follow it. Some religions, like Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, invite anyone to join. Others, like Judaism and Hinduism, are woven into a particular people and place, so you usually grow up in them. And a big group of people today follow no religion at all.
eli10.analogy: Think of the world's religions like the world's languages. A good language atlas tells you where each language is spoken, how it is written, and how many speakers it has, without declaring any language the 'best' one. A fair guide to religions does the same: it maps and describes, but it does not rank.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy has limits. Languages are mainly tools for communication, while religions make claims about meaning, right and wrong, and what happens after death, so people often hold them far more deeply than they hold a language. And unlike languages, some religions actively seek new followers while others do not, so the map of 'who joins how' works differently.

workedExample: Suppose a historian is handed a claim to evaluate: 'Islam is the world's oldest religion and its holiest.' Working descriptively, the historian separates the parts. 'Oldest' is a datable question: Islam arose in the seventh century CE, while Judaism and Hinduism took shape more than a thousand years earlier, so the age claim is simply false. 'Holiest' is a truth-and-value claim that no document can settle and that a historian will not rank, so it is set aside as outside the discipline. The historian then rewrites the sentence into something evidence supports: 'Islam, which began in the seventh century CE in Arabia, is today one of the two largest religions, with about 2.0 billion adherents in 2020 according to Pew Research Center.' Notice what changed: a dated origin replaced a false superlative, a value judgment was removed, and the population figure was attributed and dated.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a religion's teaching as a historical fact, for example writing 'God revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad' as a plain statement.
commonMistakes.correction: Attribute the belief to its holders: 'Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad.' Historians describe what traditions claim without asserting the claim.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the largest religion is also the oldest, or ranking traditions by importance.
commonMistakes.correction: Age, size, and significance are separate. Judaism and Hinduism are far older than the larger Christianity and Islam, and historians rank traditions only by measurable things like adherent counts, which must be attributed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Giving an adherent figure with no date or source, such as 'there are 2 billion Muslims.'
commonMistakes.correction: Cite the survey and year, for example 'about 2.0 billion Muslims in 2020 (Pew Research Center),' because counts are estimates that change and differ by source.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every large tradition a religion that seeks converts.
commonMistakes.correction: Distinguish universalizing religions, which invite converts, from ethnic religions like Judaism and Hinduism, which are generally joined by birth and community rather than recruitment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing the 'religiously unaffiliated' as if it were a single religion.
commonMistakes.correction: The unaffiliated are a demographic category that includes atheists, agnostics, and people with no particular affiliation, not one organized tradition.

compareContrast.distinction: A universalizing religion (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism) presents its message for everyone and seeks converts; an ethnic religion (Judaism, Hinduism, many folk traditions) is tied to a particular people or place and is usually joined by birth.
When and where a tradition formed can be documented and is the historian's domain; whether its teachings are true is a matter of faith that historians describe but do not adjudicate.

Both are Abrahamic and monotheistic, but Judaism formed among the ancient Israelites more than two millennia earlier and centers on the Tanakh, while Christianity began in first-century Roman Judea around the life of Jesus and adds the New Testament.

keyTakeaway: Historians describe religions rather than judge them: for each tradition they record its origins, core ideas, sacred texts, and dated, attributed adherent numbers, and they distinguish universalizing religions that seek converts from ethnic religions bound to a particular people or place.

questionBank.prompt: According to Pew Research Center estimates for 2020, which religion had the largest number of adherents worldwide?
options: Islam
Christianity
Hinduism
Buddhism
questionBank.explanation: Pew estimated about 2.3 billion Christians (28.8%) in 2020, more than any other group; Muslims were second at about 2.0 billion (25.6%), Hindus about 1.2 billion, and Buddhists about 324 million.
questionBank.skill: Recalling attributed religious-demography figures

questionBank.prompt: In Pew Research Center's 2020 estimates, the religiously unaffiliated made up about 24.2 percent of the world's population. Where did that place them among global groups?
options: The largest group overall
The smallest group measured
Tied with Hindus
The third-largest group, after Christians and Muslims
questionBank.explanation: At about 1.9 billion people (24.2%), the unaffiliated were the third-largest group after Christians (28.8%) and Muslims (25.6%). They were not the largest or smallest, and they far outnumbered Hindus (14.9%).
questionBank.skill: Interpreting attributed demographic rankings

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures the distinction between a universalizing religion and an ethnic religion?
options: A universalizing religion seeks converts across cultures, while an ethnic religion is tied to a particular people or place
An ethnic religion seeks converts across cultures, while a universalizing religion is tied to one people
A universalizing religion is always older than an ethnic religion
An ethnic religion is always monotheistic, while a universalizing religion is not
questionBank.explanation: Universalizing religions (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism) present their message for everyone and welcome converts; ethnic religions (Judaism, Hinduism, many folk traditions) are bound to a particular people or place. The distinction is about outreach and membership, not age or monotheism.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing two categories of religion

questionBank.prompt: A historian maps a tradition whose adherents are concentrated almost entirely within one people and homeland and that generally does not seek converts, joined instead through birth and community. Judaism is a classic example. Which category does this describe?
options: A universalizing religion
An Abrahamic religion by definition
An ethnic religion
A religion that must be monotheistic

title: Medieval Societies
in30Seconds: The Middle Ages, or medieval period, runs roughly 500-1500 CE. That label is European: it names a stretch of European history, and the old 'Dark Ages' idea of total decline is now rejected, since the Islamic world, Tang and Song China, and the Byzantine Empire were flourishing at the same time. In western Europe, loose feudal arrangements bound lords and vassals, serfs worked the manors, and the Christian Church was the central institution — through wars like the Crusades, the Black Death, and the slow rise of towns and universities.
whyItMatters: Medieval Europe is the bridge between the ancient world and the modern one, so history, literature, art, and political-thought courses keep returning to it. Studying it well trains a specific skill: refusing lazy shorthand. 'The Dark Ages' is exactly the kind of myth historians teach you to dismantle — the period had real institutions, learning, and long-distance trade, and calling it 'dark' mostly reveals that the label was coined by later Europeans looking down on their own past. Getting medieval societies right also means keeping the whole globe in view, because while parts of Europe rebuilt, the Islamic caliphates and East Asian empires were among the most advanced societies on earth.
learningObjectives: Explain why 'medieval' and 'Middle Ages' are European periodization labels and why historians reject the 'Dark Ages' framing.
Define feudalism and manorialism and describe the roles of lords, vassals, and serfs as a loose set of arrangements rather than a rigid system.
Describe the central role of the Christian Church and the place of the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire in the medieval world.
Place the Crusades and the Black Death in time with verified dates and state basic facts about each.
Explain the gradual growth of towns, trade, and universities toward the period's end, and situate Europe within a flourishing wider world.

collegeVersion.heading: What 'medieval' means — and the 'Dark Ages' myth
collegeVersion.body: The medieval period, or Middle Ages, is conventionally dated from roughly 500 to 1500 CE — from about the fall of the western Roman Empire (traditionally placed in 476) to about 1500, when the Renaissance, printing, and European ocean voyages mark a shift. Those endpoints are conventions, not sharp lines, and different textbooks nudge them a few decades either way. The word itself is a clue to a trap. 'Medieval' comes from Latin for 'the middle age,' and 'Middle Ages' was coined by later European scholars who saw themselves as reviving classical antiquity across a dull gap in between. In other words, the label describes European history from a particular later viewpoint; it is not a neutral name for what the whole world was doing between 500 and 1500. The harsher version of that viewpoint — the 'Dark Ages,' a period of decline and ignorance — is now rejected by historians. The early Middle Ages did see the western Roman state fragment and cities shrink, but it also built lasting institutions, preserved and copied classical texts, and stayed connected to a wider world. Al-Andalus in Muslim Spain was a multireligious, multiethnic society tied into Mediterranean trade and diplomacy, which OpenStax calls 'a testament to the global context of the early Middle Ages.' Beyond Europe, the Islamic caliphates, Tang and Song China, and the Byzantine Empire were among the most advanced societies on earth. So the age was not globally 'dark' — the phrase mostly reveals the prejudices of the people who invented it.

collegeVersion.heading: Feudalism and the manor: a loose set of arrangements
collegeVersion.body: After centralized Roman authority receded in the West, power in much of western Europe rested on personal bonds and on land. Historians describe this with two linked terms. Feudalism was a collection of practices that bound lesser lords to greater lords through land and privileges given in return for personal and military support. A greater lord granted a fighter — a vassal — a piece of land called a fief, whose produce the vassal could enjoy; in return the vassal swore loyalty and owed military service and counsel. It is important not to picture this as a tidy, uniform legal pyramid. It was a flexible, unequal, and locally variable set of arrangements that looked different from region to region and changed over time; the neat diagrams in old textbooks impose more order than really existed. Underneath the warrior class sat the economy that fed everyone: manorialism. Under the manor system — named for the manor house where the lord lived — agricultural production was directed by a lord and carried out mostly by serfs, unfree peasants who owed labor to the lord, lived under his authority, and were tied to the land they worked. Serfs were gathered into manor villages where labor and tools could be shared. Not everyone was unfree — some peasants owned land and worked for themselves — but in western Europe most rural laborers were servile. Feudal and manorial relationships together organized medieval European society from the top warrior down to the village field.

collegeVersion.heading: The Church, the papacy, and the Byzantine East
collegeVersion.body: The Christian Church was the central institution of medieval western Europe. It converted the Germanic peoples who had settled the former Roman provinces, preserved and copied classical and religious texts in its monasteries, educated clergy and administrators, and lent legitimacy to rulers — most famously when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, emperor in 800, reviving the idea of a Roman emperor in the West. The Church was governed through the papacy, centered on Rome. But Christianity was not united. In the Great Schism of 1054, after the pope's envoy and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, the eastern and western churches formally separated into what became the Eastern Orthodox Church and the Roman Catholic Church. That eastern church belonged to a different medieval power: the Byzantine Empire, the continuation of the eastern Roman state. Greek-speaking and Christian, centered on Constantinople, it existed from 330 to 1453 and was the longest-lasting medieval power. Under the emperor Justinian (reigned 527-565) it reached a cultural height, codifying Roman law in the Code of Justinian and building the great domed church of Hagia Sophia. The empire finally ended on 29 May 1453, when the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople. Remembering Byzantium is a good corrective on its own: for most of the 'Middle Ages,' a wealthy Roman-descended empire flourished in the East while western Europe was rebuilding.

collegeVersion.heading: The Crusades and the Black Death
collegeVersion.body: Two events from the later medieval centuries are named again and again, and both deserve to be stated factually rather than mythologized. The Crusades were religiously motivated military campaigns that began when Pope Urban II, responding to a Byzantine request for aid, called at the Council of Clermont in France in 1095 for a war to help eastern Christians and 'liberate Jerusalem.' The First Crusade reached and captured Jerusalem in the summer of 1099. Further crusades followed over roughly two centuries, aimed mainly at the eastern Mediterranean, until the fall of the port city of Acre in 1291 ended the last of the Crusader States. The Black Death was a plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Spreading from central Asia along Silk Road caravans and Black Sea shipping, it reached the ports of Europe in 1346-1347 — arriving at Messina and Genoa in the summer of 1347 — and swept the continent in the years around 1347-1351. It killed roughly 30 percent of Europe's population, perhaps as many as twenty-four million people. In its terror, Jewish communities were falsely blamed for spreading the plague by poisoning wells and suffered widespread persecution that escalated in several cities into massacres, even though Jewish people were dying of the disease alongside everyone else. That scapegoating is a documented atrocity, not a matter of dispute.

collegeVersion.heading: Towns, trade, universities — and the wider world
collegeVersion.body: The later medieval centuries were not static. Towns grew, long-distance commerce revived — the Crusades and renewed Mediterranean trade helped stimulate it — and a new institution appeared: the university. The first European universities emerged in the 11th and 12th centuries, with Bologna founded about 1088, followed by Paris and Oxford, offering advanced study in law, theology, medicine, and the liberal arts. Here even-handedness matters. The world's oldest continuously operating university is not European at all: it is Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, founded in the 9th century and recognized as such by UNESCO and Guinness World Records — older than Bologna by more than two centuries. Some historians reserve the word 'university' for the specifically European institution and call Al-Qarawiyyin a madrasa; the honest move is to note the debate rather than to pretend higher learning began in Europe. That is the throughline of the whole topic. The Middle Ages were a real, developing period in European history, not a blank 'dark' interval — and Europe was one region among several thriving centers of a connected world, not its lone flame in the dark.

vocabulary.definition: The era of European history conventionally dated from roughly 500 to 1500 CE; the name was coined by later scholars who saw it as a 'middle' age between classical antiquity and their own time.

An outdated, pejorative label for the early Middle Ages that portrayed it as a time of total decline; now rejected by historians because the period had real institutions and learning and the wider world was flourishing.

A collection of practices that bound lesser lords to greater lords through land (fiefs) and privileges given in return for personal and military support — a flexible, locally variable set of arrangements, not a single rigid system.
A fighter who received a fief from a lord and in return swore loyalty and owed military service and counsel.
A grant of land (and its income) given by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service.
The medieval economic system in which agricultural production on an estate was directed by a lord and carried out mainly by serfs and other unfree laborers gathered into manor villages.
An unfree peasant who owed labor to a lord, lived under the lord's authority, and was tied to the land — not enslaved property, but not free to leave.
The continuation of the eastern Roman Empire, Greek-speaking and Christian, centered on Constantinople; it existed from 330 to 1453.
The formal split of Christianity into the western (Roman Catholic) and eastern (Eastern Orthodox) churches after mutual excommunications between the pope's envoy and the patriarch of Constantinople.
Religiously motivated military campaigns, beginning with the call at the Council of Clermont in 1095, aimed mainly at the eastern Mediterranean and the Holy Land.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: 'The Middle Ages' is a nickname later Europeans gave to about a thousand years of their own history, from around 500 to 1500. Some people used to call it the 'Dark Ages,' as if nothing good happened, but that is wrong: people built things, wrote books, traded, and started universities, and huge parts of the world — the Muslim empires, China, and the Byzantine Empire in the east — were doing brilliantly the whole time. In western Europe, powerful lords gave land to fighters who promised to serve them, and farmers called serfs worked that land without being allowed to leave. The Christian Church was the biggest and most important organization around. Two events get mentioned a lot: the Crusades, which were religious wars over the Holy Land, and the Black Death, a plague in the 1340s that killed about a third of Europe.
eli10.analogy: Think of medieval Europe like a school with no single principal after the old head teacher leaves. Instead, senior students (lords) each protect a group of younger ones (vassals) in exchange for help, and everyone answers to one big club — the Church — that everybody belongs to.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy is loose. A school is one building with shared rules, but medieval Europe had no single government at all, and the deals between lords and vassals varied wildly from place to place. And a friendly student hierarchy leaves out the harshest part: serfs were not free to walk away from the land, which no ordinary school membership resembles.

workedExample: Suppose you are handed four facts about medieval Europe and asked to put them in order and label each: (1) Charlemagne is crowned emperor; (2) the eastern and western churches split; (3) the First Crusade takes Jerusalem; (4) the Black Death sweeps Europe. Verify the dates one at a time. Charlemagne's coronation was in 800; the Great Schism was in 1054; the capture of Jerusalem was in 1099; and the Black Death's main sweep was around 1347-1351. So the sequence is 800, 1054, 1099, then 1347-1351 — Charlemagne, schism, crusade, plague. Notice that all four fall well inside the roughly 500-1500 span, and that they are spread across the whole period rather than bunched at the start, which is itself evidence against a 'nothing happened' picture of the age.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the whole period the 'Dark Ages' and assuming nothing important happened.
commonMistakes.correction: Historians reject that label. The Middle Ages had lasting institutions, learning, and trade, and the wider world — the Islamic caliphates, China, and the Byzantine Empire — was flourishing, so the era was not globally 'dark.'

commonMistakes.mistake: Picturing feudalism as one rigid, uniform legal pyramid that worked the same everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: Feudalism was a loose, locally variable set of personal arrangements binding lords and vassals through land and service. It differed by region and changed over time; the neat charts overstate its order.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing serfs with enslaved people, or thinking they could freely leave.
commonMistakes.correction: Serfs were unfree peasants tied to the land who owed labor to a lord and lived under his authority, but they were not owned as property and could not simply be sold apart from the land. They were also not free to leave at will.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the Roman Empire vanished entirely in 476 and that Europe was the medieval world's only center.
commonMistakes.correction: The eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued until 1453, and the oldest continuously operating university is Al-Qarawiyyin in Morocco (9th century), older than Europe's. Europe was one region among several thriving centers.

compareContrast.distinction: Feudalism describes the political-military bonds among lords and vassals (land and service for loyalty); manorialism describes the economic system of the estate, where serfs worked the lord's land. One organizes the warriors, the other the fields.

After the Great Schism of 1054 the western church (Latin, led by the pope in Rome) and the eastern church (Greek, led by the patriarch of Constantinople and tied to the Byzantine Empire) were formally separate branches of Christianity.

The Crusades were deliberate religious military campaigns (1095-1291) aimed at the Holy Land; the Black Death (c. 1347-1351) was an unplanned plague pandemic that killed about a third of Europe. One was a human undertaking, the other a biological catastrophe.

keyTakeaway: The Middle Ages (c. 500-1500) is a European label, not a global 'Dark Age': western Europe was organized by loose feudal and manorial arrangements under a powerful Christian Church, while the Byzantine Empire and the Islamic and East Asian worlds flourished at the same time — an era of real development, named factually through Charlemagne, the Great Schism, the Crusades, and the Black Death.

options: A centralized empire in which a single emperor directly governed all of Europe
An economic theory holding that land should be owned in common by peasant villages
A loose, locally variable set of arrangements binding lesser lords to greater lords through land (fiefs) and privileges in return for military and personal service
A body of Church law issued by the pope to govern monasteries

Option A is wrong because medieval Europe had no single emperor governing it all. Option B misdescribes it as communal ownership. Option D confuses it with canon law.

About 5 percent
About 90 percent
About 30 percent

questionBank.prompt: A serf lives in a manor village and wants to move to a nearby town to look for other work. Under the manorial system as it typically operated in western Europe, what was his situation?
options: As an unfree peasant tied to the land, he owed labor to the lord and was not free to leave at will
As a free wage laborer, he could relocate whenever he wished with no obligations
As the lord's legal property, he could be sold individually to a buyer in the town
As a vassal, he owed the lord military service but was otherwise free to travel
questionBank.explanation: Serfs were unfree peasants who owed labor to the lord, lived under his authority, and were tied to the land, so they could not simply leave. Option B describes a free laborer, which most western European peasants were not. Option C wrongly equates serfdom with chattel slavery — serfs were bound to the land, not sold as individual property. Option D confuses a serf with a vassal (a fighting man who held a fief).

questionBank.prompt: Which statement about the Byzantine Empire is accurate?
options: It was a short-lived Germanic kingdom that collapsed shortly after 476 CE
It was the Greek-speaking, Christian continuation of the eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, that lasted until 1453
It was the western European empire founded by Charlemagne in 800
It was a Muslim caliphate that ruled Spain during the early Middle Ages
questionBank.explanation: The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the eastern Roman state — Greek-speaking, Christian, centered on Constantinople — and existed from 330 until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453. Option A is wrong because Byzantium long outlasted the western empire's fall. Option C describes Charlemagne's Frankish realm. Option D describes al-Andalus, a different society.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the Byzantine Empire

questionBank.prompt: Historians reject the label 'Dark Ages' for the early Middle Ages. Which piece of evidence best supports that rejection?
options: Written records from the period were completely destroyed, so nothing can be known about it
The western Roman Empire's institutions continued unchanged, so there was no disruption at all
Europe was cut off from every other region, proving it developed entirely on its own
While parts of Europe rebuilt, the Islamic caliphates, China, and the Byzantine Empire were flourishing, and Europe kept trade and learning alive — so the era was neither empty nor globally 'dark'
questionBank.explanation: The 'Dark Ages' label fails because the wider world was thriving and Europe itself preserved learning and stayed connected through trade — the era was one of development, not a blank. Option A is false (the period is well documented). Option B overstates continuity — Roman institutions did fragment in the West. Option C is the opposite of the truth: Europe was connected to a wider world, as al-Andalus's Mediterranean ties show.
